kyr_shinodaya.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation. The signature chuka-soba is wheat ramen noodles in a soy-based (wheat shoyu) broth, and the famous sara-mori features a breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet plus a curry-udon-style ankake sauce — all wheat-heavy. This is a traditional 1904 family diner with no allergen program; not celiac-safe.
kyr_shinodaya.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly option. The chuka-soba broth is chicken-based, the tare is soy/wheat shoyu, and the menu centers on pork cutlet, beef-and-onion curry sauce, and other meat/fish dishes. No vegan menu or substitutions noted.
kyr_shinodaya.hours_raw: Tabelog: Mon–Fri & Sun 11:30–15:00; Saturday closed. (A secondary source lists 11:00–15:00 / 16:30–19:00 with Friday closing at 15:00; hours may vary — confirm locally.)

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1904 (Meiji 37) and now run by the fourth generation, Shinodaya is a beloved retro shokudo just east of the Sanjo Ohashi bridge, steps from Sanjo Keihan Station. The shop name comes from Shinoda Village in Aichi, the founder's home. The current owner Kutsumi Shuichi works the kitchen and counter alongside his wife Midori and his mother Tsugiko — three generations keeping a sturdy old wooden building (its thick central pillar reputedly kept every dish in place during the 1995 Hanshin earthquake) and its recipes essentially unchanged for over a century.
chef_bio.philosophy: Continuity and care: traditional cooking methods (rice cooked in a clay okudosan oven), unchanged recipes, and a warm family-run welcome where Kyoto families have built memories across generations.
chef_bio.specialty: Two signature bowls define the place. The chuka-soba is a clear, gentle chicken-and-soy broth with thin, custom-made straight noodles — a plain, nostalgic ramen that regulars come back for again and again. The other icon is the sara-mori: a heaping plate of rice with a lard-fried pork cutlet, blanketed in a piping-hot, curry-udon-style ankake sauce with green onion and beef. It looks like katsu curry but tastes nothing like roux curry.

anecdotes.text: The famous sara-mori began as an off-menu request from Keihan Railway workers about 30 years ago — rice topped with a cutlet and curry-udon sauce. Customers asked for it on a plate so it would cool faster, and it joined the official menu roughly 25 years ago.
The shop's solid traditional construction, anchored by a heavy central pillar (daigokubashira), is said to have come through the 1995 Hanshin-Awaji earthquake without a single dish falling.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hot Pepper Mesitsu confirms 篠田屋 was founded in 1904 (Meiji 37), is 4th-generation, run by Kutsumi Shuichi with wife Midori and mother Tsugiko; the name derives from Shinoda Village, Aichi; it sits seconds from Keihan Sanjo Station by the Kamogawa; sara-mori arose ~30 years ago from Keihan railway workers and joined the menu ~25 years ago; the heavy central beam kept every bowl in place in the 1995 Hanshin-Awaji quake; rice is cooked on an okudosan clay oven.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The chuka-soba broth is a soy-based (shoyu) chicken stock; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills, century-old neighborhood lunch counter run by an older family; little to no English, so it is most comfortable with a guide or some Japanese and a relaxed, respectful manner.

kyr_yamanoya.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. The chuka-soba is built on wheat noodles in a soy-tare/pork-style broth, and the kitchen also turns out udon, katsu curry and other wheat-and-fry dishes. There is no celiac-safe offering and no indication the kitchen accommodates gluten avoidance. Not suitable for anyone who needs to avoid wheat or gluten.
kyr_yamanoya.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly place. The signature chuka-soba comes with char siu (pork) and kamaboko (fish cake) over an animal-based broth, and the wider menu is meat-, fish- and egg-centric (katsu curry, nabeyaki udon, rice bowls). No dedicated vegan or vegetable-only ramen is offered.
kyr_yamanoya.hours_raw: Mon-Fri 11:00-22:00; Sat 11:00-16:30; Sun & public holidays closed. (Hours and closed days may change; check before visiting.)
kyr_yamanoya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Yamanoya is an old-school neighborhood eatery (machi-chuka shokudo) that has been feeding the Shijo-Kawaramachi crowd for well over half a century, tucked onto the Ayakoji-Miyukicho corner right behind the Fujii Daimaru department store. Despite sitting in one of Kyoto's busiest

chef_bio.background: Yamanoya is an old-school neighborhood eatery (machi-chuka shokudo) that has been feeding the Shijo-Kawaramachi crowd for around seventy years, tucked onto the Ayakoji-Miyukicho corner right behind the Fujii Daimaru department store. Despite sitting in one of Kyoto's busiest shopping districts, it has kept the unpretentious feel of a working-people's lunch counter rather than a specialist ramen bar.
chef_bio.philosophy: Tasty, genuinely cheap, everyday food you could happily eat any day — the comfort of a real local diner over any specialist gimmick.
chef_bio.specialty: Chuka-soba: a gentle, everyday bowl of springy, chewy wheat noodles in a mild broth topped with bean sprouts, green onion, char siu and kamaboko (fish cake) — a homey, cafeteria-style take rather than a fashionable ramen.

anecdotes.text: Regulars and writers single out the Showa-retro atmosphere: it feels like a nostalgic neighborhood gohan-ya, and the chuka-soba's char siu and fish-cake toppings mark it as a homey diner dish rather than a serious ramen-ya creation. The broth is praised as so gentle you could eat it every day.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi (KLAw8) describes 山の家 as an over-70-year-old machi-chuka behind Fujii Daimaru at the Ayakoji/Miyukicho corner, with a Showa-era casual feel; its chuka-soba has chewy, flavorful noodles topped with bean sprouts, negi, char siu and kamaboko, and a gentle broth 'you could eat every day.'

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The chuka-soba uses wheat noodles in a soy-style broth; standard Japanese soy sauce and tare contain wheat. No wheat-free preparation is offered.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: SOY-SAUCE WARNING INVENTED FROM GENRE — 'chuka-soba, therefore soy-style broth'. Nothing on the cited page or anywhere found says shoyu, and 'clear and 淡麗' is equally consistent with a shio tare. Also guard against the sibling-transplant risk: KLAw8 profiles EIGHT shops (山の家, 萬福, かどや食堂, 篠田屋, まるせ, みや

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills neighborhood shokudo with a Showa-retro feel and little English; basic Japanese or pointing at the menu will carry you through comfortably.

kyr_shisentei.gf_detail: Not safe for celiac. The core dishes are tantanmen and shiru-nashi tantanmen built on straight wheat noodles (sourced from a noodle factory), a sesame-paste tare, and Sichuan seasonings that typically include wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free noodle, menu, or preparation is offered, and the tiny 10-seat counter kitchen has no separate gluten-free workflow.
kyr_shisentei.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly option. Every dish centers on sweet ground pork: the tantanmen, shiru-nashi tantanmen, mapo tofu/mapo rice, and Chinese-style broth all use meat. There is no plant-based bowl on the menu.
kyr_shisentei.notes: [Mom & Pop] A specialist tantanmen counter shop near Mototanaka Station in Kyoto's Sakyo ward, relocated to its current Tanaka Satononaicho address in January 2024. It keeps a deliberately tight focus: just ten counter seats and a short menu built around Sichuan-style dan dan noodles.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Sakyo-ku (Mototanaka), specializing in Sichuan-influenced tantanmen.
chef_bio.background: A specialist tantanmen counter shop near Mototanaka Station in Kyoto's Sakyo ward, relocated to its current Tanaka Satononaicho address in January 2024. It keeps a deliberately tight focus: just ten counter seats and a short menu built around Sichuan-style dan dan noodles.
chef_bio.philosophy: A single-minded focus on tantanmen done well: rich sesame depth balanced against stimulating Sichuan spice, served from a small counter where each bowl gets full attention.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the shiru-nashi tantanmen (soupless dan dan noodles): straight wheat noodles topped with a mountain of green onions, a sweet ground-pork mince, sesame, and Sichuan peppercorns, with adjustable heat across five levels. The brothy tantanmen (rich sesame Chinese-style broth) and a mini mapo-rice set are equally popular.

anecdotes.text: The shop is repeatedly singled out as one of Kyoto's best tantanmen specialists, with the soupless version cited as the dish that turns first-timers into regulars.
A professional chef who runs a Korean restaurant is quoted calling Shisentei 'Kyoto's best (京都一) dan dan noodles.'
Reviewers note the heat is adjustable across five levels; the brothy tantanmen is approachable while the soupless tantanmen is noticeably spicier and considered the more flavor-concentrated choice.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: anna-media confirms 四川亭 is a 10-seat counter shop at Tanaka Satononaicho, Sakyo-ku, with a soupless tantanmen (green onion + Sichuan pepper, 'addictive'), a brothy sesame tantanmen offered as a mini-mapo-rice set, 5 adjustable heat levels, and a Korean owner-chef's endorsement calling it '京都一.'

gf_cross_contamination.text: All bowls use straight wheat noodles sourced from a noodle factory; there is no gluten-free noodle and the entire menu is wheat-based.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dishes are Sichuan-style tantanmen and mapo, which conventionally use wheat-based soy sauce in the tare and sauces; no wheat-free soy sauce is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every dish uses sweet ground pork and Chinese-style meat broth, including the tantanmen, soupless tantanmen, and mapo tofu/rice; no plant-based option exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 10-seat, cash-only neighborhood counter shop with a short Japanese menu and no reservations: comfortable if you can order simply in Japanese and follow counter etiquette.

kyr_ramen_daiei_honten.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. This is a traditional Kyoto ramen shop: wheat noodles (sourced from a local noodle maker), a soy-sauce or miso tare almost certainly made with wheat-based shoyu/miso, and a pork-based broth. No dedicated fryer, no allergen menu, and no indication of celiac awareness. Not safe for celiac diners; cross-contamination from shared noodle water and a single small counter kitchen is essentially certain.
kyr_ramen_daiei_honten.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The broth is pork-based (豚骨/豚清湯) and bowls are built around generous chashu pork; free toppings are chives and grated garlic. There is no vegetable or vegan broth option. Vegans and vegetarians have no viable bowl here.
kyr_ramen_daiei_honten.hours_raw: Mon–Sat 11:00–14:30, 18:30–21:30 / closed Sun (some sources note that Saturday dinner service is shortened)
kyr_ramen_daiei_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] A neighborhood ramen institution in the Kujo area just south of Kyoto Station, in business for more than 40 years (locally cited as founded in 1981). It is the original 'honten' of the Daiei name and remains a small, independently run counter shop that draws lines even on weekday

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood ramen institution in the Kujo area just south of Kyoto Station, in business for more than 40 years (founded in the early 1980s). It is the original 'honten' of the Daiei name and remains a small, independently run counter shop that draws lines even on weekday afternoons.
chef_bio.philosophy: A minimalist, value-driven menu (essentially shoyu and miso) executed consistently for decades, prized for volume, balance, and a clean pork broth rather than novelty.
chef_bio.specialty: Generously loaded bowls built on a pork-based broth: the shoyu ramen and the miso ramen are the signatures. Both come piled with thinly sliced chashu (often more than ten slices, even on a regular bowl), local Kujo green onions, and bean sprouts, over medium-thick springy noodles from nearby Kondo Seimen. Free chives and grated garlic at the counter let regulars tune the flavor.

anecdotes.text: Regulars describe the bowls as overflowing with thin-sliced chashu and topped with Kujo negi, with free chives and grated garlic at the counter to change up the flavor mid-meal.
The miso ramen is noted for a subtle acidity and a clean, refreshing finish over a pork broth ('ほんのり酸味を感じ、スッキリとした美味しさ').

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi (bAeHF) describes ラーメン大栄本店 in Kujo/Minami-ku as a 40-plus-year honten with a compact ~10-seat counter, shoyu and miso ramen piled with 10+ chashu slices, Kujo negi and bean sprouts, noodles from nearby 近藤製麺 (Kondo Seimen), free chives and grated garlic, and a miso ramen with 'ほんのり酸味' and a clean finish.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water in a single small counter kitchen; gluten cross-contamination is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Shoyu and miso ramen are the house specialties; the soy-sauce/miso tare is almost certainly wheat-based, as is standard for this style. No wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-based and bowls are built around chashu pork; no vegan or vegetarian broth is offered, so all items share animal-based stock.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, busy, cash-only neighborhood counter shop with a Japanese-only menu and no English service expected; comfortable for visitors who can order simply in Japanese or point at the menu.

kyr_chuugokusai_taihou.gf_detail: No gluten-free provision. The tantanmen and ramen use wheat noodles (the dry tantanmen uses thin Kagawa-style wheat udon noodles), and the kitchen is a Sichuan/Chinese operation built on soy-sauce-based sauces, fried dishes, and wheat-containing seasonings. No dedicated gluten-free menu, no allergen handling claims found in any source. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_chuugokusai_taihou.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian operation. The menu centers on meat and animal-based dishes: glazed-pork teridon, beef mapo tofu, Shanghai sweet-and-sour pork, drunken chicken, and meat/pork-and-chili tantanmen. No vegan ramen or dedicated plant-based options were found in any source.
kyr_chuugokusai_taihou.hours_raw: 11:30–14:15 / 17:30–21:00 (L.O. 20:30). Closed Tuesdays, with occasional additional Wednesday closures some months.
kyr_chuugokusai_taihou.notes: [Mom & Pop] Founded in 1974 near Nijo Station, the shop reached its 50-year milestone in 2024. It is run by a parent-and-child team: the first generation built its reputation as a beloved casual neighborhood Chinese restaurant (machichuka), and the second generation studied Sichuan cooking,

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1974 near Nijo Station, the shop reached its 50-year milestone in 2024. It is run by a parent-and-child team: the first generation built its reputation as a beloved casual neighborhood Chinese restaurant (machichuka), and the second generation studied Sichuan cooking, layering authentic Sichuan flavors over the original homey menu.
chef_bio.philosophy: A flavor for everyone, from children to seniors: sweet-and-savory comfort cooking that keeps the room full at both lunch and dinner, with the second generation's Sichuan training giving the menu real depth and heat alongside the nostalgic favorites.
chef_bio.specialty: The house signature is the teridon (照り丼) family of glazed-pork rice bowls, especially the teridon kinshi topped with silky egg ribbons and richly glazed pork in a sweet-savory sauce. On the noodle side, the kitchen offers both a brothed tantanmen and a sesame-free dry tantanmen (汁なし担々麺) built on thin Kagawa wheat noodles dressed with Sichuan chili and Sichuan pepper aromatics; the beef mapo tofu is another standout.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant has earned the Michelin Bib Gourmand, recognition for great food at a friendly price.
Locals consider it an indispensable name in Kyoto Chinese cooking; lines regularly form for both the midday and evening services.
The dry tantanmen is made without sesame and uses thin Kagawa-prefecture wheat noodles topped with Sichuan chili and Sichuan pepper.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: v-trip confirms 中國菜 大鵬 was founded in 1974 (50th anniversary in 2024) near Nijo Station, holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand, is loved across all ages, and is famous for its teridon glazed-pork bowls (six variations including teridon-kinshi with egg strips). gcjapan documents the sesame-free 汁なし担々麺 on thin Kagawa noodles with Sichuan chili and pepper.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Noodles are wheat-based (the dry tantanmen uses thin Kagawa wheat noodles), and the kitchen runs Sichuan/Chinese dishes with soy-based sauces and fried items, so heavy gluten cross-contact is inherent.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is meat-forward (glazed pork, beef mapo tofu, chicken, pork tantanmen); no vegan dishes or separated plant-based prep were documented.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: 「てりどんきんし地獄盛り … 錦糸玉子の上に旨タレが絡む豚肉がたっぷりと。」「牛肉麻婆豆腐 1,760円 … ぷりっと豆腐と牛肉」「軍鶏のよだれ鶏 ハーフ 1,100円」. The 汁なし担々麵 entry describes only 「香川県産の細いうどんに四川の唐辛子と山椒の香りが絡みあう」 — no pork is named.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, locals-packed neighborhood Chinese spot with no indication of English service; basic Japanese or a translation tool will make ordering smoother.

kyr_nishiazabu_curry_tsukeme.gf_detail: Not safe for celiac/gluten-free. Every signature dish is wheat-noodle based — the noodles are custom wheat noodles from Asakusa Kaikaro — and the curry broths and tare standardly contain wheat. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no published allergen handling. Avoid if you require strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_nishiazabu_curry_tsukeme.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian option. The curry broths are built on beef cheek and a seafood/fish dashi base, and the dishes center on meat-and-fish curry. No vegan or vegetarian bowls are advertised, and the kitchen is animal-broth based.
kyr_nishiazabu_curry_tsukeme.hours_raw: Tabelog: 11:30–16:00, 18:00–21:00. Closed days: irregular. Blog sources note earlier hour formats (e.g. 11:30–15:00, 17:00–23:00 with Monday closures); hours have varied over time, so confirm before visiting.
kyr_nishiazabu_curry_tsukeme.notes: [Mom & Pop] A curry-noodle specialist that carries the Nishi-Azabu name in its full title — 西麻布カレーつけ麺 なんだっ亭. The owner trained at a Tokyo Nishi-Azabu curry-ramen specialist before opening here, and is described as a former French chef who crossed over into noodles, which shows in the layered

chef_bio.background: A curry-noodle specialist that carries the Nishi-Azabu name in its full title — 西麻布カレーつけ麺 なんだっ亭. The owner is a former French chef who crossed over into ramen, training at a Tokyo Nishi-Azabu curry-ramen specialist (しゅういち) before opening here — a background that shows in the layered, refined curry broths. The shop sits down a quiet Shinkyogoku-area side street near Kyoto-Kawaramachi, an unassuming little counter that has built a loyal regular following.
chef_bio.philosophy: A small, focused counter built around one idea executed carefully — curry-and-noodles done with a chef's attention to broth-building rather than a big menu.
chef_bio.specialty: Curry tsukemen — the signature bowl. The dipping broth is a curry built on slow-cooked beef cheek and a seafood/fish dashi base, balancing gentle sweetness against spice, with a milky, almost coconut-like roundness. It is paired with custom medium-thick, chewy wheat noodles ordered from the long-established Asakusa Kaikaro (開花楼). Curry ramen (カレーらぁ麺) and curry abura-soba round out the lineup; a finishing scoop of rice into the leftover broth is a beloved ritual that shows off the soup's depth.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a former French chef who retrained in ramen at a Nishi-Azabu (Tokyo) curry-ramen specialist (しゅういち) before opening in Kyoto.
Diners are encouraged to drop a small bowl of rice into the leftover curry dipping broth at the end — locals say that finish is where the quality of the soup really shows.
The noodles are custom-made by Asakusa Kaikaro (開花楼), a renowned long-established noodle maker, giving them a notably chewy, substantial texture.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kareota confirms なんだっ亭's owner is a former French chef who transitioned to ramen after training at Nishi-Azabu curry-ramen shop しゅういち; the curry broth uses 牛ほほ肉・魚介 (beef cheek + seafood) with coconut-milk smoothness; noodles are Asakusa 開花楼's medium-thick curly type; menu spans curry tsukemen, curry ramen and curry abura-soba, finished by adding rice to the leftover broth.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All signature dishes use custom wheat noodles from Asakusa Kaikaro; there is no gluten-free noodle option and no separate preparation, so cross-contamination with wheat is unavoidable.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Curry broths are made from beef cheek and a seafood/fish dashi base, so all bowls share an animal-and-fish broth; no vegan/vegetarian preparation exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 13-seat counter shop tucked in a Shinkyogoku side street; comfortable for an independent traveler but expect Japanese-language ordering and a no-frills local pace.

kyr_ichiwan_seiemon.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. This is wheat-noodle ramen, and the signature bowl is dressed with a blend of two soy sauces (from a local Gosho-nishi maker) — Japanese soy sauce normally contains wheat. The kitchen is a single small counter operation with no documented gluten-free accommodation or dedicated prep, so cross-contact with wheat is unavoidable.
kyr_ichiwan_seiemon.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian options found. The signature bowls are built on a dashi-forward broth with chashu made from Iga mochi pork; the miso bowl uses rendered beef fat. Animal protein is central to every bowl on the menu.
kyr_ichiwan_seiemon.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner trained as a kappo chef in Japanese haute cuisine before his love of ramen grew strong enough that he opened this small counter shop near Imadegawa to pursue it full-time.

chef_bio.background: The owner trained as a kappo chef in Japanese haute cuisine before his love of ramen grew strong enough that he opened this small counter shop near Imadegawa to pursue it full-time.
chef_bio.philosophy: To let the umami of carefully chosen ingredients carry the bowl rather than leaning on heavy seasoning — ramen approached with the restraint and ingredient focus of a kappo kitchen.
chef_bio.specialty: The 京醤油らぁ麺 (Kyoto soy sauce ramen) is the signature bowl: a refined, dashi-forward broth seasoned with a blend of two soy sauces from the noted Gosho-nishi maker Sawai Shoyu (澤井醬油本店), topped with chashu made from prized Iga mochi pork prepared with traditional kappo technique. The shop also offers a 極塩らぁ麺 (salt) and a spicy miso らぁ麺 using white and red miso from a historic maker with Sichuan pepper and star anise.

anecdotes.text: The proprietor's kappo (Japanese haute cuisine) training shows in the details: the chashu is cut from Iga mochi pork and finished with traditional Japanese culinary technique, and the soy tare blends two soy sauces from the Gosho-nishi maker Sawai Shoyu for a mellow, smooth mouthfeel.
He opened the shop because his passion for ramen outgrew his kappo career, building a small counter near Imadegawa to serve refined, dashi-led bowls at lunch.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi (WjuV5) confirms 一盌 清右衛門's owner trained in 割烹料理 before opening near Imadegawa; the 京醤油らぁ麺 blends two soy sauces from 御所西 maker 澤井醬油本店 for a mellow, dashi-like broth topped with Iga mochi-pork chashu; the lineup also has 極塩らぁ麺 and a spicy miso らぁ麺 using white/red miso (石野) with Sichuan pepper and star anise.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single small counter kitchen serving wheat-noodle ramen; no dedicated gluten-free prep or separate equipment is documented, so wheat cross-contact is effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature Kyoto soy sauce bowl is seasoned with a blend of two soy sauces from a local maker; Japanese soy sauce normally contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths and toppings are animal-based (dashi-forward broth, Iga mochi pork chashu; the miso bowl uses rendered beef fat), so no vegan-safe path on the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny lunch-only counter shop run by a chef who is described as bright and attentive; basic Japanese for ordering will go a long way, and there is no indication of English support.

kyr_kyoto_tantanmen_kinshiro.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle tantanmen shop (the noodles are hand-cut crimped wheat noodles from Sano, Tochigi), and tantanmen tare/sauce typically contains wheat-based soy sauce. There is no gluten-free offering and no allergen information published. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_kyoto_tantanmen_kinshiro.vegan_detail: Tantanmen here is built on a sesame-rich creamy broth and topped with coarsely ground meat miso (pork), so the signature bowls are not vegan. No vegan or plant-based option is advertised; ask if you want to know whether the broth can be modified.
kyr_kyoto_tantanmen_kinshiro.hours_raw: 11:00-14:30 (L.O. 14:00) daily except Sunday; dinner service 17:00-20:30 (L.O. 20:00) Thursday and Friday only. Closed Sundays.
kyr_kyoto_tantanmen_kinshiro.notes: [Mom & Pop] 京都担担麺 金鵄楼 (Kinshiro) opened on March 25, 2024 in the quiet Gosho-minami neighborhood at the Sakaicho-Ibikawa corner of Nakagyo Ward, a stylish counter-only shop that quickly drew lunchtime lines from its 11:00 opening.

chef_bio.background: 京都担担麺 金鵄楼 (Kinshiro) opened on March 25, 2024 in the quiet Gosho-minami neighborhood at the Sakaicho-Ibikawa corner of Nakagyo Ward, a stylish counter-only shop (about six seats) that quickly drew lunchtime lines soon after opening.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focused single-dish specialist: do tantanmen well, let guests dial in their own heat and numbing spice, and keep an intimate counter where solo diners feel welcome.
chef_bio.specialty: Tantanmen offered three ways - with broth (汁あり), without broth (汁なし), and chilled (冷やし). The signature bowl is a sesame-rich, lightly whipped creamy white broth that stays surprisingly light on the palate, paired with chewy thick (rather than the usual thin) noodles for a strong textural presence, and crowned with a praised coarsely ground meat miso. Diners customize noodle firmness, chili oil (rayu) and Sichuan pepper (花椒) levels on an order slip.

anecdotes.text: Became a local craze soon after opening, with lines forming regularly - the shop earned a reputation for being addictively good among Kyoto tantanmen fans.
Goes against the tantanmen norm by using chewy thick noodles - hand-cut crimped wheat noodles sourced from Sano City, Tochigi - that hold their own against the creamy broth.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi (yQyRk) confirms 金鵄楼 is a counter-only (~6-seat) shop in Nakagyo's Gosho-minami area serving tantanmen three ways (汁あり/汁なし/冷やし) with a sesame-rich, slightly frothy creamy broth, thick noodles, and a standout 肉みそ, all customizable. gcjapan (kinshilou) gives the 2024-03-25 opening and states the noodles are hand-cut crimped noodles from Sano City, Tochigi.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tantanmen tare is typically made with wheat-containing soy sauce; no allergen breakdown is published for this shop, so wheat should be assumed present in the sauce as well as the noodles.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is sesame-rich and bowls are topped with pork meat miso; no separate vegetarian/vegan preparation is described.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny counter-only specialist popular with locals and solo diners; ordering is via a customization slip, so a few words of Japanese and patience with possible lines help, but it is approachable.

kyr_seikatei.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation indicated. This is a wheat-heavy Chinese kitchen: gyoza/shumai/spring-roll wrappers, Chinese noodles and fried rice seasonings, and wheat-based soy sauce/seasoning are central. The signature sesame gyoza even has roasted sesame kneaded into a wheat wrapper. Not suitable for celiac diners; no dedicated handling found.
kyr_seikatei.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly venue. Pork is central to the menu (gyoza, shumai, fried rice, noodle dishes), and dishes are seasoned with soy oil, sake and likely meat/seafood-based stocks. No vegan-specific options or labeling were found.
kyr_seikatei.hours_raw: Tue–Sun & holidays (except days before a holiday) 17:00–23:00 (last order 22:30). Closed Mon, and the 1st & 3rd Tue.
kyr_seikatei.notes: [Mom & Pop] Seikatei opened in 1982 in the quiet temple district near Ginkaku-ji. Its roots run back to 盛京亭 (Seikyotei), a Beijing-style restaurant founded in 1951 in the heart of Gion's hanamachi (geisha district). The founder's father served as head chef at Seikyotei and was sent to run a

chef_bio.background: Seikatei opened in 1982 in the quiet temple district near Ginkaku-ji. Its roots run back to 盛京亭 (Seikyotei), a Beijing-style restaurant founded in 1951 in the heart of Gion's hanamachi (geisha district). The founder's father served as head chef at Seikyotei, and the son went on to open this independent shop, carrying most of the original menu with it.
chef_bio.philosophy: A Kyoto take on Chinese food: because the original Gion shop cooked for geiko and refined patrons, it deliberately dialed back heavy aromatics like garlic and excess oil. Seikatei keeps that restraint — light white-pressed soybean oil (shirashime-yu), local Matsui-brewery sake instead of cooking wine, and clean, delicate flavors over punch.
chef_bio.specialty: Goma-gyoza (sesame dumplings): roasted sesame is kneaded right into the wrapper, with a filling of only cabbage, Chinese chives, pork and sake, then pan-fried in a heavy cast iron pan until the surface turns crisp. It began as an off-menu request from a regular and became the house signature.

anecdotes.text: The famous sesame gyoza started life as an off-menu dish made for a customer's request before becoming the shop's signature.

The shop traces back to 盛京亭, opened in Gion's flower district in 1951, where the founder's father was head chef; the garlic-light, oil-light style was developed to suit the refined palates of Gion's patrons.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: serai confirms 盛華亭 opened in 1982 near Ginkaku-ji (Jodoji), founded by the son of a head chef from 盛京亭 (Gion, est. 1951); current owner 佐々木幸司 (Sasaki Koji); the kitchen avoids strong aromatics, uses 白絞油 (white-pressed soybean oil) and 京都松井酒造 sake; the 胡麻餃子 has sesame kneaded into the wrapper, a cabbage/chive/pork/sake filling, cast-iron pan-fry, and began as a customer request.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat is pervasive: gyoza, shumai and spring-roll wrappers, Chinese noodles, and fried-rice/stir-fry seasonings all involve wheat, with shared woks and fryers typical of a town-Chinese kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are seasoned in the Chinese-Japanese style; standard soy sauce/seasonings contain wheat. No wheat-free seasoning is indicated.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: Wrong in both directions at once. 'No wheat-free seasoning is indicated' is false — the cited page's whole point is a house style of salt, Kyoto sake (Matsui Shuzo seisyu, rice-brewed and wheat-free) and white-pressed soybean oil, with strong spices deliberately avoided; gf_detail's 'wheat-based soy

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork is used throughout (gyoza, shumai, fried rice, noodle dishes) and stir-fries share oil and pans, so genuine vegan separation is not provided.

positives.text: Cooking is intentionally light on garlic and heavy oil — a gentler, cleaner style of Chinese food, though this is about palate rather than allergen safety.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional local Kyoto-Chinese restaurant where Japanese is the working language; a few words of Japanese and a relaxed, polite manner will serve you well.

kyr_chuka_no_sakai_honten.gf_detail: This is a traditional town-Chinese (machi-chuka) noodle shop whose signature bowls are wheat-based: the famous cold noodles (冷麺) use custom wheat noodles dressed in a vinegar-and-sesame sauce, and the chuka-soba is a wheat-noodle soy-broth noodle. Wheat is fundamental to the core menu and the sauces, with no gluten-free preparation indicated. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_chuka_no_sakai_honten.vegan_detail: The house specialty cold noodles are topped with roast pork (焼豚), cucumber, and seaweed, and the kitchen is a meat-and-fish Chinese kitchen. No vegan ramen or vegan menu is indicated. Not a vegan-friendly destination.
kyr_chuka_no_sakai_honten.hours_raw: Wed-Fri 11:00-15:00 (L.O. 14:45) & 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:30); Sat-Sun 11:00-16:00 (L.O. 15:30) & 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:30). Lunch may end earlier if sold out. Closed Mon & Tue (open if a public holiday).
kyr_chuka_no_sakai_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] Founded in 1939 (Showa 14) as a coffee shop, the business reinvented itself during wartime as a Western-style restaurant and, after the war, became a specialist Chinese noodle shop. Traces of those earlier lives still linger on the menu in the form of kissaten-style cafe items ke

chef_bio.origin: Murasaki / Shin-Omiya shopping street, Kita-ku, Kyoto, near Daitoku-ji
chef_bio.background: Founded in 1939 (Showa 14) as a coffee shop, the business reinvented itself during wartime as a Western-style restaurant and, after the war, became a specialist Chinese noodle shop. Traces of those earlier lives still linger on the menu in the form of kissaten-style cafe items kept on as a nod to the past.
chef_bio.philosophy: Quietly perfectionist about the basics: the cold-noodle sauce is built on honjozo vinegar of the grade used in Kyoto's high-end kaiseki kitchens, and the noodles themselves were dialed in over dozens of trial batches in collaboration with a local noodle maker so they would marry perfectly with the sauce.
chef_bio.specialty: The legendary cold noodles (冷麺) — roast pork, cucumber and seaweed over custom wheat noodles in a vinegar-and-sesame sauce. Unusually, the shop serves them year-round rather than only in summer, and roughly 90% of customers order them. The other pillar is a classic soy-based chuka-soba.

anecdotes.text: The signature cold noodles were created by the current owner's parents, who refined an earlier recipe that had included shrimp and egg ribbons down to a spare trio of pork, cucumber and seaweed; getting the custom noodles right reportedly took dozens of failed attempts and plenty of arguing with the noodle manufacturer.
A favorite insider move: pay about 100 yen extra to swap your rice for fried rice, then pour the leftover cold-noodle sauce over it for a surprisingly delicious finish.

Because it started life in 1939 as a cafe before becoming a Chinese restaurant, the shop has long kept some kissaten-style cafe dishes (like omurice and cream soda) on the menu as a remnant of its origins.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The chuka-soba is a traditional soy-based Chinese noodle soup; soy sauce in this style of cooking is conventionally wheat-based, though the shop publishes no specific allergen details.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is a meat-and-fish Chinese kitchen and the signature cold noodles are topped with roast pork, so cross-contact with animal products is pervasive.

cultural_comfort.note: A beloved local town-Chinese institution where most ordering is in Japanese and lines of regulars are common; a little Japanese or pointing at the famous cold noodles goes a long way.

kyr_nibodamashii_ramen_gion_.gf_detail: This is a niboshi (dried sardine) ramen specialist serving thick curly wheat noodles in a fish-based broth. As with virtually all Japanese ramen, the noodles are wheat, the tare is almost certainly a wheat-based shoyu, and there is no indication of any gluten-free option or accommodation. Not suitable for celiacs or anyone requiring strict gluten avoidance. No dedicated GF preparation, menu, or cross-contamination controls are advertised.
kyr_nibodamashii_ramen_gion_.vegan_detail: The entire concept is built on a dried-sardine (niboshi) fish broth, with chashu pork, soft-boiled egg, and nori as standard toppings. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on offer, and the broth itself is fish-based, so even broth-free items cannot be assumed plant-based. Not a vegan-friendly destination.
kyr_nibodamashii_ramen_gion_.hours_raw: Tabelog lists: Tue/Wed/Thu/Fri/Sat/Sun (& holidays) 22:00–07:00 (last order 06:30); closed Mon & Sun. May close early. Opening-era shop/blog info also lists 20:00–05:00 (next day), closed Sun & Mon; as it is a late-night operation, hours may vary.
kyr_nibodamashii_ramen_gion_.notes: [Mom & Pop] にぼ魂 opened on August 8, 2025 in the heart of Gion, just north of Gion-Shijo Station off Nawate-dori, taking over a space that previously housed a katsudon-style shop. It was conceived from the start as a deep-night niboshi-ramen stop — a bowl to land in after an evening out in Gi

chef_bio.background: にぼ魂 opened on August 8, 2025 in the heart of Gion, just north of Gion-Shijo Station off Nawate-dori, taking over a space that had until then housed a kasu-udon shop (かすうどん). It was conceived from the start as a deep-night niboshi-ramen stop — a bowl to land in after an evening out in Gion's bars and teahouses, when most kitchens have long closed, running from around 8pm into the early-morning hours.
chef_bio.philosophy: Lean into the niboshi rather than tame it — a punchy, sea-forward bowl built for the late-night palate, served bright and clean in a small room. Diners can dial the flavor themselves with the tabletop kit of spiced tare, black and white pepper, and niboshi vinegar, and free extra-large noodle portions reward a hungry post-drinking crowd.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the Special Nibodamashii Ramen (特製にぼ魂ラーメン): an unapologetically bitter, dried-sardine (niboshi) broth ladled over thick, curly noodles, finished with marbled chashu, a soft-boiled egg, nori, and a single whole niboshi as garnish. The kitchen deliberately leaves the sardine heads and innards in the stock rather than removing them to soften the bitterness.

anecdotes.text: Where many niboshi shops carefully pull the sardine heads and guts to tame the bitterness, にぼ魂 leaves them in the broth on purpose, embracing the sharp bitterness as the point of the bowl rather than a flaw to correct.
Every table is set with a niboshi-forward condiment kit — spiced tare, black pepper, white pepper, and niboshi vinegar — so guests can tune the intensity of the dried-sardine flavor to taste.
Opened August 8, 2025 as a late-night destination for Gion's after-hours crowd, occupying a former kasu-udon shop and running into the early morning.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A wheat-noodle ramen shop with fried side dishes prepared in a tiny shared kitchen; no gluten-free handling or separation is indicated, so cross-contact with wheat is effectively certain.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare is a Japanese ramen seasoning, which is overwhelmingly a wheat-containing shoyu base; no wheat-free soy sauce is advertised.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are built on a dried-sardine fish broth with pork chashu and egg; there is no plant-based broth or vegan preparation, so no item can be considered free of animal cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, cash-only late-night ramen counter in Gion with no sign of English support — basic Japanese and pointing at the menu will go furthest, and quiet ordering etiquette is appreciated.

kyr_ganso_ramen_daiei.gf_detail: This is a traditional Kyoto pork-bone-shoyu ramen shop. The bowls are built on wheat noodles (custom-made by Kondo Seimen) plus a soy-based tare, which is virtually always wheat-containing. There is no indication of any gluten-free options, gluten-free noodles, or celiac handling. Not safe for those who must strictly avoid gluten.
kyr_ganso_ramen_daiei.vegan_detail: Every bowl is built on a pork-and-bone broth (described as crystal-clear shoyu tonkotsu made from premium Iga pork), and chashu pork is the signature topping. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu; even a plain bowl uses animal broth. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_ganso_ramen_daiei.hours_raw: Mon–Sat 11:30–14:00 / 15:30–18:00; Sun & holidays 11:30–14:00 (closes when sold out). Closed the 2nd, 4th & 5th Sun.
kyr_ganso_ramen_daiei.notes: [Mom & Pop] The original Ramen Daiei was founded in 1980 in Kyoto's Minami ward. The current owner is the founder's nephew, who apprenticed under him for about 20 years before opening this Kawaramachi-Marutamachi shop in 2003 to carry the lineage forward. When the founder passed away in 2017

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (lineage from Daiei Ramen, Minami ward)
chef_bio.background: The original Ramen Daiei was founded in 1980 in Kyoto's Minami ward. The current owner is the founder's nephew — raised by his uncle from childhood and apprenticed to him for close to two decades — who then went independent and opened this Kawaramachi-Marutamachi shop around 1998 (it reached its 20th year in 2018) to carry the lineage forward. When the founder passed away in 2017, he left a charge to keep the recipe alive.
chef_bio.philosophy: The founder's words guide the shop: 'ラーメンはスープが命' (the broth is the soul of ramen). The kitchen keeps the broth pure and clean - made only from premium pork and bones, with no cloudiness, bitterness, or gaminess - aiming for a refreshing, never-tiring bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: A clear, aromatic Kyoto-style shoyu tonkotsu ramen crowned with a mountain of freshly hand-sliced chashu and a generous heap of Kujo negi. The popular order is the shoyu chashu-men with extra negi; a miso version is also offered, and a yaki-meshi (fried rice) set rounds out the menu.

anecdotes.text: The broth uses Iga mochibuta premium pork and noodles made to order by Kondo Seimen; the chashu is sliced fresh to order so it stays tender and full of umami.
Beneath the generous Kujo negi, crisp green mung bean sprouts add a textural contrast, and free condiments at the counter include spicy nira, beni-shoga, and fresh garlic to customize each bowl.
Just steps from the Kawaramachi-Marutamachi intersection, it keeps a clean, unpretentious counter atmosphere beloved by locals and ramen fans rather than tourists.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles plus a soy-based tare; the shop and broth are not designed around gluten avoidance, so cross-contamination from shared pots and noodle water should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature is a shoyu (soy sauce) tonkotsu broth; Japanese soy sauce almost always contains wheat, so the tare should be treated as wheat-containing.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls use a pork-and-bone broth and pork chashu; there is no vegan/vegetarian preparation, so no vegan-safe option exists.

positives.text: The broth is made only from premium pork and bones with no additives or muddiness, so ingredients are simple and transparent; toppings like Kujo negi, mung bean sprouts, and chashu are clearly identifiable.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills, cash-only local counter ramen shop favored by regulars; a friendly greeting and a few words of Japanese will go a long way, with no English menu expected.

kyr_tonryu_kitashirakawa_hon.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. Both signature bowls use house-made egg (wheat) noodles, and the 福仙楼そば is shoyu-seasoned (wheat-based soy sauce). Broths are pork-bone and chicken-gara based. No gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle substitution, and no allergen handling is mentioned in any source. A celiac diner cannot safely eat the ramen here.
kyr_tonryu_kitashirakawa_hon.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian friendly. The 東龍そば broth is built on pork bone, chicken carcass and maple-leaf (chicken feet) gelatin; the 福仙楼そば is a pork-bone/chicken paitan. Toppings include pork-belly chashu and braised tendon/minced pork. Noodles are egg noodles. No plant-based bowl is offered.
kyr_tonryu_kitashirakawa_hon.notes: [Mom & Pop] 東龍 opened in December 2000 in the Kitashirakawa neighborhood of Kyoto's Sakyo Ward. The owner had previously worked as a manager at Karako, a well-known ramen shop in Higashiyama, and brought that pedigree to his own counter on the quiet north-eastern edge of the city.

chef_bio.background: 東龍 opened in December 2000 in the Kitashirakawa neighborhood of Kyoto's Sakyo Ward. The owner had previously worked as a manager at Karako, a well-known ramen shop in Higashiyama, and brought that pedigree to his own counter on the quiet north-eastern edge of the city.
chef_bio.philosophy: An emphasis on hand-made work and fresh ingredients runs through the kitchen, down to the rice — the owner serves Koshihikari grown on his family's farm in Kutsuki.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is 東龍そば, described as a kind of 'kaiseki in a bowl' — a creamy salt-based broth simmered from pork bone, chicken carcass, chicken-feet gelatin and around ten kinds of vegetables, served with house-made curly egg noodles, Kyotamba-highland pork-belly chashu and Kujo green onion. A second house specialty, 福仙楼そば, is a Taiwanese-street-stall-inspired pork-and-chicken paitan in a shoyu key with slow-braised tendon and minced pork over flatter, thicker egg noodles.

anecdotes.text: A sister shop, Fukusenro, operated next door from April 2009 until May 2020; when it closed, its Taiwanese-style bowl was folded into the main 東龍 menu, which is why diners can now order both the salt 東龍そば and the shoyu 福仙楼そば under one roof.
The owner studied Taiwanese noodle dishes in order to recreate the street-stall flavors of the 福仙楼そば.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The 福仙楼そば is described as a 醤油味 (soy-sauce-seasoned) bowl; standard ramen shoyu tare is wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are animal-based (pork bone, chicken carcass, chicken-feet gelatin) and noodles are egg noodles, so the entire ramen line is cooked in shared animal-derived stock.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual neighborhood ramen counter where a little Japanese smooths things along; no English service is indicated, and the parking-friendly suburban setting draws mostly local regulars.

kyr_tsukemen_yumenchu.gf_detail: Tsukemen specialist. Homemade wheat noodles, fish-and-pork-bone (魚介豚骨) dipping broth typically built on wheat-based shoyu tare, and side dishes finished with soy reduction. No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodation indicated. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_tsukemen_yumenchu.vegan_detail: The entire menu is built on a fish-and-pork-bone broth, with pork chashu toppings and butter rice. No plant-based bowls or vegetarian options indicated. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_tsukemen_yumenchu.hours_raw: Mon/Tue/Thu/Fri/Sat 11:00–14:30 (last order 14:30) / 18:00–21:00 (last order 21:00); Sun 11:30–14:30 (last order 14:30). Closed Wed.
kyr_tsukemen_yumenchu.notes: [Mom & Pop] Yumenchu is a much-loved Yamashina tsukemen shop with a comeback story. The original shop near Miryoji closed for roughly three years while the owner recovered from an injury; it reopened on October 1, 2018, in a roomier space near Kyoto Pharmaceutical University, drawing a line

chef_bio.background: Yumenchu is a much-loved Yamashina tsukemen shop with a comeback story. The original shop near Miryoji closed for roughly three years while the owner recovered from an injury; it reopened on October 1, 2018, in a roomier space near Kyoto Pharmaceutical University, drawing a line of around 50 people on opening day.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than chasing the heaviest possible broth, the shop aims for a cleaner, balanced dip where both the fish and pork-bone umami read clearly, with a touch of acidity and citrus, an approachable style meant to win over tsukemen newcomers as much as devotees.
chef_bio.specialty: Tsukemen only. The house bowl pairs thick, angular, homemade noodles with a fish-and-pork-bone broth, including a charred burnt-oil version (焦がしつけ麺) that adds aromatic depth. A torch-seared butter rice topped with chashu and a soy reduction is a popular side.

anecdotes.text: After about three years dark while the owner recovered from injury, the shop returned on October 1, 2018, with roughly 50 people queuing on reopening day.
The dip is described as cleaner and more balanced than a typical heavy tonkotsu tsukemen, framed as friendly to first-time tsukemen eaters.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Tsukemen-only shop: homemade wheat noodles in a fish-and-pork-bone broth with wheat-based soy seasoning typical of the style. No gluten-free handling or separation is described.
gf_cross_contamination.why: SOY-SAUCE WARNING INVENTED FROM GENRE — the exact defect pattern. The tsuke-jiru's described flavour driver is MISO (mackerel simmered in miso, blended into the broth), not shoyu, and the record aims a wheat warning at a seasoning nobody has documented. Two clauses do survive and should become the w

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Side dishes such as the butter rice are finished with a soy (shoyu) reduction; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No tamari/GF soy is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is fish-and-pork-bone based with pork chashu toppings; no plant-based preparation exists, so cross-contact is inherent to the whole menu.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, queue-heavy local tsukemen counter where ordering and a few words of Japanese go a long way; no English service is indicated.

kyr_abura_soba_nekomata.gf_detail: No gluten-free option. Abura soba is built on wheat (中華麺) noodles tossed in a soy-sauce-based tare (almost always wheat-containing shoyu) with sesame oil; toppings include pork chashu and menma. There is no published gluten-free menu or dedicated handling, and the entire dish is wheat-centric. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_abura_soba_nekomata.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The standard bowls use pork chashu, a soy/animal-savory tare, and a popular onsen-egg topping; this is a meat-and-egg abura soba specialist with no advertised vegan or vegetarian version. Confirm directly if you must, but plan to eat elsewhere.
kyr_abura_soba_nekomata.hours_raw: 10:00–20:00 (last order 19:45); irregular closures. Note: other sources list 11:00–21:00 closed Wednesdays, and a 10:00–15:00 daily window — hours appear to vary, so confirm before visiting.
kyr_abura_soba_nekomata.notes: ねこまた bills itself as Kansai's first dedicated abura-soba specialist, tucked into the slope below Kiyomizu-dera on the well-trodden path between Gojo and Shijo along Higashioji-dori. It is the kind of small, serious noodle counter that holds its own amid the souvenir shops and tem

chef_bio.background: ねこまた bills itself as Kansai's first dedicated abura-soba specialist, tucked into the slope below Kiyomizu-dera on the well-trodden path between Gojo and Shijo along Higashioji-dori. It is the kind of small, serious noodle counter that holds its own amid the souvenir shops and temple crowds, drawing both local regulars and curious travelers.
chef_bio.philosophy: Eat it the shop's way: dig the tare and oil up from the bottom and toss everything together so the noodles, oil, and toppings bind into one concentrated, savory mouthful — the chilled raw onion is kept cold until service for crunch and contrast.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the 元祖油そば (ganso abura soba) — a brothless bowl where flat, chewy kishimen-like noodles are dressed at the bottom of the bowl with a fragrant dashi oil and a soy-based tare, then mixed thoroughly with pork chashu, menma, scallion, naruto and a generous handful of cold, crisp diced raw onion. Variations include a spicy miso (辛味噌) version and an ebi-shio (shrimp salt) version. Adding an onsen egg and mixing it through turns the bowl rich and creamy, close to carbonara.

anecdotes.text: Despite being surrounded by Kiyomizu tourist traffic, it keeps genuine noodle-shop credentials, pulling in both neighborhood enthusiasts and international visitors.
The onsen-egg topping is a fan favorite: mixed into the noodles it turns the bowl into something close to a cream sauce, carbonara-like.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Abura soba is fundamentally a wheat-noodle dish in a soy/wheat-based tare; no gluten-free handling is published.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare is described as a soy-sauce (醤油) based seasoning, which in Japan is virtually always wheat-containing shoyu.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Standard bowls include pork chashu and an onsen-egg topping; no vegan/vegetarian version is advertised.

positives.text: English menu available, easing communication for non-Japanese-speaking diners.

cultural_comfort.note: Sitting in the heart of the Kiyomizu tourist district, the shop is used to international visitors and offers an English menu, so a non-Japanese-speaking diner can order comfortably.

kyr_ramen_fuji_kyoto_honten.gf_detail: Not safe for celiac/gluten-free. As a noodle-factory-direct shop (近藤製麺), the bowls center on wheat ramen noodles, and the soy-based tare/broth almost certainly contains wheat-based shoyu. No gluten-free noodle or menu option is indicated, and there is no allergen-handling information. Should be avoided by anyone requiring strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_ramen_fuji_kyoto_honten.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly shop. The signature bowl is built on a pork-bone soy (豚骨醤油) broth with pork toppings; gyoza and pork rice (豚めし) are also pork-based. No plant-based ramen is offered. A vegan diner could not be reliably accommodated here.
kyr_ramen_fuji_kyoto_honten.hours_raw: 10:00-19:00 (closed Thursdays; 3rd Wednesday closes earlier ~17:00). Note: Tabelog lists 10:00-22:00, but the official site and multiple recent blog reports state 10:00-19:00 continuous service — the 19:00 close reflects current operation.
kyr_ramen_fuji_kyoto_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] A beloved old-guard Kyoto ramen shop founded in the early 1970s (1973, with some sources citing 1972), Ramen Fuji has fed the south-Kyoto neighborhood for over half a century. It is the flagship of a small local family of shops, with branches around the city (Fushimi Ote, Gojo, F

chef_bio.origin: Minami-ku, Kyoto — near Jujo Station along Shin-Jujo-dori
chef_bio.background: A beloved old-guard Kyoto ramen shop founded in the early 1970s (1973, with some sources citing 1972), Ramen Fuji has fed the south-Kyoto neighborhood for over half a century. It is the flagship of a small local family of shops, with branches around the city (Fushimi Ote, Gojo, Fukuchiyama, Kyotanabe).
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's edge is the noodle itself: it is run as a direct outlet of Kondo Seimen (近藤製麺), the family noodle factory a few minutes' walk away. That factory has long supplied the noodles behind some of Kyoto's most storied ramen names, so the springy, well-cut house noodle is the heart of every bowl here.
chef_bio.specialty: A classic Kyoto-style pork-bone-and-soy bowl: a 豚骨醤油 broth in the clear (清湯) idiom — rich yet transparent, savory with a clean soy finish — piled with green onion and bean sprouts over thin, straight noodles. Beyond the standard ramen there is a 特製 (special), a miso version, and a menma bowl, with gyoza and a pork rice bowl (豚めし) on the side.

anecdotes.text: Ramen Fuji is the direct retail face of Kondo Seimen, the Kyoto noodle maker said to supply heavyweights of the local scene such as Daiichi Asahi and Shinpuku Saikan — so the noodles are made by people who have shaped Kyoto ramen for decades.
The room keeps a thick Showa-era mood: a wooden counter with an open kitchen — a working-class Kyoto ramen counter rather than a polished modern shop.
A playful local tradition: on days when the rain probability is 70% or higher, the shop has offered free noodle refills (kaedama) — a small wink to its neighborhood regulars.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A noodle-factory-direct shop built around wheat ramen noodles; flour is central to the operation and cross-contact with wheat is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a soy-based 豚骨醤油 tare; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, so the soup base should be assumed to contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth and toppings are pork-based (pork-bone soy broth, pork rice, gyoza); no plant-based options noted.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills, cash-only neighborhood ramen counter where ordering is done verbally in Japanese; a little Japanese and an easygoing attitude go a long way, and there is no English support to rely on.

kyr_ramen_to_mazesoba_no_omi.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The core menu is wheat ramen and mazesoba noodles (sourced from Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teigaku / 棣鄂) served with wheat-based shoyu and curry sauces. No gluten-free noodle or dedicated preparation is advertised, and a busy single-counter kitchen means heavy shared-equipment cross-contact. There is no indication staff can accommodate a gluten allergy.
kyr_ramen_to_mazesoba_no_omi.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian options. Ramen broths are chicken and pork-bone (and chicken-seafood) based; mazesoba and the keema curry use ground pork/meat, homemade bacon, egg yolk, cheese and pork back fat. There is no plant-based bowl on the menu.
kyr_ramen_to_mazesoba_no_omi.hours_raw: Tue–Sun & holidays: 11:30–15:00 (last order 14:30), 18:00–23:00 (last order 22:30). Closed Mon.
kyr_ramen_to_mazesoba_no_omi.notes: [Mom & Pop] Lee started life in May 2021 as 'Curry Shop Lee,' a curry-focused spot on the gaikanjō ring road in the Natsutsuji neighborhood of Yamashina, near Aeon Town. Over time the kitchen leaned more and more into noodles, and in May 2024 it fully rebranded into a ramen-and-mazesoba shop

chef_bio.background: Lee started life in May 2021 as 'Curry Shop Lee,' a curry-focused spot on the gaikanjō ring road in the Natsutsuji neighborhood of Yamashina, near Aeon Town. Over time the kitchen leaned more and more into noodles, and in May 2024 it fully rebranded into a ramen-and-mazesoba shop while keeping its curry roots front and center.
chef_bio.philosophy: Curry expertise carried into the noodle bowl — the keema curry is built to be spice-forward but balanced, 'spicy without being overwhelming,' reflecting the shop's years as a curry kitchen. The clean, café-like counter room is a deliberate departure from the typical ramen-shop feel.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the keema curry mazesoba: springy Y-shaped 'wing' noodles from the long-established Kyoto maker Teigaku (棣鄂) tossed with a layered keema curry, finished with egg yolk, cheese, house-made bacon, pork back fat, tomato and parsley. Staff ask each guest about garlic before serving it. Alongside it sit a gyokai-shoyu mazesoba and a Taiwan mazesoba, plus three ramen styles: tori-niboshi (chicken-sardine), tori-tonkotsu (rich chicken and pork bone), and gyokai tori-tonkotsu.

anecdotes.text: The keema curry mazesoba layers egg yolk, cheese, house-made bacon, pork back fat, tomato and parsley over Teigaku's grippy 'wing' noodles, and the counter asks your garlic preference before it goes out.

Lee began as 'Curry Shop Lee' in May 2021 and completed its turn into a dedicated ramen-and-mazesoba shop in May 2024; the curry-based mazesoba is popular enough that it can sell out, leaving only the chilled and niboshi bowls late in service.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen and mazesoba noodles from Kyoto maker Menya Teigaku (棣鄂) are the base of every bowl, cooked in a shared single-counter kitchen, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Bowls use wheat-based shoyu/curry sauces (e.g. gyokai-shoyu mazesoba and shoyu-seasoned ramen), which contain wheat.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: The exact pattern to watch for, and it lands on the wrong bowl. The record extends a soy-sauce warning to 'shoyu-seasoned ramen' at a shop whose own cited page says the ramen it tasted was seasoned ほんのり塩味 - lightly SALTY. A coeliac is not helped by being told the salt bowl is a soy bowl, and the sho

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are chicken/pork-bone based and mazesoba/keema use ground meat, house-made bacon, egg yolk, cheese and pork back fat; no plant-based preparation exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A small 11-seat counter ramen shop in a residential Yamashina neighborhood; expect Japanese-only ordering and menu, so a translation app or pointing helps.

kyr_nippon_ramen_rin_kyoto.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The bowls are built on house-made wheat noodles (blends such as Haruyokoi and Kitahonami) and a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which is brewed from wheat. There is no gluten-free noodle or tare option and no indication of allergen accommodation, so a strict gluten-free or celiac diner cannot safely eat here.
kyr_nippon_ramen_rin_kyoto.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The signature broths are chicken-based (clear chicken shoyu/shio, plus a chicken-paitan variant), finished with chashu pork, wonton, and similar animal toppings. There is no vegan or vegetarian bowl on the menu.
kyr_nippon_ramen_rin_kyoto.hours_raw: 11:00–15:00 / 17:30–21:30 (closed Tue). Schedule changes are announced on Instagram/Twitter.
kyr_nippon_ramen_rin_kyoto.notes: [Mom & Pop] Producer Hiroshi Hiraoka built his reputation in Sapporo with Lab Q, known for crystal-clear, multi-layered broths. He travels around Japan to meet producers in person and source ingredients, then works out the flavor pairings and techniques himself before they reach the bowl.

chef_bio.origin: An offshoot of the celebrated Sapporo shop Japanese Ramen Noodle Lab Q, brought to Kyoto as the brand's first Kansai venture; the Shijo-Karasuma shop (Nakagyo-ku) opened on April 9, 2022.
chef_bio.background: Producer Hiroshi Hiraoka built his reputation in Sapporo with Lab Q, known for crystal-clear, multi-layered broths. He travels around Japan to meet producers in person and source ingredients, then works out the flavor pairings and techniques himself before they reach the bowl.
chef_bio.philosophy: Summed up in the shop's motto 温故知新・日本の食材・醸造文化・伝統を丼の中に — honoring the old to create the new by gathering Japanese ingredients and the country's fermentation (brewing) culture into a single bowl, a modern reconstruction of classic Japanese shoyu ramen.
chef_bio.specialty: Clear chicken shoyu ramen (醤油らぁ麺) built from prized Japanese poultry — jidori from around the country such as Hinai-jidori (Akita) and Nagoya Kochin (Aichi) — alongside a salt (shio) version and a limited chicken-paitan; bowls come plain or dressed up with wonton or chashu, on fine house-made Hokkaido-wheat noodles that stay firm.

anecdotes.text: Hiraoka's stated wish was to 'gather ingredients from all over Japan and make the very best ramen possible,' which is why he personally visits producers nationwide rather than buying off a supplier list.
The dining room is deliberately calm — one craftsman works the line with a couple of helpers, and staff even see guests to the door — so the focus stays on the bowl rather than bustle.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bowls are served on house-made wheat noodles (wheat blends such as Haruyokoi and Kitahonami), so wheat is central to the kitchen and there is no gluten-free preparation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature tare is a soy-sauce (shoyu) base; Japanese shoyu is brewed from wheat, so the broth itself contains gluten.

source_independence.note: This source reprints shop marketing rather than reporting a visit (a curated hub or a press release). It corroborates that a claim was MADE, not that it was verified.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are chicken-based (clear chicken shoyu/shio and a chicken-paitan), with pork chashu and wonton among the toppings; the kitchen is built around animal products with no vegan option.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet, refined counter ramen-ya in central Kyoto that draws international visitors; staff are gracious but the room is calm and Japanese-first, so a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu go a long way.

kyr_menya_yamahide_kyoto_sho.gf_detail: This is a Taiwanese maze-soba (brothless mixed noodle) specialist built on house-made medium-thick wheat noodles, finished with a savory tare and spicy pork mince — all classic wheat-and-soy components. No gluten-free menu, gluten-free noodles, or allergen accommodation is mentioned on the official site, the shop's listings, or any review. Not suitable for celiacs; assume heavy gluten throughout.
kyr_menya_yamahide_kyoto_sho.vegan_detail: The core dishes are animal-based: the signature 台湾まぜそば is topped with spicy minced pork and raw egg yolk, and the other house specialty is a chicken paitan (鶏白湯) ramen. No vegan or vegetarian option is advertised anywhere. Not a place a vegan can eat.
kyr_menya_yamahide_kyoto_sho.notes: [Mom & Pop] An offshoot of a Nara maze-soba house, this Kyoto outpost opened on November 26, 2022 in the quiet Shogoin neighborhood near Kumano Shrine and Kyoto University Hospital, a short walk from Jingu-Marutamachi Station. It took over a former beauty salon in a residential apartment blo

chef_bio.origin: A branch of Menya Yamahide, whose main shop is in Nara.
chef_bio.background: An offshoot of a Nara maze-soba house, this Kyoto outpost opened on November 26, 2022 in the quiet Shogoin neighborhood near Kumano Shrine and Kyoto University Hospital, a short walk from Jingu-Marutamachi Station. It took over a former beauty salon in a residential apartment block, and the room keeps that pale-wood, almost cafe-like calm rather than the usual steamy ramen-shop bustle.
chef_bio.philosophy: A noodle-first shop: the kitchen makes its own noodles and treats the texture and how the sauce grips them as the whole point of maze-soba.
chef_bio.specialty: Taiwanese maze-soba (brothless mixed noodles): house-made medium-thick noodles deliberately scuffed as they boil so the surface turns glossy and clings to the sauce, then piled with spicy minced pork, raw egg yolk, garlic, nori and bonito for a punchy, savory-spicy mix you stir together yourself — with a scoop of rice to chase the leftover sauce at the end. A chicken-paitan shio ramen and a chuka soba round out the board.

anecdotes.text: The shop occupies a converted former hair salon in an apartment building, giving it an unusually bright, white-wood, cafe-like feel for a ramen counter, and it draws both neighborhood regulars and travelers staying at nearby guesthouses.
The medium-thick noodles are scratched at the surface while boiling so they turn silky and hold the heavy maze-soba sauce, served at around 200g per bowl.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Maze-soba tare is built on a soy-sauce-based savory seasoning, which in Japan is overwhelmingly brewed with wheat; no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature bowl is topped with spicy minced pork and raw egg yolk, and the alternate house bowl is a chicken paitan; the kitchen is animal-broth and meat based throughout.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, walk-in-only noodle counter where ordering is simple and a few friendly words of Japanese go a long way; it sits in a guesthouse-heavy pocket near Kumano Shrine so foreign diners are not unusual.

kyr_tsukemen_kyoto_watanabe.gf_detail: A wheat-noodle tsukemen specialist. The dipping broths are built on a pork-chicken bone and seafood base (the five options include rich seafood, vegetable-potato, spicy minced meat, curry, and shrimp), and tsukemen tare almost always contains wheat-based soy sauce. There is no dedicated gluten-free menu, gluten-free noodles, or stated allergen handling, so this is not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_tsukemen_kyoto_watanabe.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian establishment. All broths derive from a pork-chicken bone stock with seafood umami, and even the vegetable-potato (ベジポタ) option is built on the same animal base. No vegan or vegetarian bowl is offered.
kyr_tsukemen_kyoto_watanabe.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tsukemen specialist tucked on a backstreet a one-minute walk from Hankyu Saiin Station. The shop has long roots in the Saiin neighborhood, where it formerly operated under the name Watanabe Seimen (渡辺製麺) before becoming Tsukemen Kyoto Watanabe.

chef_bio.background: A tsukemen specialist tucked on a backstreet a one-minute walk from Hankyu Saiin Station. The shop has long roots in the Saiin neighborhood, where it formerly operated under the name Watanabe Seimen (渡辺製麺) before becoming Tsukemen Kyoto Watanabe.
chef_bio.philosophy: A 'new-sensation' tsukemen format where the diner customizes broth and noodle to taste, served continuously from late morning through the evening.
chef_bio.specialty: Choose-your-own tsukemen: five dipping broths built on a pork-chicken bone and seafood base — rich seafood (濃厚魚介), vegetable-potato (ベジポタ), spicy minced meat (辛肉ミンチ), curry (カレー), and shrimp (えび) — paired with a choice of three noodle styles: thick, medium-thick, and flat thick.

anecdotes.text: At lunch the shop offers a complimentary small bowl of rice (一口ライス) so diners can finish their leftover dipping broth risotto-style.
The counter is lined with autographed cards from entertainers, a mark of the shop's local fame.
Formerly known as Watanabe Seimen, the shop has been a familiar fixture in the Saiin area for years.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tsukemen dipping tare is conventionally based on wheat-containing soy sauce; no allergen breakdown is published for this shop.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All five broths share a pork-chicken bone and seafood base, including the vegetable-potato option, so no broth is free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locally beloved counter-and-table tsukemen shop on a backstreet by the station; English support is not advertised, so a little Japanese or pointing at the broth/noodle choices helps.

kyr_chugoku_shisen_ryori_rak.gf_detail: This is a Sichuan noodle and stir-fry house: the tantanmen and soupless tantanmen are wheat noodles, and Sichuan staples lean on doubanjiang (broad-bean/chili paste), tianmianjiang (sweet wheat-flour paste) and soy-based seasonings that typically contain wheat. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented; not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_chugoku_shisen_ryori_rak.vegan_detail: Core dishes are built on pork mince, dried shrimp, scallop and animal-based broths (tantanmen mince blends scallop, dried shrimp, sweet miso and pork; mapo tofu and yun-bai-rou are meat dishes). No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented; not a plant-based-friendly destination.
kyr_chugoku_shisen_ryori_rak.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-13:45 (last order); Dinner 17:30-20:45 (last order). Closed Mondays (open if holiday) and 1st & 3rd Tuesdays (open if holiday).
kyr_chugoku_shisen_ryori_rak.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tiny, long-running Sichuan counter tucked into the Kitashirakawa/Chayama neighborhood beside Kyoto University of the Arts. The owner-chef trained in Yokohama's Chinatown before opening Rakuda, which has been serving authentic Sichuan food in the same spot for well over fifteen

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Sakyo-ku); cuisine rooted in Sichuan, China, by way of Yokohama Chinatown training.
chef_bio.background: A tiny, long-running Sichuan counter tucked into the Kitashirakawa/Chayama neighborhood beside Kyoto University of the Arts. The owner-chef trained in Yokohama's Chinatown before opening Rakuda, which has been serving authentic Sichuan food in the same spot for well over fifteen years.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking real, unapologetically numbing-and-spicy Sichuan food in an intimate room rather than chasing a crowd — the kind of place enthusiasts mean when they say 'in Kyoto, there is Rakuda.'
chef_bio.specialty: Tantanmen and the soupless tantanmen (汁なし担々麺) drenched in fragrant chili oil, plus a benchmark mapo tofu made with local Kyoto tofu, Sichuan peppercorn and doubanjiang. The yun-bai-rou (雲白肉, 'cloud white meat') is the most popular appetizer.

anecdotes.text: Among Sichuan-food lovers there is a saying, '京都に駱駝あり' ('In Kyoto, there is Rakuda'), nodding to its reputation as a destination for the real thing.
The owner trained in Yokohama's Chinatown before opening Rakuda, which has run for around 17 years.

The soupless tantanmen uses chili oil as its tare, with the star-anise aroma of genuine Sichuan cooking clinging to every noodle; the soup tantanmen runs intensely hot, its mince layered with scallop, dried shrimp, pickled mustard greens, sweet miso, star anise, cinnamon and peanuts.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sichuan seasonings used here (doubanjiang, sweet wheat-flour paste, soy-based sauces) typically contain wheat, and the tantanmen noodles are wheat; assume wheat throughout.
soy_sauce_wheat.source_wording: 「たぶん『ホタテ・ヤーサイ・ザーサイ・干しエビ・甘みそ・ハッカク・シナモン・ピーナッツ』など多くの食材を練りこんでおり、複雑ながらも統一感のある味になっていました。」 plus 「タレは油だけかなと思ったら、何かペーストが入っていました。なにか分かりませんでしたが、麺に適度に絡んで…」

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are built on pork, dried shrimp and scallop; the tantanmen mince and broths are animal-based.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: 「ミンチは色々な食材で作られた甘みそを使った逸品になってもいました。たぶん『ホタテ・ヤーサイ・ザーサイ・干しエビ・甘みそ…』など多くの食材を練りこんで…」 — scallop and dried shrimp in the tantanmen mince. The shop's own menu adds フカヒレ海鮮丼 (shark-fin seafood bowl).

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood Sichuan counter where Japanese is the working language; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu go a long way.

kyr_chuka_soba_rantan.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The ramen uses custom wheat noodles made with whole-grain flour (全粒粉入りの特注麺), and the signature 鰹昆布水つけ麺 noodles incorporate tapioca but are still wheat-based. Broths are chicken/bonito/dried-sardine (鶏・鰹・煮干) and the tare is aged soy sauce (熟成醤油), which is conventionally wheat-fermented. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodation. A celiac diner should not eat here.
kyr_chuka_soba_rantan.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Every bowl is built on animal-derived dashi — chicken, bonito (鰹), and dried sardines (煮干) — and menu items feature duck fat, shellfish dashi (貝ダシ), and egg-based dishes such as TKM and the "まんげつ濃厚卵." There is no vegan or vegetable-broth option noted.
kyr_chuka_soba_rantan.notes: [Mom & Pop] Chuka Soba Rantan is a light, clear-broth (tanrei) chuka soba specialist that opened on May 31, 2024, at Sanjo Kiyamachi (Kiyamachi-dori Sanjo Agaru). With a calm, deep interior reminiscent of a Japanese restaurant, it aims to offer a bowl to be savored as a dish of dashi rather than merely ramen.

chef_bio.origin: 京都・三条木屋町（三条駅近く、木屋町三条上ル）
chef_bio.background: 中華そば らんたんは2024年5月31日に三条木屋町（木屋町通三条上ル）にオープンした淡麗系の中華そば専門店です。和食店を思わせる落ち着いた奥行きのある店内で、ラーメンというより一杯の出汁料理として味わえる一品を目指しています。
chef_bio.philosophy: 「わざわざ食べに行きたいお店」として、味のクオリティーだけでなくおもてなしと高級感のある趣を大切にしている。秋田県大潟村直送のあきたこまちや濃厚な『まんげつ濃厚卵』など素材にもこだわる。
chef_bio.specialty: 看板は鰹昆布水つけそば。北海道産がごめ昆布と土佐清水の鰹（宗田節）からとった昆布水に全粒粉入りの特注中細麺を浸し、熟成醤油と国産鴨脂を合わせたつけ汁で味わう。レギュラーの熟成醤油中華そば（900〜1000円）は国産鶏・鰹・煮干から引いたクリアで力強いスープに柚子が香る淡麗系の一杯。

anecdotes.text: 全粒粉入りの特注麺は中細でツルっとした食感とすすり心地のよさが特徴。
鰹昆布水つけそばは、北海道産がごめ昆布と土佐清水産の鰹（宗田節）でとった昆布水につけ、熟成醤油と国産鴨脂のつけ汁で食べる京都ではまだ貴重な昆布水つけ麺。
国産鶏と鰹・煮干から抽出されるクリアながらも力強い味わい、秋田県大潟村直送のあきたこまち、濃厚な『まんげつ濃厚卵』を使用。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyo-soku と kyotopi が2024年5月31日開店・木屋町三条・全粒粉低加水麺・熟成醤油鰹昆布水つけそばを確認。公式PR Times（prtimes 023）が北海道産がごめ昆布と土佐清水の宗田節による昆布水、国産鴨油、大潟村直送あきたこまち、まんげつ濃厚卵を明記。

gf_cross_contamination.text: Custom wheat noodles made with whole-grain flour (全粒粉入りの特注麺) are the core of every bowl; the kitchen is a wheat-noodle ramen operation with no gluten-free handling noted.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature ramen is built on an aged soy sauce tare (熟成醤油 中華そば), and the tsukemen dipping sauce uses aged soy sauce (熟成醤油) — conventionally wheat-fermented.

source_independence.note: This source reprints shop marketing rather than reporting a visit (a curated hub or a press release). It corroborates that a claim was MADE, not that it was verified.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are animal-based (国産鶏・鰹・煮干 — chicken, bonito, dried sardine); the tsukemen uses 国産鴨脂 (domestic duck fat) and shellfish dashi (貝ダシ) and egg dishes appear on the menu. No vegetable broth offered.

source_independence.note: This source reprints shop marketing rather than reporting a visit (a curated hub or a press release). It corroborates that a claim was MADE, not that it was verified.

cultural_comfort.note: A small 14-seat counter-style ramen shop near Sanjo-Kiyamachi where a friendly greeting in Japanese goes a long way, though the simple point-and-order format makes it manageable for visitors with little Japanese.

kyr_kyoto_nijo_menya_susuru.gf_detail: A ramen specialist based on wheat chuka noodles and an aged soy-sauce (wheat-derived) tare; no gluten-free accommodation could be confirmed. The soup is centered on Japanese dashi such as chicken, bonito flakes, and dried sardines, and wheat noodles are used across the board, including tsukemen and tantan. No bowl that can be safely served to celiac/gluten-intolerant guests could be confirmed; consider it fundamentally not possible.
kyr_kyoto_nijo_menya_susuru.vegan_detail: Two dedicated animal-free items are permanently offered: 'Vegan Paitan Ramen' (soy-milk and aromatic-vegetable soup, topped with ganmodoki and red mizuna / about 1,200 yen) and 'Vegan Tantan Ramen' (about 1,250 yen). However, the same kitchen prepares large volumes of animal-based dishes such as chicken clear soup, dried sardine, A5 wagyu, and pork gyoza, and there is no stated management of shared noodle-boiling water, shared utensils, or cross-contact. They can be ordered as plant-based, but strict vegans or those with severe allergies should always confirm at the time of visit.
kyr_kyoto_nijo_menya_susuru.notes: Opened October 16, 2025, in Jurakumawari Minami-cho close to JR Nijo Station, a new ramen specialist. It is run by Efried Co., Ltd. (representative Ryota Adachi, founded 2019), headquartered in Nagoya, opening under the slogan 'Ramen connecting the world and Kyoto.'

chef_bio.background: 2025年10月16日、JR二条駅からほど近い聚楽廻南町に開業した新しいラーメン専門店。名古屋に本社を置く株式会社エフリード（代表・安達亮太、2019年5月設立）が手がけ、『世界と京都をつなぐラーメン』を掲げてオープンしました。
chef_bio.philosophy: 『伝統と革新』がコンセプト。日々の一杯を求める地元客、思い出の一食を求める旅行者、本物の日本文化に触れたい訪日客の三者すべてに応えることを目指しています。
chef_bio.specialty: 看板は『熟成醤油らぁ麺』。国産鶏からていねいに引いた澄んだ鶏清湯に、鰹節・煮干し・昆布の和出汁を重ね、まろやかな熟成醤油のかえしを合わせた一杯。クリアでありながら奥行きのある旨味と、熟成醤油の豊かな香りが身上です。

anecdotes.text: 看板の熟成醤油らぁ麺に加え、濃厚鶏白湯、自家製胡麻だれと香味油の胡麻担々、A5ランクの和牛ローストビーフをのせた『A5和牛らぁ麺』まで、幅広い一杯を揃える。さらに動物性不使用の『ヴィーガン白湯らぁ麺』『ヴィーガン担々らぁ麺』も常設し、プラントベースの来店者にも対応する。
開業を記念し、10月16〜17日にはInstagramフォロワー向けに看板の熟成醤油らぁ麺を通常900円のところ500円で提供するなど、地域とSNSを通じたオープン企画も実施した。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: 公式PR Times（prtimes 057）と kyo-soku が2025年10月16日開店・中京区聚楽廻南町・JR二条駅至近・メニュー（熟成醤油らぁ麺900円、鶏白湯、胡麻担々、A5和牛1800円、ヴィーガン各種）・500円オープン企画を確認。運営は株式会社エフリード（名古屋、2019年5月設立、代表 安達亮太）。

kyr_menya_ikku.gf_detail: This is a standard ramen shop built on wheat noodles (sourced from Menya Teigyaku), wheat-based shoyu tare, and a long-simmered chicken (tori-paitan) broth. Wheat is present in the noodles and almost certainly in the soy-based tare. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, gluten-free tare, a dedicated fryer, or any celiac accommodation. Not safe for celiacs.
kyr_menya_ikku.vegan_detail: The entire menu is built around chicken (tori-paitan / chicken clear soup made from three heritage chicken breeds including Nagoya Cochin simmered ~8 hours) plus pork and chicken chashu toppings. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options noted; even the broths are animal-based.
kyr_menya_ikku.hours_raw: Mon-Fri 11:00-14:30 and 18:00-21:00; Sat 11:00-14:30 (lunch only); closed Sunday. (Some sources list slightly different evening/Saturday hours; Tabelog's listing used here.)
