chef_bio.origin: 京都市左京区・岡崎（平安神宮の北東）
chef_bio.background: A craftsman ramen shop born from a yatai (hand-pushed food cart). Founder Ryohei Morikawa, originally from Ishikawa Prefecture, had worked as a materials dealer and a taxi driver before learning to make ramen by volunteering unpaid for five months — late nights after his own shift work — at a shop called Homin (芳眠) in Kamikatsura. In 1972 he began pushing a hinoki-wood cart along Marutamachi-dori in Okazaki, opening each evening around the time the first star appeared, which gave the shop its name, Ichibanboshi ("first star"). After about three years he took over a brick-walled space left by a closing nearby steakhouse and put down permanent roots; the ivy-covered, café-like brick exterior near Heian Shrine is now the local landmark.
chef_bio.philosophy: Morikawa credits his customers for the recipe itself: "お客さんのほうがラーメンにくわしいんです。こだわりのあるお客さんのアドバイスをたくさん取り入れて、今の味になりました" — "Customers know ramen better than I do; I took in a lot of advice from discerning regulars, and that's how today's flavor came to be." He says the taste evolved over the years alongside the regulars who eat it.
chef_bio.specialty: A single bowl: chuka-soba. A clear (seiyu) broth of pork bones blended with chicken carcasses, soy-based and a touch sweet, with fine, soft noodles, house-made chashu and house-made menma, plus bean sprouts and green onion. House-made pickles are served alongside to refresh the palate after the bowl. Rice is the only other thing on the menu.

anecdotes.text: The shop is named for the cart's opening time: Morikawa rolled out his hinoki-wood yatai around dusk, when the first star (一番星) appeared in the sky.
He learned the craft by working unpaid for five months at a shop called Homin in Kamikatsura, taking the late shifts after his own day's work.
He shaped the broth around long-time regulars' feedback, adjusting it over the years until it settled into today's flavor.
The brick, ivy-covered storefront — taken over from a closed steakhouse — feels more like a retro kissaten than a ramen shop: "レトロなレンガ調で、まるで喫茶店のような店内."

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hankei500 (detailed profile) confirms Morikawa's Ishikawa origin, prior work as a materials dealer and taxi driver, five months' unpaid training at 芳眠 in Kamikatsura, the 1972 hinoki yatai on Marutamachi-dori in Okazaki opening ~6:30pm when the first star appears, the move after ~3 years into a former steakhouse's brick building, the soy-based pork-bone-and-chicken broth with house chashu and menma, and the quote お客さんのほうがラーメンにくわしいんです…今の味になりました; kyotopi describes the retro, kissaten-like brick interior.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single-item wheat-noodle ramen shop with one small kitchen; wheat noodles are handled throughout, so any dish would face cross-contamination. No gluten-free handling is offered.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a soy-based (醤油/清湯) chuka-soba; Japanese shoyu used in such tare is virtually always wheat-containing. No wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone and chicken-carcass based with house-made pork chashu; the kitchen is built entirely around animal products, so no vegan separation exists.

positives.text: House-made pickles (お漬物) are served with the bowl to refresh the palate, and chashu and menma are made in-house — a sign of a careful, hands-on kitchen, though not an allergen accommodation.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, cash-only, decades-old neighborhood ramen counter run by an attentive owner with a single set menu and no English or allergen support, so a first-time GF/vegan visitor should not attempt it without a Japanese-speaking guide.

kyr_jiei.gf_detail: This is a classic wheat-noodle Kyoto chukasoba shop. The bowl is built on wheat (komugi) straight noodles plus a tonkotsu-shoyu broth whose tare is almost certainly standard wheat-based soy sauce, with no gluten-free menu, no separate prep, and a shared boiling pot. Not suitable for celiac diners. No GF information is published anywhere.
kyr_jiei.vegan_detail: A single-bowl pork-based shop: the broth is tonkotsu-shoyu (pork bone) and every bowl is topped with pork-belly chashu, with rice/egg-over-rice as the only sides. There is no vegetarian or vegan ramen option and no published accommodation.
kyr_jiei.hours_raw: 11:30–14:30 / 17:30–22:00 (closed Mon, with additional irregular days off)
kyr_jiei.notes: [Mom & Pop] Jiei opened on February 4, 2016 in a quiet residential pocket of Mototanaka in Sakyo Ward, just north of Kyoto University's agriculture campus, taking over a small storefront that earlier sources describe as a former bistro/izakaya space. Now approaching its tenth year, it has be

chef_bio.background: Jiei opened in February 2016 in a quiet residential pocket of Mototanaka in Sakyo Ward, about five minutes' walk from Mototanaka Station and just north of Kyoto University's agriculture campus, taking over a small storefront that earlier housed a Western-style (yoshoku) restaurant called Kitchen Gorilla. Now approaching its tenth year, it has become a low-key neighborhood fixture rather than a tourist destination.
chef_bio.philosophy: Do one bowl, and do it carefully. The taciturn owner is described as working quietly and methodically, plating a nostalgic, old-fashioned (昔ながらの) Kyoto ramen meant to feel homely and warming rather than flashy.
chef_bio.specialty: A single classic Kyoto-style chukasoba (中華そば) in a style that reviewers liken to the Takara-ya (宝屋) / Taiei (大栄) Kyoto-ramen tradition: a tea-colored tonkotsu-shoyu broth with mellow, comforting umami, served over medium-thin straight noodles and topped with thick-cut pork-belly chashu, menma (bamboo shoots) and freshly hand-cut scallions. Offered as regular or large, plus a chashu version; rice rounds out the short menu.

anecdotes.text: The shop occupies a space that earlier housed a Western-style restaurant called Kitchen Gorilla before becoming Jiei, part of its low-profile, residential-street character.
The owner is reported to have previously worked as a manager at the Kyoto ramen shop Daioh Ramen (大王ラーメン), which reviewers tie to Jiei's nostalgic, Takara-ya/Taiei-style Kyoto ramen.
The space leans into Showa-era nostalgia, down to a television playing in the corner of the small counter room.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms the 2016 opening in Mototanaka (~5 min from Mototanaka Station), the single tonkotsu-shoyu chukasoba with medium-thin straight noodles, large pork-belly chashu, menma and hand-cut scallions, the taciturn proprietor and TV-in-the-corner nostalgia, and that the space previously held a Western restaurant 'Kitchen Gorilla'; osumituki reports the owner was formerly manager at 大王ラーメン and likens the ramen to 大栄ラーメンや宝屋系.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bowl is built on wheat straight noodles boiled in a shared pot, with a tonkotsu-shoyu broth and (standard wheat) soy-based tare; no gluten-free preparation exists.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Broth is a tonkotsu-shoyu (pork bone + soy sauce) base; soy sauce in a traditional Kyoto chukasoba tare is wheat-based unless stated otherwise, and no allergen labeling is published.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every bowl uses pork-bone broth and is topped with pork-belly chashu; there is no animal-free option.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny counter-only neighborhood ramen shop with a quiet owner, cash only, no English and no menu accommodations expected — best approached with a guide or basic Japanese and a willingness to just order the one bowl.

kyr_konbu_to_men_kiichi.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The noodles are wheat — a custom whole-grain blend built on Hokkaido "Haruyo Koi" first-grade flour — so the core dish contains gluten. Unusually for ramen, the signature kombu ramen broth is described by the shop as using no meat and no kaeshi (no soy-sauce tare), built only from blended ma-/rausu-/rishiri kombu plus seafood and bonito; that removes the usual wheat-shoyu tare risk from the broth, but the wheat noodles themselves rule out a gluten-free meal. No gluten-free noodle option and no dedicated GF handling is indicated.
kyr_konbu_to_men_kiichi.vegan_detail: Not vegan and not vegetarian. Although the signature kombu ramen broth uses no meat stock (a kombu-and-seafood dashi), it is built on bonito (katsuo) flakes and other seafood, so it is not vegetarian/vegan. The gagome kombu tsukemen is also described with pork chashu and a soy-sauce tare in at least one account. There is no stated vegan or vegetarian option.
kyr_konbu_to_men_kiichi.hours_raw: 3-seating reservation system: ① from 11:00, ② from 12:00, ③ from 13:00 (three time slots, 10 seats each, reservation-only), each seating ~45 minutes. Arrive by the 10-minutes-prior assembly time or entry is denied. Tabelog lists Sunday closed; official site notes irregular closures — confirm via Instagram @kiichi5224 before going.
kyr_konbu_to_men_kiichi.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kiichi is the ramen room of Itutuji no Konbu, a Kyoto kombu specialist founded in 1902 (Meiji 35) on Nishi-Itsutsuji in Kamigyo-ku. The ramen counter sits on the second floor above the family's historic kelp shop, near Kitano Tenmangu.

roles: Operated by 五辻の昆布 (Itutuji no Konbu)
chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, in the Kitano-Hakubaicho / Kitano Tenmangu district of Kamigyo-ku.
chef_bio.background: Kiichi is the ramen room of Itutuji no Konbu, a Kyoto kombu specialist founded in 1902 (Meiji 35) on Nishi-Itsutsuji in Kamigyo-ku. The ramen counter sits on the second floor above the family's historic kelp shop, near Kitano Tenmangu.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop exists to help people rediscover the value of kombu: 昆布専門店が『昆布の価値を再認識してもらう』ために作った『昆布らぁめん』 — a kombu specialist's answer to falling kelp consumption and changing kitchens.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature 昆布らぁめん (kombu ramen) is built on a broth blending ma-kombu, rausu and rishiri kelp, lifted with bonito and seafood (squid and shellfish) and — unusually for ramen — made with no meat stock. The other headline bowl is the がごめ昆布つけ麺 (gagome kombu tsukemen), whose dipping water leans on sticky gagome kelp; whole-grain wheat noodles built on Hokkaido 'Haruyo Koi' first-grade flour are made to the shop's own spec.

anecdotes.text: Each seating is a guided experience, not just a meal: diners first water-taste three kelp varieties side by side, then watch oboro-kombu shaved fresh by hand and laid over the noodles, finishing with a kombu rice ball and the shop's tsukudani.
Since June 2023 a 'One Kombu' rule asks every guest to buy at least one product from the kelp shop downstairs, tying the ramen experience back to the 120-year-old family trade.
The fresh oboro kombu is described as just-shaved and still soft (削り出された出来立てホヤホヤのおぼろ昆布), demonstrated live with the shop's own equipment.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: itutuji (official) confirms 五辻の昆布 founded Meiji 35 (1902) at 西五辻東町, the 2nd-floor ramen counter (reservation, three seatings of ~10), the 昆布らぁめん on ma/rausu/rishiri kelp with bonito, squid and shellfish and no meat stock/additives over 春よ恋 Hokkaido first-grade whole-wheat noodles, the three-kelp water tasting, hand-shaved oboro kombu, kombu tsukudani rice ball, and the ワンコンブ制 since June 2023; noodlers describes the just-shaved oboro kombu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The dish is wheat-noodle ramen/tsukemen with no gluten-free alternative noted, so cross-contamination is moot for celiacs — the meal itself contains gluten.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature kombu ramen is stated to use no kaeshi / no soy-sauce tare (かえしは不使用), so the flagship broth avoids the usual wheat-shoyu seasoning; however, an account of the gagome kombu tsukemen describes a soy-sauce tare.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth relies on bonito and seafood (and at least one bowl uses pork chashu), so it is not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.

positives.text: The signature kombu ramen broth uses no additives and no meat stock — a purely kombu-and-seafood dashi (添加物、肉類、かえしは不使用), unusually transparent and animal-stock-free for ramen.

cultural_comfort.note: A reservation-only, fixed-timing seating with a guided kombu tasting and a one-product purchase rule — smoothest if you can manage the online booking and follow along in Japanese, though the experience is welcoming.

kyr_inaho_shokudo.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is advertised. The kitchen leans on naturally rice-based Southeast Asian dishes — Khao Man Gai (jasmine rice with poached chicken), pho and pad thai (rice noodles), and green curry over rice — which can be lower-gluten than the wheat-noodle ramen the street is known for. However, Thai/Vietnamese cooking commonly uses fish sauce, oyster sauce, and soy-based seasonings, and no cross-contamination handling is documented. A celiac diner must ask about each sauce; treat as not verified safe.
kyr_inaho_shokudo.vegan_detail: Some plant-forward items exist (green salad, chilled tofu, vegetable salads, and green curry described as having a vegetarian option), and the building's ground floor is an organic vegetable market that supplies the kitchen. But Thai/Vietnamese dishes here typically use fish sauce, chicken broth, and egg, so a strict vegan must confirm preparation; full vegan is not guaranteed.
kyr_inaho_shokudo.notes: Inaho Shokudo sits on the second floor of a small building in Ichijoji, above a ground-floor organic vegetable market and below a guesthouse — a layout that shapes the whole experience: produce comes from just downstairs, and travelers staying upstairs drift in, giving the room a

chef_bio.background: Inaho Shokudo sits on the second floor of a small building on the Takano/Ichijoji fringe of Sakyo Ward, above a ground-floor organic vegetable market and below a guesthouse — a layout that shapes the whole experience: produce is sold just downstairs, and travelers staying upstairs drift in, giving the room an easy international mix. Rather than a ramen counter, it is an Asian 'no-borders' (mukokuseki) dining bar leaning hard into Thai and Vietnamese home cooking, making liberal use of fresh herbs and seasonal vegetables.
chef_bio.philosophy: Lunch is framed as Asian street food in a plant-filled, greenery-draped space; evenings turn into a relaxed dining bar with music, drinks, and food. The cooking emphasizes fresh herbs and seasonal vegetables, with an organic vegetable market right downstairs in the same building.
chef_bio.specialty: Khao Man Gai — jasmine rice cooked in concentrated chicken broth, topped with poached chicken and served with Thai chili and scallion sauces — is the dish reviewers single out. Khao Soi (Chiang Mai curry noodles), pho, pad thai, and green curry round out the noodle-and-rice section, with crispy herb-filled spring rolls and Yam Woon Sen among the small plates.

anecdotes.text: The building stacks an organic vegetable market on the ground floor, the restaurant on the second, and a guesthouse on the third — so produce is sold in the same building and the crowd skews international.
Despite standing near Ichijoji's famous ramen street, the kitchen serves Thai and Vietnamese-inspired dishes — Khao Man Gai, Khao Soi, pho, green curry — rather than ramen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto.tips describes the building as an organic vegetable market (1F), the restaurant (2F) and a guesthouse (3F) at Takano Tamaoka-cho, a mukokuseki/Thai-leaning kitchen using fresh herbs, ~25 seats, and highlights the カオマンガイ (Khao Man Gai); Tabelog's menu lists Khao Soi, pho, pad thai, green curry, spring rolls and Yam Woon Sen.

positives.text: Many menu items are naturally rice-based rather than wheat-noodle — Khao Man Gai (jasmine rice + poached chicken), pho and pad thai (rice noodles), and curries over rice — which can suit a gluten-avoiding diner better than the wheat ramen the street is known for, though sauces should still be checked.
An organic vegetable market on the ground floor supplies the kitchen, and the menu includes plant-forward salads, chilled tofu, and a green curry with a vegetarian option.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, foreigner-friendly spot (a guesthouse occupies the floor above, so international guests are common), but English support is limited — a few words of Japanese go a long way.

kyr_komugi_no_kirameki_komug.gf_detail: Not safe for celiacs. The house specialty is in-house-milled, in-house-made wheat noodles (a four-wheat blend), and the bowls pair them with chicken-paitan broth and typically wheat-based shoyu/miso tare. The flagship dish, Komugi no Chikara, is a thick-noodle Jiro-style mazesoba — entirely wheat. No gluten-free noodle or dedicated preparation was found, and no allergen program is advertised.
kyr_komugi_no_kirameki_komug.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly stop. The broth is a chicken-paitan (creamy chicken) base and the Taiwan mazesoba is built on pork mince, egg yolk, and chicken-derived components; the Komugi no Chikara mazesoba features braised pork and back fat. No plant-based broth or vegan option was found on the menu.
kyr_komugi_no_kirameki_komug.notes: [Mom & Pop] A Kami-Katsura neighborhood ramen shop in Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, this is one branch of the fast-growing Kirameki group, which began with its flagship Kirameki no Tori in Marutamachi and has spread across Kyoto and into Osaka. The shop sits about a 7-minute walk from Kamikatsura S

chef_bio.background: A Kami-Katsura neighborhood ramen shop in Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, this is one branch of the fast-growing Kirameki group, which began with its flagship Kirameki no Tori in Marutamachi and has spread across Kyoto and into Osaka. The shop sits about a 7-minute walk from Kamikatsura Station on the Hankyu Arashiyama line, with on-site parking.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name means roughly 'the sparkle of wheat,' and the shop leans hard into the noodle itself: noodles are milled and made in-house in a glass-fronted production room, using a custom wheat blend prized for its bite — thick and chewy for mazesoba, medium for ramen.
chef_bio.specialty: Two pillars: a creamy tori-paitan (chicken) ramen offered in salt, soy, and miso, and richly built mazesoba. The signature bowl is Komugi no Chikara ('the power of wheat'), a Jiro-style thick-noodle mazesoba piled with bean sprouts, menma, and big chunks of tender pork and back fat. The Taiwan mazesoba layers pork mince, egg yolk, garlic, chives, scallion, nori, and fish powder.

anecdotes.text: Komugi no Chikara, the house Jiro-style mazesoba, is offered at only a handful of the group's Kyoto shops, making this branch one of the places to try it.
Noodles are produced on-site behind glass in the shop's own noodle room, which gives it its 'sparkle of wheat' identity.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: genjitsutouhi confirms the Kamikatsura branch of the Kirameki group (flagship Kirameki no Tori in Marutamachi), 7-min walk from 上桂駅 on the Hankyu Arashiyama line, on-site parking, glass-fronted in-house noodle production, tori-paitan (soy/salt) with thick white chicken broth, the Taiwan mazesoba 'Chokutaro' and Komugi no Chikara oil-based mazesoba (up to 500g); osumituki notes Komugi no Chikara is available at only some group shops.

gf_cross_contamination.text: House noodles are wheat (a four-wheat blend), milled and made in-house, and used across every bowl; there is no gluten-free noodle and no allergen-handling program advertised, so cross-contamination from shared noodle water and prep is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soy- and miso-tare ramen are on the menu; standard ramen tare and miso in Japan are wheat-containing, and no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is chicken-paitan and dishes feature pork, egg yolk, and fish powder; no plant-based options were found, so vegan diners cannot eat here safely.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual ticket-machine ramen shop — buy a meal ticket at the vending machine before sitting; a smile and a few Japanese words go a long way, though the system is easy to navigate visually.

kyr_ramen_viska.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle tonkotsu shop with no gluten-free offering. The noodles are wheat, the tare is almost certainly wheat-based shoyu, and the menu (kotteri/assari/tsukemen) is built around standard ramen components. No celiac-safe option and no published allergen handling. Not suitable for anyone requiring strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_ramen_viska.vegan_detail: Every bowl is built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth and topped with roast-pork chashu; there is no vegetable or vegan broth and no meat-free option on the menu. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_ramen_viska.hours_raw: 11:00-14:00 / 18:00-20:00 (sources also list the dinner block as 17:30-19:30). Open until sold out. Closed Wednesdays and Thursdays plus irregular holidays.
kyr_ramen_viska.notes: [Mom & Pop] Ramen Viska opened in summer 2023 (July 14) in a quiet residential pocket behind Takano Post Office, on the fringe of Ichijoji's famously crowded ramen battleground. It is a true one-person shop: the owner cooks, serves, and chats single-handedly. The space is a renovated former

chef_bio.background: Ramen Viska opened on July 14, 2023, in a quiet residential pocket behind Takano Post Office, on the fringe of Ichijoji's famously crowded ramen battleground. It is a true one-person shop: the owner cooks, serves, and chats single-handedly. The space is a renovated former snack bar with a glossy high bar-style counter of about five seats, and the owner greets guests in a suit and tie rather than the usual ramen-cook garb. There is no noren curtain out front.
chef_bio.philosophy: A minimalist, single-minded devotion to tonkotsu done well — quality broth over a broad menu, served personally and explained in detail to anyone curious.
chef_bio.specialty: Super-rich kotteri tonkotsu: a pork-bone broth simmered until thick enough that, as locals joke, the spoon could stand up in it, yet it stays mild and clean on the palate with no porky funk, drinking almost like a potage. The lineup is deliberately spare — kotteri (rich), assari (a remarkably clear, transparent tonkotsu, finished with yuzu zest), a Bisuro (ビス郎) bowl, and tsukemen — paired with medium-straight noodles and well-seasoned roast-pork chashu. The focus is entirely the bowl.

anecdotes.text: The shop name 'Viska' comes from Catalan, used as a celebratory cheer meaning roughly 'long live!' / 'banzai / hooray!'
Among the table condiments sits an unexpected jar of harissa, the North African chili paste, which regulars say melds surprisingly well with the rich pork broth.
The owner works solo, and diners can self-serve rice from a cooker and add takana and pickled ginger, with free small meat and green-onion top-ups offered.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms the summer-2023 opening behind Takano Post Office, no noren, bar-like interior, suit-and-tie owner, the こってり 'spoon might stand up' mild tonkotsu 'like potage', and the harissa on the table; noodlers confirms the one-person operation, ex-snack-bar space, assari/kotteri/Bisuro/tsukemen, clear yuzu-accented assari, self-serve rice with takana and beni-shoga and free top-ups; Retty listing gives the July 14, 2023 opening and the Catalan 'banzai' meaning of the name.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water, making the broth and any shared utensils unsuitable for strict gluten avoidance.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tare/seasoning is standard ramen-shop shoyu, which is wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are pork-bone based and every bowl is cooked in the same tonkotsu kitchen with pork chashu; no vegan-safe preparation exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny counter run single-handedly by an approachable owner; ordering is done in Japanese when he comes out to greet you, and a little Japanese goes a long way in this snug local spot.

kyr_menya_sawaki.gf_detail: Standard ramen here uses wheat noodles (Goto noodles for the iekei bowl) and a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare that almost certainly contains wheat, plus pork broth. No gluten-free noodles or menu are offered, and there is no indication of celiac-safe handling.
kyr_menya_sawaki.vegan_detail: All bowls are built on pork-bone (tonkotsu) or pork-clear broth with chashu and other animal toppings; no vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.
kyr_menya_sawaki.hours_raw: Mon, Wed-Sat: 11:00-14:00, 18:00-23:30; Tue: 11:00-14:00; Sun: 11:00-14:00, 18:00-22:00 (one source lists 11:00-14:00, 18:00-22:00, closed Mondays). Hours subject to change.
kyr_menya_sawaki.notes: [Mom & Pop] Menya Sawaki sits on Ichijoji's famous 'ramen street,' a stretch in northeast Kyoto packed with competing shops. It first opened in 2021 as Chuka Soba Nishiki (中華そば 錦) and was rebranded as Menya Sawaki in October 2023, making it one of the area's notable iekei (Yokohama-style) en

chef_bio.background: Menya Sawaki sits on Ichijoji's famous 'ramen street,' a stretch in northeast Kyoto packed with competing shops. It first opened in 2021 as Chuka Soba Nishiki (中華そば 錦) and was rebranded as Menya Sawaki in October 2023, making it one of the area's notable iekei (Yokohama-style) entrants in a district better known for Kyoto's heavier back-fat shoyu and assari styles.
chef_bio.philosophy: A deliberately wide-ranging menu - iekei, Hakata, Kyoto shoyu, classic chuka soba and more - so that a single counter can satisfy very different ramen cravings, with evening service leaning toward small plates for a casual izakaya-style stop.
chef_bio.specialty: Iekei ramen: a shoyu-tonkotsu (pork-bone-and-soy) bowl described as rich yet surprisingly clean, served over thick Goto-style noodles and topped with pork chashu, spinach, nori, chopped white negi and a quail egg. A popular add-on set brings karaage and rice. The kitchen also ranges across Hakata yatai-style thin-noodle tonkotsu and a classic chuka-soba shoyu bowl.

anecdotes.text: Diners single out the karaage as unusually fluffy and soft rather than the typical crisp-shelled style, a small signature alongside the ramen.
The iekei bowl is praised as 'looks thick but tastes clean,' a balance the shop aims for in its shoyu-tonkotsu broth.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: gcjapan confirms the 2021 opening as 中華そば 錦, the October 2023 rebrand to Menya Sawaki, the wide menu (iekei, Hakata, Kyoto shoyu, chuka soba and more), and the iekei bowl on Goto-made thick noodles with chashu, spinach, negi, nori and quail egg plus a karaage set; note (yk317ss) describes the soft karaage and the 'looks thick, tastes clean' iekei broth.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are shoyu-tonkotsu based; the soy-sauce tare used in this style of ramen standardly contains wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A small local ramen counter on Ichijoji's ramen street; little to no English, so a few Japanese phrases or pointing at the menu will smooth the visit.

kyr_goriki.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. This is a tantanmen specialist: wheat noodles (curly noodles from the noted maker Teikaku/棣鄂), a sesame-and-nut tare that in dandan noodles is typically built on wheat-based soy sauce and miso, and pork. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is advertised, and the standard rice-based finish is cooked together with the same sauce and toppings. A celiac diner cannot eat safely here.
kyr_goriki.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The bowls are built around ground pork and char siu, and there is no advertised vegan or vegetarian tantanmen. The shop highlights a vegetable-forward dumpling and some vegetable-topped variations, but the broth/sauce and proteins are meat-based throughout. No plant-based option is offered.
kyr_goriki.hours_raw: 11:30-15:00 / 17:30-21:00. Monday is lunch service only (no dinner). Closed for Obon (around Aug 16) and New Year holidays, plus occasional temporary closures.
kyr_goriki.notes: [Mom & Pop] Goriki opened in 2016, back when dedicated tantanmen counters were still a rarity in Kyoto, taking over a space that had previously run as a night-only spot before expanding into lunch service. It has since grown into a fixture among the city's dandan-noodle lovers.

chef_bio.background: Goriki opened in 2016, back when dedicated tantanmen counters were still a rarity in Kyoto, taking over a space that had previously run as a night-only spot before expanding into lunch service. It has since grown into a fixture among the city's dandan-noodle lovers.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen aims for a broth that is concentrated and smooth (noko de maroyaka) rather than punishingly hot, letting the Sichuan-pepper aroma and sesame depth carry the bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: The house specialty is its tantanmen built on a thick yet mellow sesame-and-nut sauce, balancing the numbing-and-spicy 'karashibi' character with nutty richness rather than chasing pure heat. The lineup runs from THE Tantanmen to a brothless (shirunashi) version, dipping-style tsukemen, the chili-heavy Karashibi, and a stamina version, plus seasonal limiteds.

anecdotes.text: Goriki's signature move is the shime finish: after you have worked through most of the noodles, the staff scrape the remaining meat and toppings into a bowl and cook it down with rice and a raw egg over the table's built-in burner, turning it into a fragrant, bibimbap-style 'second dish' whose egg mellows the lingering spice.
The brothless tantanmen uses curly noodles from the well-regarded Kyoto noodle maker Teikaku (棣鄂), tossed with minced meat, char siu, bean sprouts, scallions and nuts.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms the 2016 opening, the five tantanmen varieties (THE担々麺, 汁なし, つけ麺, カラシビ, スタミナ) plus seasonal limiteds, the spice-fragrant sesame sauce, the 汁なし bowl on Teikaku (棣鄂) noodles with minced meat, char siu, bean sprouts, scallions and nuts, and the tabletop-IH-burner rice-and-raw-egg bibimbap-style shime finish.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dandan-noodle tare is conventionally built on wheat-based soy sauce and miso; no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bowls are built around ground pork and char siu and share a meat-based sauce; no plant-based separation is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual neighborhood noodle counter with no indication of English support, so a little Japanese or pointing at the menu will smooth the visit.

kyr_marutan_ogawa.gf_detail: This is a tantanmen (dandan noodle) specialist. The bowls are built on wheat noodles (straight thin noodles from a noodle supplier) in a sesame/miso/pork-based spicy broth, which in this style virtually always contains wheat-based shoyu/miso tare. No gluten-free options or gluten-free preparation were found, and there is no indication of a dedicated fryer or any cross-contamination control. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_marutan_ogawa.vegan_detail: A meat-based tantanmen shop: bowls feature ground meat (挽肉) and the broth is built on a pork/sesame/miso base. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is advertised. Not suitable for vegans.
kyr_marutan_ogawa.notes: [Mom & Pop] Marutan Ogawa began life as a yatai-style operation, with the owner serving tantanmen from the garage/parking space of his own home in a quiet residential pocket of Katsura. A few years ago, after renovating the house, the food-cart setup was converted into a proper indoor shop o

chef_bio.background: Marutan Ogawa began life as a yatai-style operation, with the owner serving tantanmen from the garage/parking space of his own home in a quiet residential pocket of Katsura. A few years ago, after renovating the house, the food-cart setup was converted into a proper indoor shop on the same spot — but it has kept the intimate, handmade, hole-in-the-wall feel of its food-cart roots.
chef_bio.philosophy: A small, personal kitchen focused on doing one thing — tantanmen — well, in a casual, home-style setting that grew straight out of a neighborhood food cart.
chef_bio.specialty: Spicy 'uma-kara' (delicious-spicy) tantanmen. The miso tantanmen pairs a miso-and-sesame broth with ground meat, bamboo shoots, Chinese greens and bean sprouts over straight thin noodles; seasonal bowls include a chilled tantanmen served over ice and topped with kimchi and crunchy vegetables, and a brothless (shiru-nashi) version.

anecdotes.text: What started as the owner serving noodles out of his own home garage in food-cart style was turned into an indoor shop a few years ago when he renovated the house.

The shop sits in a residential neighborhood near Route 9 that you basically need a car to reach; regulars include students from the nearby Kyoto University Katsura campus, who are on friendly terms with the owner.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Tantanmen here is made with wheat noodles in a sesame/miso/pork-based broth; this style of tare is wheat-based, so the dish is not gluten-free and no GF handling is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth and toppings are meat-based (ground meat plus a pork/sesame/miso broth), so vegan diners cannot be accommodated.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run neighborhood tantanmen counter on a residential street; expect a Japanese-only experience and a warm, regulars-driven atmosphere, so a few words of Japanese or a translation app will help.

kyr_kyogame.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The lunch bowls are standard wheat ramen noodles, and the kitchen is built around motsunabe with chicken/garlic broths and soy-based seasonings — no gluten-free noodles, dedicated handling, or allergen accommodation is advertised. Cross-contamination with wheat is effectively guaranteed in a shared ramen and hotpot kitchen.
kyr_kyogame.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly destination. The house identity is beef offal (motsu) and the ramen leans on offal, clams, duck, and chicken broth; even the cabbage-heavy "hormone ramen" is built on meat/animal stock. No plant-based ramen or vegan set is offered.
kyr_kyogame.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-14:00 (L.O. 13:30); Dinner 17:00-23:30 (L.O. 23:00). Wed & Thu dinner only (no lunch). Ramen is a lunch-only offering.
kyr_kyogame.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kyogame occupies a restored Kyoto machiya townhouse along Imadegawa-dori, a short walk from Demachiyanagi. The owner, known affectionately as Kame-san, runs it less like a polished restaurant and more like a friend's home — courtyard garden, tatami rooms where you can stretch you

chef_bio.background: Kyogame occupies a restored Kyoto machiya townhouse along Imadegawa-dori, a short walk from Demachiyanagi. The owner, known affectionately as Kame-san, runs it less like a polished restaurant and more like a friend's home — courtyard garden, tatami rooms where you can stretch your legs, and the unhurried feel of an old popular izakaya.
chef_bio.philosophy: Generous, unfussy, and deliberately affordable — the lunch bowls are priced so that students and regulars can come often, in a room meant to feel like dropping by someone's house rather than dining out.
chef_bio.specialty: The house centerpiece is a hearty garlic motsunabe: select beef offal in a quality chicken-bone broth, offered in white-miso, soy, or salt versions, alongside other izakaya sides. At lunch the kitchen turns to ramen — the signature being a cabbage-piled hormone (offal) ramen, alongside a light clam (asari) salt bowl and, in summer, a cold duck-and-vegetable bowl, all served with a generous 1.5 portions of noodles.

anecdotes.text: A writer who once worked at a related shop describes the owner Kame-san as encouraging and supportive of his staff's ambitions, the kind of proprietor people stay loyal to.
The cabbage-heavy hormone ramen and the affordable lunch sets are pitched as a welcome deal for students.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi and genjitsutouhi confirm a machiya motsunabe-ya on Imadegawa-dori run by 'Kame-san': garlic motsunabe (white-miso/soy/salt, ~14 pieces offal per 2-serving order), a spicy cabbage-piled hormone ramen (850 yen), clam salt and cold-duck lunch bowls with 1.5 noodle portions; official kamerin.jp confirms the garlic motsunabe in chicken broth.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Lunch ramen uses standard wheat noodles and shares a kitchen with motsunabe and fried sides, so wheat cross-contact is unavoidable; no gluten-free option is mentioned anywhere.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Broths and seasonings are soy- and miso-based (a soy-shoyu motsunabe option is offered), which in Japan normally means wheat-containing soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Even the vegetable-forward cabbage 'hormone ramen' is built on beef offal and animal-based broth; all advertised bowls contain meat, clams, duck, or chicken stock.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual neighborhood machiya izakaya where ordering and any dietary questions will go most smoothly in Japanese; an English menu is not advertised.

kyr_raamen_miyako_gion_honte.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop. The bowls use the house 低温熟成細麺 (low-temperature aged thin wheat noodles), a paitan broth built on chicken and vegetables, and tare options including soy (醤油, typically wheat-based) and miso, finished with pork chashu. There is no gluten-free menu, no published allergen handling, and no indication of a dedicated gluten-free preparation area. Not safe for celiac diners; cross-contamination from shared noodle water and broth is effectively unavoidable. Confirm directly with the shop if you must, but treat as not gluten-free.
kyr_raamen_miyako_gion_honte.vegan_detail: The signature broth is a chicken-and-vegetable paitan (鶏白湯) and bowls come standard with pork chashu, egg, and other animal toppings; the broth itself is animal-based. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen offering noted on any source. Not suitable for vegans.
kyr_raamen_miyako_gion_honte.hours_raw: Mon–Thu & Sun 11:00–22:00 (last order 21:30) / Fri & Sat 11:00–03:00 next day (last order 02:30 next day). Note: hours may be temporarily changed for the time being (please confirm). No regular closing days.
kyr_raamen_miyako_gion_honte.notes: [Mom & Pop] The Gion honten is the flagship of the Raamen Miyako (らぁ～めん京) group, which has since grown to additional locations including Hyogo and Shiga, and runs a much-praised stall in Kyoto Station's Kyoto Ramen Koji (ramen alley), where it opened in June 2023.

roles: Gion flagship of a small Kyoto-based group
chef_bio.origin: Gion, Higashiyama — the main shop sits just north of Yasaka Shrine in the heart of Kyoto's old geisha district.
chef_bio.background: The Gion honten is the flagship of the Raamen Miyako (らぁ～めん京) group, which has since grown to additional locations including Hyogo and Shiga, and runs a much-praised stall in Kyoto Station's Kyoto Ramen Koji (ramen alley), which opened in June 2023.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen states it uses only carefully selected ingredients and does meticulous prep every day, slowly drawing chicken umami and vegetable sweetness into a broth that is rich yet light enough to drink to the bottom.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the 'ぎをん白湯' (Gion paitan) — a chicken-and-vegetable white broth, slightly enriched with back-fat for body without heaviness, paired with the shop's own low-temperature aged thin noodles. The 'みやこらぁ～めん' tops it with a wide slice of chashu, soft egg, scallion and menma.

anecdotes.text: The broth is described as having solid body from chicken and a touch of back-fat, yet staying savory rather than heavy — 'finished enough to drink down as the close of a meal.'
The shop developed its own 'low-temperature aged thin noodles' (低温熟成細麺) prized for a chewy-yet-smooth texture that clings to the Gion paitan broth.
Its side-dish fried rice uses rice from the noted Kyoto brand Hachidaime Gihey, and the group's bowl was a top seller at Kyoto Station's ramen alley.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Bowls are built on house wheat thin noodles boiled in shared water, with soy/miso tare and chicken-vegetable broth; no gluten-free preparation is offered.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Soy (醤油) is one of the standard tare options; ordinary Japanese shoyu contains wheat, and no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The base broth is animal (chicken paitan) and bowls include pork chashu and egg; no vegan option is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy walk-in ramen counter beside Yasaka Shrine in Gion; tourists are common, but a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu go a long way, and it is cash-only.

kyr_ramen_mentaiken.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle ramen and town-Chinese shop. The bowls are built on medium-thick wheat ramen noodles in a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare over an animal-based broth, plus fried rice and other Chinese dishes — all standard sources of gluten. Soy-sauce tare is essentially always wheat-containing, and there is no indication of any gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs; anyone strictly gluten-free should avoid.
kyr_ramen_mentaiken.vegan_detail: The core menu is built on an animal-based (pork/meat) dashi broth with pork chashu toppings, and the shop is a meat-forward town-Chinese ramen place. No vegan or vegetable-broth ramen is indicated. Not a vegan-friendly option.
kyr_ramen_mentaiken.notes: [Mom & Pop] Mentaiken is a small neighborhood 'machi-chuka' (town-Chinese) ramen shop in central Kyoto, the kind of unpretentious local counter where regulars come for a comforting bowl. It is run essentially as a near one-person operation, with the owner-chef handling most of the cooking.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Shimogyo ward, near the Shijo-Horikawa intersection and Omiya Station)
chef_bio.background: Mentaiken is a small neighborhood 'machi-chuka' (town-Chinese) ramen shop in central Kyoto, the kind of unpretentious local counter where regulars come for a comforting bowl. It is run essentially as a near one-person operation, with the owner-chef handling most of the cooking.
chef_bio.philosophy: In-store signage sums up the aim as making 'memorable ramen that stays in your heart' — a straightforward, regulars-first approach to a satisfying everyday bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the ginger ramen (生姜ラーメン / 生姜中華そば): an animal-based broth seasoned with soy-sauce tare and finished with a generous amount of freshly grated ginger, so that a soup which looks mild actually delivers a real punch of ginger warmth. It is served with medium-thick, low-hydration straight noodles that have a chewy bite (extra-firm available on request) and sliced pork chashu with chopped green onion. The shop also serves a 'Kyoto black' deep-soy-sauce ramen, ramen-and-fried-rice sets, spicy mala noodles, and negi-chashu.

anecdotes.text: The shop expanded its set options with a 'nami-nami set' (regular ramen plus regular fried rice) so customers could finally order full-size portions of both together, rather than only the smaller combinations offered before.
The ginger ramen is described as especially popular with women, its grated-ginger soup giving a flavor punch that belies the broth's mild appearance.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All ramen is built on wheat noodles and a soy-sauce tare, and the kitchen also makes fried rice and Chinese dishes, so shared cookware and gluten exposure throughout are inherent.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen, including a 'Kyoto black' deep-soy-sauce style; soy-sauce tare for ramen is essentially always wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is animal-based dashi with pork chashu; no vegan/vegetable-broth option is indicated.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locals' town-Chinese ramen counter where ordering in basic Japanese (or by pointing at the menu) is expected; no English service indicated.

kyr_ramen_sugichiyo.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation. This is a classic Kyoto-style ramen shop: the noodles are wheat, the tare (seasoning) is soy-sauce based (typically wheat-containing shoyu), and the broth is a pork-bone and chicken soy-sauce base. There is no published allergen handling, no gluten-free noodle option, and no dedicated prep area. A celiac diner cannot eat safely here.
kyr_ramen_sugichiyo.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. Every bowl is built on an animal broth (pork bone / chicken bones) and topped with chashu (braised pork). The menu is limited to ramen, chashu ramen, rice and green onion add-ons; there is no plant-based broth or vegetable ramen.
kyr_ramen_sugichiyo.hours_raw: Weekdays 11:30-15:00 / 17:00-23:00; Saturdays & holidays roughly 11:30-23:00; Sunday until 22:30. Sources vary on exact midday break and on a possible Monday closure — confirm locally before a special trip.
kyr_ramen_sugichiyo.notes: [Mom & Pop] Sugichiyo is the revival of a legendary Kyoto ramen shop. The original opened in 1999 in the Uzumasa area of western Kyoto and drew daily lines for roughly a decade before it closed at the end of 2009 — reportedly because the crowds it attracted had become difficult to sustain. A

chef_bio.background: Sugichiyo is the revival of a legendary Kyoto ramen shop. The original opened in 1999 in the Uzumasa area of western Kyoto and drew daily lines for roughly a decade before it closed at the end of 2009 — reportedly because the crowds it attracted had become difficult to sustain. After about twelve years dormant, the name returned in June 2021 in a renovated spot down a Takase River alley just west of Shijo-Kawaramachi, in the heart of central Kyoto's nightlife district. The current team is said to have inherited the complete original recipe directly from the founder.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithfully carry forward a beloved recipe rather than reinvent it — a nostalgic, unpretentious bowl served with quiet, courteous hospitality instead of the high-intensity style of many modern ramen shops.
chef_bio.specialty: Chashu ramen — the bowl that built the shop's reputation. The pork-bone soy-sauce broth carries the deep richness of Kyoto-style ramen with a thin veil of back fat on top, yet drinks lighter and cleaner than its color suggests; the soy tare is comparatively restrained, letting the broth's umami lead. It comes over low-hydration straight thin noodles, finished with melt-tender homemade chashu (made by the founder's original slow-braise method), menma, nori and green onion. A touch of chili pepper is added by default, giving a gentle heat from the first sip.

anecdotes.text: Sugichiyo's flavor was famous enough that Nissin Foods produced it as a cup-noodle product — a rare nod from a major manufacturer.
The original shop closed in 2009 reportedly because of complaints about the long lines it generated, and was reborn in 2021 at Shijo-Kawaramachi.
The current operators say they received the full original recipe from the founder 'without any leaks,' aiming to reproduce the legendary taste exactly.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare base; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, and the shop publishes no gluten-free or wheat-free tare.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls use animal broth (pork bone / chicken) and pork chashu; no separate vegetable stock or vegan prep is mentioned.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, classic counter ramen shop where ordering is straightforward but staff and menu are Japanese; a little Japanese or pointing goes a long way.

kyr_torisoba_223_tsutsumi.gf_detail: This is a salt ramen specialist built on wheat noodles (curly noodles supplied by Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teigaku/麺屋棣鄂), so the core dish is not gluten-free. The broth is chicken-based and the seasoning is a salt (shio) tare rather than a wheat-shoyu tare, which avoids one common wheat source, but the noodles themselves contain wheat and there is no indication of a gluten-free noodle option, dedicated prep, or celiac-level cross-contamination control. Not suitable for celiac diners; a wheat-allergic diner should treat it as off-limits unless they confirm directly.
kyr_torisoba_223_tsutsumi.vegan_detail: Every bowl is built on a chicken broth (described as roughly 99% chicken stock, using Tanba black chicken bones and Kyoto red-breed chicken) with chicken chashu and egg toppings. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu and the entire concept is animal-based, so it does not work for vegans.
kyr_torisoba_223_tsutsumi.hours_raw: Tue–Sun 08:00–15:00; additional evening service Sunday 18:00–21:00; closed Mondays. May close early when the day's soup stock runs out.
kyr_torisoba_223_tsutsumi.notes: [Mom & Pop] Torisoba 223 is a one-man salt-ramen specialist that opened in 2020 in a renovated storefront just south of the Kyoto Botanical Garden, a short walk from Kitaoji. The shop's odd name is a play on the owner's surname: 2-2-3 reads as 'tsu-tsu-mi' (Tsutsumi).

chef_bio.background: Torisoba 223 is a one-man salt-ramen specialist (seven counter seats) that opened in 2020 in a renovated storefront just south of the Kyoto Botanical Garden, a short walk from Kitaoji. The shop's odd name is a play on the owner's surname: 2-2-3 reads as 'tsu-tsu-mi' (Tsutsumi).
chef_bio.philosophy: Tsutsumi openly states his goal is to be 'No.1 in salt ramen.' He is a certified salt sommelier and blends four salts (including Andes rock salt and a sea salt) to build a smooth, layered savoriness rather than a sharp saltiness, and avoids chemical seasonings.
chef_bio.specialty: An unusually delicate, additive-free (無化調) salt ramen built on a clear chicken broth made from Tanba black-chicken bones and Kyoto red-breed chicken meat, finished with fragrant chicken oil and paired with curly wheat noodles from Kyoto maker Menya Teigaku. Bowls carry playful Italian-flavored names (e.g. 'Milano no Asahi'), and a table-side olive/special sauce lets diners shift the flavor mid-bowl.

anecdotes.text: The shop name 223 is read 'Tsutsumi' after the owner's surname.
The owner is a certified salt sommelier who blends four kinds of salt (including Andes rock salt) to design the broth's seasoning.
It opens early at 8:00 for ramen-as-breakfast and is treated as a morning-ramen spot in Kyoto.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are seasoned with a salt (shio) tare rather than a soy-sauce tare, so wheat soy sauce is not the primary seasoning; however this is not a substitute for being gluten-free because the noodles are wheat.

positives.text: No chemical seasonings are used (無化調); the broth is a clear chicken stock.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 7-seat counter shop run by one owner where Japanese is the working language; basic Japanese or a translation app helps, and ordering is straightforward once seated.

kyr_menya_shinano.gf_detail: Not gluten-free and not suitable for celiacs. This is a classic ramen shop: wheat noodles served in a chicken paitan or fish-soy broth finished with soy-sauce-based tare (Japanese soy sauce / white soy sauce, both wheat-containing). Tsukemen (dipping noodles) is also wheat. No gluten-free menu, no documented allergen accommodation.
kyr_menya_shinano.vegan_detail: No vegan options. The signature bowls are built on a chicken-based broth (whole chicken and chicken bones), with chashu, flavored egg, and other animal toppings; the fish-soy ramen uses fish-flake dashi. Nothing on the menu is plant-based.
kyr_menya_shinano.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 / 17:00-20:30 (L.O. 20:00). Wednesday and Sunday evenings closed (calendar-dependent). Lunch served daily.
kyr_menya_shinano.notes: [Mom & Pop] 麺屋 しな埜 began life in February 2020 as TETSUpan Style+ しな埜, a yakisoba specialty shop, before reinventing itself as a ramen-focused restaurant in March 2021 with chicken paitan as its new signature. A further full renovation in September 2024 refreshed the menu and the space. It s

chef_bio.background: 麺屋 しな埜 began life in February 2020 as TETSUpan Style+ しな埜, a yakisoba specialty shop, before reinventing itself as a ramen-focused restaurant in March 2021 with chicken paitan as its new signature. A further full renovation in September 2024 refreshed the menu and the space. It sits, almost unexpectedly, in a quiet residential pocket of Matsugasaki near the ward office, drawing queues to a converted white single-family house with sunlit counter seating and a breezy balcony area.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than the heavier bowls Kyoto is often known for, the shop leans on technique and restraint, using the whipped-foam broth and carefully drawn dashi to keep flavors smooth and the finish clean.
chef_bio.specialty: The house bowl is the 泡白湯 (awa paitan): a broth simmered from whole chicken and chicken bones, then whipped into a creamy, mousse-like foam and finished with a Japanese-style soy tare for a surprisingly clean, light aftertaste. The kitchen also offers a chicken paitan, a fish-soy (gyokai-shoyu) ramen built on a low-temperature dashi of three fish flakes, kombu and dried shiitake with chicken oil, and a rich fish-pork tsukemen.

anecdotes.text: The shop is a renovated white house with second-floor counter seating and a beach-house-style balcony, and it has become a quiet favorite among neighbors and nearby university students who line up despite the out-of-the-way residential location.

Visitors note the broth's creamy, foamed texture is achieved with an espuma-style whipping technique, accented with coarse black pepper, giving a lighter, less-salty profile than typical for the city.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi and osumituki confirm the timeline (yakisoba TETSUpan Style+ しな埜 opened 16 Feb 2020, ramen pivot 22 Mar 2021, full renovation 1 Sept 2024), the Matsugasaki white-house/balcony setting, the 泡白湯 whipped-foam chicken broth with Japanese soy tare, a three-fish/kombu/shiitake gyokai-shoyu, and a pork-fish tsukemen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broths are finished with soy-sauce-based tare (Japanese soy sauce / white soy sauce), which is wheat-containing, and the noodles are wheat ramen noodles.

cultural_comfort.note: A small residential-neighborhood ramen shop with friendly, attentive staff; ordering is straightforward but expect a Japanese-only experience, so a little Japanese or a translation app helps.

kyr_chuka_soba_akky.gf_detail: This is a pork-broth chuka soba (ramen) shop built around wheat noodles and a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, both of which contain wheat. The signature bowls are a back-fat "black" soy ramen and a back-fat tonkotsu-shoyu ramen. There is no published gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no statement about gluten handling. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner cannot safely eat the core menu here.
kyr_chuka_soba_akky.vegan_detail: The shop's entire identity is a 100% pork broth ("豚100％のスープ"), with back fat, chashu pork, and pork-bone soy bases across every bowl. There are no vegetarian or vegan ramen options on the published menu and no plant-based broth offered.
kyr_chuka_soba_akky.hours_raw: Mon 10:30–14:30; Tue closed; Wed–Fri 10:30–14:30 and 17:00–20:30; Sat 10:30–14:30; Sun 08:00–14:30. Note: evening service is suspended for the time being, so currently lunch-only daytime hours apply.
kyr_chuka_soba_akky.notes: [Mom & Pop] Akky is a Kyoto native who became well known across the city's ramen scene as a food creator, running the YouTube channel 'Mr.京都アッキーのぶらり飲食店巡り' along with TikTok, Instagram and X, where he tirelessly reviewed Kyoto ramen shops. Before opening this place he spent about two years ru

chef_bio.chef_name: Mr.京都アッキー (Mr. Kyoto Akky)
chef_bio.background: Akky is a Kyoto native who became well known across the city's ramen scene as a food creator, running the YouTube channel 'Mr.京都アッキーのぶらり飲食店巡り' along with TikTok, Instagram and X, where he tirelessly reviewed Kyoto ramen shops. Before opening this place he spent about two years running a ramen shop on borrowed premises in Fushimi, learning the craft hands-on, before launching his own standalone shop in Shimogamo in August 2025.
chef_bio.philosophy: Akky builds everything on a 100% pork broth simmered carefully from early morning, drawing out the depth of pork bone and pork meat while keeping the finish clean rather than heavy. He describes the goal as a soup that is rich yet sharp ('コクがありながらもキレのある'), an everyday bowl that people of all ages can enjoy.
chef_bio.specialty: His signature is the 'Triple GO' back-fat black chuka soba (トリプルGO 背脂ブラック中華そば) - a dark soy-and-back-fat bowl in the classic Kyoto 'black' style - alongside a back-fat tonkotsu-shoyu chuka soba.

anecdotes.text: His shop is a personal homage to the three Kyoto ramen styles he loves most, blending the black broth of Shinpukusaikan, the pork-bone style of Dai-ichi Asahi, and the back-fat-forward approach of Masutani into one bowl of what he himself most wants to eat.
Among Kyoto ramen fans he is described as someone 'there isn't a single ramen lover in Kyoto who doesn't know' - a familiar face who turned his fandom into his own shop.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are built on a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, including a dark-soy 'black' version; standard Japanese shoyu is brewed with wheat.
soy_sauce_wheat.source_wording: Own menu page, 背脂ブラック: 「完全オリジナルで厳選したたまり醤油に、じっくり仕込んだチャーシューの旨みを移した特製醤油を重ね合わせた、コク深い黒いスープが特徴の京都ラーメンです。」 Header line: 「アッキー流 中華そば — たまり醤油を使ったコクと旨みあるこだわりの味」

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every broth is a 100% pork soup with back fat and pork toppings, so there is unavoidable animal content throughout the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny counter-only neighborhood ramen shop run by a local owner; expect Japanese-only service and a quick, casual lunch flow, so a little Japanese or a translation app helps.

kyr_ambitious_hana.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. This is a tsukemen specialist: the signature noodles are wheat-based (with tapioca flour blended in, but still wheat), and the rich pork-and-fish (豚骨魚介) dipping broth is built on wheat-containing shoyu/miso tare — the spicy "辛醤つけめん" is miso-based. There is no mention anywhere of gluten-free options, a separate fryer, or any celiac accommodation. A celiac diner cannot eat safely here.
kyr_ambitious_hana.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The core product is a thick pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) dipping broth, and add-ons include raw egg; the menu centers on animal-based tsukemen and ramen with no plant-based broth or noodle option mentioned. No vegan offering is advertised.
kyr_ambitious_hana.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, independent tsukemen specialist tucked into the Shimogamo neighborhood of Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, just west of where Shimogamo-hondori meets Kitaoji. It has built a loyal following among nearby students and locals as a destination for serious, rich dipping noodles.

chef_bio.background: A small, independent tsukemen specialist tucked into the Shimogamo neighborhood of Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, just west of where Shimogamo-hondori meets Kitaoji. It has built a loyal following among nearby students and locals as a destination for serious, rich dipping noodles.
chef_bio.philosophy: Generous and unfussy — large portions (up to 400g) are offered at the same price as a regular serving, and diners customize noodle thickness and garlic to taste.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a thick, rich pork-bone-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) tsukemen with a pronounced seafood depth, served with chewy noodles made by blending tapioca flour into the dough. Its calling card is the dipping broth served bubbling in a clay/stone pot (土鍋・石鍋): the pot is brought to a boil and its heat retention keeps the tsukejiru piping hot from the first bite to the last.

anecdotes.text: The defining feature is the screaming-hot dipping broth: it is brought to the table in a clay/stone pot kept at a rolling boil, so the tsukejiru stays piping hot (アツアツ) right to the end of the meal instead of cooling off the way ordinary tsukemen broth does.

The noodles are made with tapioca flour worked into the dough for a distinctive chew, and the broth is a thick pork-and-seafood (豚骨魚介) style; portions run up to 400g at the same price, making it a favorite of the area's students.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dipping broth is a thick pork-bone-and-seafood tare-based tsukejiru, and the spicy version is miso-based (辛醤つけめん); these standard ramen/tsukemen seasonings contain wheat-based soy/miso.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, ticket-machine ramen counter popular with local students; minimal English and a fast-paced lunch flow, so a little Japanese (or pointing at the machine) goes a long way.

kyr_tanpopo.gf_detail: This is a classic Kyoto pork-and-chicken-bone soy ramen shop. The bowl is built on wheat noodles with a soy-sauce tare and a pork/chicken-bone broth enriched with pork back-fat, so it is not celiac-safe. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, a gluten-free tare, or any allergen accommodation, and the kitchen is a single shared ramen line. A celiac diner should treat this as off-limits; even the signature chili topping and the soy-and-pepper fried rice involve wheat-based seasoning.
kyr_tanpopo.vegan_detail: The entire menu centers on a long-simmered pork-bone and chicken-bone broth finished with pork back-fat, and the bowls come with pork chashu and menma; the fried rice is cooked with pork and egg-style seasoning. There is no plant-based broth or vegan option here. A vegan diner has nothing to eat at this shop. The chili topping can be omitted on request, but that does not change the animal-based broth.
kyr_tanpopo.notes: [Mom & Pop] Tanpopo is a Kyoto ramen institution out near the western end of Kitayama-dori, in the Murasakino/Kinugasa pocket toward Kinkaku-ji. Sources describe it as a shop loved by Kyoto residents for around 70 years, with a founding commonly cited as 1947, making it one of the old-guard

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, in the Kita-ku Murasakino area near Bukkyo University and Kitayama-dori.
chef_bio.background: Tanpopo is a Kyoto ramen institution out near the western end of Kitayama-dori, in the Murasakino/Kinugasa pocket toward Kinkaku-ji. Sources describe it as a shop loved by Kyoto residents for around 70 years, with a founding commonly cited as 1947, making it one of the old-guard shops that carry the history of Kyoto-style ramen into the present.
chef_bio.philosophy: A deceptively dramatic, comforting bowl: the chili makes a strong first impression, but the flavor underneath is the deep, fatty, soy-rich savoriness of classic Kyoto ramen. The shop leans into a warm, unpretentious neighborhood feel rather than polish.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a Kyoto back-fat soy-sauce ramen famous for a topping of red chili spread across the entire surface, so the bowl arrives looking fiery red. The broth is a rich pork-bone soup simmered for many hours and finished with sweet pork back-fat; the chili sits on top rather than being cooked into the soup, so the actual heat is mild-to-moderate rather than punishing. Medium noodles, pork-belly chashu that turns crumbly-tender, green onion and menma round it out. The other house favorite is an old-fashioned, hearty fried rice (yakimeshi) with pork and onion, popular as a ramen-and-fried-rice set.

anecdotes.text: The bowl is famous for being blanketed in red chili so it looks intensely spicy, but because the chili is sprinkled on top rather than mixed into the broth it is only mildly spicy, and you can order it with the chili left off entirely while the soup stays delicious on its own.

Described as loved by Kyoto people for about 70 years and as a legend shop conveying the history of Kyoto ramen, with a retro exterior, humorous handwritten signs around the room, and a regular crowd of locals rather than tourists.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are cooked in shared boiling water on a single ramen line, so any bowl carries gluten and cross-contact risk; no gluten-free preparation is mentioned anywhere.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop is a Kyoto soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen specialist; the tare is a standard soy-based seasoning, which in this style is wheat-containing soy sauce, with no gluten-free alternative noted.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every bowl is built on a multi-hour pork-bone and chicken-bone broth finished with pork back-fat and topped with pork chashu, so the cooking line is fundamentally animal-based with no separate vegan preparation.

positives.text: The signature chili topping can be omitted on request, since it is sprinkled on top rather than cooked into the broth.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills, cash-only neighborhood ramen counter run for locals with no English service, so come prepared to point at the menu and keep it simple.

kyr_ramen_yu.gf_detail: This is a classic Kyoto-style soy-sauce ramen shop. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles, a wheat-based shoyu tare, and a pork-driven broth — none of which is gluten-free, and there is no indication of any GF accommodation. Not suitable for celiacs. The only other listed item is gyoza (wheat wrappers). Assume cross-contamination throughout a single shared kitchen.
kyr_ramen_yu.vegan_detail: The menu is limited to shoyu and miso ramen built on a pork-based (旭系) broth with chashu pork, plus gyoza. There are no vegan or vegetarian options and no plant-based broth. Not a vegan-friendly destination.
kyr_ramen_yu.hours_raw: 11:00–19:00. Closed Mondays and Thursdays. (One listing notes possible irregular Sunday closures; confirm before a Sunday visit.)
kyr_ramen_yu.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, time-worn ramen counter tucked into the Shichijo-Omiya block near Umekoji Park and Umekoji-Kyoto-Nishi Station. It belongs to Kyoto's beloved 'Akira-kei' (旭系) lineage — the nostalgic Kyoto soy-sauce ramen tradition associated with the famous Daiichi-Asahi. The owner is s

chef_bio.origin: 京都市下京区 七条大宮・梅小路
chef_bio.background: A small, time-worn ramen counter tucked into the Shichijo-Omiya block near Umekoji Park and Umekoji-Kyoto-Nishi Station. It belongs to Kyoto's beloved 'Akira-kei' (旭系) lineage — the nostalgic Kyoto soy-sauce ramen tradition associated with the famous Daiichi-Asahi. The owner is said to have trained at a shop called Taiki before opening his own counter, and the place has the lived-in, slightly aged storefront of a long-standing local fixture.
chef_bio.philosophy: A taciturn owner with a quiet, single-minded devotion to ramen — no frills, no trend-chasing, just an honest bowl in the old Kyoto idiom. Regulars describe the flavor as deeply nostalgic, evoking long-gone neighborhood shops.
chef_bio.specialty: Kyoto-style shoyu ramen — a clear, pork-forward broth where the pig's umami and richness are balanced against a restrained soy edge, served over soft medium-thick straight noodles that soak up the broth, finished with loin chashu, a generous pile of scallions and bean sprouts. A miso version and a notably good spicy miso are also offered.

anecdotes.text: Regulars often pitch it as the under-the-radar alternative to the famous station-side Daiichi-Asahi: its broth is described as sitting between the intensity of Daiichi-Asahi and Ganso Ramen Taiee, refreshing yet rich.
The clientele skews to local regulars, salarymen, and older customers rather than a young crowd — a true neighborhood ramen stop.

One Kyoto food guide notes the bowl tastes remarkably close to a now-defunct beloved shop ('Big Ramen') near the Higashino (東野) intersection in Yamashina, and singles out the abundant loin chashu and excellent spicy miso.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: priceless-kyoto confirms the 旭系 lineage, the owner having trained at 'Taiki', a 12-seat counter of regulars/salarymen/older locals, and a broth judged between Daiichi-Asahi and Ganso Ramen Taiee; kyoto-gourmet.info likens the taste to a defunct shop ('Big Ramen') near the Higashino intersection in Yamashina and praises the loin chashu and spicy miso.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single small counter kitchen built entirely around wheat ramen noodles, wheat-based shoyu tare, and gyoza; no separation possible and no GF handling mentioned.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The defining flavor is a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which in a traditional Kyoto ramen shop is wheat-based; assume the broth/tare contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-based with chashu pork; no plant-based broth or vegan options, so vegan cross-contact is unavoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, old-school neighborhood counter shop frequented by taxi drivers, locals, and older regulars; a little basic Japanese and easygoing ramen-shop etiquette will go a long way, and English support should not be expected.

kyr_kyoichi_honten.gf_detail: This is a classic Showa-era Chinese-noodle diner. The signature dishes are wheat-noodle bowls — curry chuka soba and chuka soba — built on a chicken-and-secret-ingredient broth with curry roux (curry roux is itself wheat-thickened) plus, typically, wheat-based seasonings. There is no indication of any gluten-free accommodation, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiac diners; assume wheat throughout.
kyr_kyoichi_honten.vegan_detail: A meat-and-broth-centered old-style shokudo: the broth is chicken-bone based, the curry chuka is finished with braised wagyu beef, and other mains include katsudon. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered, and there is no sign of plant-based broth or accommodation. The dessert menu (zenzai, parfaits) is a legacy of the shop's origins as a sweet-bean (zenzai) shop but is not a vegan offering.
kyr_kyoichi_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] Founded in 1948 (Showa 23) at Shijo-Omiya, Kyoichi Honten has anchored the same corner for over 75 years. The shop began life as a zenzai (sweet red-bean) shop before becoming the bustling everyday diner it is today; the current building was rebuilt in 1976 but keeps its retro, t

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1948 (Showa 23) at Shijo-Omiya, Kyoichi Honten has anchored the same corner for over 75 years. The shop began life as a zenzai (sweet red-bean) shop before becoming the bustling everyday diner it is today; the current building was rebuilt in 1976 but keeps its retro, time-capsule feel. It is run by the Miyazaki family, with a hands-on female proprietor who happily steers customers toward her favorite pairings.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's long-standing motto is 'umai, hayai, yasui' — delicious, fast, and cheap — the creed of a true neighborhood diner serving locals, laborers and students alike.
chef_bio.specialty: Curry chuka soba (カレー中華) — Chinese wheat noodles buried under a glossy, spicy-sweet curry an (sauce) built from a long-simmered broth, multiple curry rouxs and secret seasonings, finished with braised wagyu beef for depth. The sauce is famously so generous it hides the noodles, and regulars drink it to the last drop. The clearer chicken-bone chuka soba is the other house favorite.

anecdotes.text: The shop's origins as a zenzai (sweet-bean) house live on in its unusually rich dessert lineup — zenzai and several parfaits — and the proprietor likes to suggest a cream dessert as the perfect cool-down after the spicy curry chuka.

The first-generation owner has remarked that along this stretch almost nothing has changed over the decades except themselves, the 'Hattori' coffee shop and the 'Yaoiso' fruit stand — a snapshot of how rooted the place is in the Shijo-Omiya streetscape.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dishes are wheat ramen noodles and a wheat-thickened curry roux sauce; gluten is unavoidable across the menu and no gluten-free handling is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is chicken-bone based and the signature curry chuka is finished with braised wagyu beef; the kitchen is built around animal stocks and meat, with no plant-based option noted.

cultural_comfort.note: A genuine local Showa-era diner where regulars, workers and students drop in — friendly and casual, but expect a Japanese-only ordering experience and no special accommodation, so a little Japanese (or pointing at the menu) goes a long way.

kyr_kanton_sankan_houhi.gf_detail: The headline dishes here are wheat-noodle plates — からしそば (mustard noodles) and 中華そば — served with house-made wheat noodles, and the kitchen leans on soy-based seasonings. Spring rolls, shumai, gyoza and fried noodles are all wheat-based as well. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodation, so this is not a safe choice for celiacs.
kyr_kanton_sankan_houhi.vegan_detail: This is a meat-and-seafood Chinese kitchen: the からしそば is built on chicken and shrimp, signature plates include からし鶏 (fried chicken), juicy pork shumai, and 酢豚 (sweet-and-sour pork), and broths/stir-fries rely on animal stock. No vegan menu or dedicated plant-based options are advertised; a vegan diner would have very little to eat.
kyr_kanton_sankan_houhi.hours_raw: 12:00-13:30, 17:00-20:00 (L.O. 19:50). Closed Tuesday and Wednesday; additional closures on the first and third Sunday-through-Wednesday of each month.
