roles: keeper of the 鳳舞系 からしそば tradition
chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (北区 紫野, on Horikawa near Kitaoji)
chef_bio.background: 鳳飛 is part of Kyoto's celebrated 鳳舞系 — the lineage of Chinese cooks who trained under master 高華吉, a Cantonese immigrant, at the legendary 鳳舞, which opened in 1967 and closed, much mourned, in 2009. 高 is remembered as a pioneer of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking who reworked Chinese food for local palates into something light, restrained and broth-forward — chicken- and kombu-based, with the oil and aggressive aromatics pulled back. Disciples who struck out on their own carried the 鳳 (phoenix) character of 鳳舞 into their own shop names; 鳳飛 is regarded as a direct heir of that tradition. (The lineage is sometimes traced further back through 高's earlier restaurants 第一樓 and 飛雲, and ultimately the Taisho-era 支那料理ハマムラ.)
chef_bio.philosophy: Gentle, unshowy, deeply Kyoto: minimal oil, no aggressive aromatics, prices kept low enough for neighbors to eat here regularly — Chinese food rebuilt as everyday comfort food rather than a feast.
chef_bio.specialty: からしそば — a noodle dish found essentially only at 鳳舞系 shops: boiled Chinese noodles tossed with mustard and bound in a lightly sweet, glossy chicken-and-kombu sauce, topped with chicken, shrimp, vegetables and scallion. The version here is known to run notably spicier than at sibling shops such as 鳳泉. The kitchen is also loved for its bamboo-shoot-packed spring rolls, shumai, からし鶏 (mustard-spiced fried chicken), and a light, never-greasy fried rice.

anecdotes.text: You order by writing the dish numbers on a paper slip; regulars line up before opening to claim the first seating in the short lunch window (roughly 12:00–13:30).
Diners describe the cooking as gentle and tender — light, lightly seasoned plates whose flavor deepens bite after bite, in keeping with the restrained Kyoto-Chinese style.
からしそば is a Kyoto noodle dish that exists essentially only within the 鳳舞 lineage of shops, of which 鳳飛 is a direct heir.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Brutus confirms からしそば exists only in Kyoto's 鳳舞系, whose 鳳舞 was founded in 1967 by Cantonese immigrant 高華吉; syu-mai.com traces the lineage (支那料理ハマムラ→第一樓/飛雲→鳳舞, closed 2009). The otaku-son blog and sakura394 confirm 鳳飛's Kitaoji-Horikawa location, paper-slip ordering, the ~90-minute lunch, its からしそば running spicier than 鳳泉's, and its gentle, light cooking as a direct 鳳舞 heir.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kyoto-Chinese noodle and stir-fry dishes here are seasoned with soy-based sauces, which in Japan are standard wheat-containing shoyu; assume gluten is present throughout.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Signature plates are chicken-, pork- and shrimp-based (からし鶏, pork shumai, 酢豚, and the chicken-and-shrimp からしそば), so animal ingredients run through the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-reservations neighborhood counter where you order by writing dish numbers on a slip of paper; little to no English, so a few Japanese phrases or a translation app will smooth the visit.

kyr_nabura.gf_detail: Standard ramen and tsukemen built on wheat noodles, and the mackerel karaage topping (tatsuta-age) is wheat-floured and fried; tare is almost certainly wheat-based shoyu. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is indicated. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_nabura.vegan_detail: The entire concept is built on a mackerel-and-kombu fish dashi (鯖と昆布の出汁) with a fried-mackerel topping, so the broth and signature dishes are fish-based and not vegan. The shop notably avoids animal/pork products and chemical seasonings (無化調), but it is a fish-broth specialist, not a vegan one.
kyr_nabura.hours_raw: 11:30-22:00 (L.O. 21:30), Tuesday-Sunday & holidays; closed Mondays (shifted to the following day if Monday is a holiday).
kyr_nabura.notes: [Mom & Pop] Nabura was opened on 8 August 2022 by a chef who spent about 35 years cooking traditional Kyoto-style Japanese cuisine (kappo/washoku) before turning that craft to ramen, in the Kitano Tenmangu / Kamishichiken area of Kamigyo-ku.

chef_bio.origin: The owner is a keen fishing enthusiast, and the shop name 'Nabura' refers to a school of small fish leaping at the sea surface as they are chased by larger fish - a fisherman's sign of opportunity and good fortune. The name was suggested by a fishing-loving staff member, and the staff wear Nabura T-shirts as a maritime good-luck symbol.
chef_bio.background: Nabura was opened on 8 August 2022 by a chef who spent about 35 years cooking traditional Kyoto-style Japanese cuisine (kappo/washoku) before turning that craft to ramen, in the Kitano Tenmangu / Kamishichiken area of Kamigyo-ku.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop deliberately keeps salt low and the broth clean and digestible so that anyone, regardless of age or gender, can eat it as an everyday meal - the owner says you can finish all the soup and still feel light afterward (誰でも美味しく食べられる).
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a completely additive-free (無化調) ramen whose broth is drawn only from kombu (kelp) and saba (mackerel) - no fish powder, no chemical seasoning - finished with a piece of fried mackerel tatsuta-age floating in the soup. Tsukemen is also a mainstay, including a rich seafood dipping broth.

anecdotes.text: The owner condensed 35 years of experience as a Kyoto Japanese-cuisine chef into this ramen, building the entire broth from just kombu and mackerel with no chemical seasonings.

The name 'Nabura' was chosen by a fishing-loving staff member after the term for a school of small fish breaking the surface while chased by bigger fish - an auspicious sign at sea - and staff wear Nabura T-shirts to carry that good-luck symbolism.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Leaf Kyoto confirms Nabura opened 8 Aug 2022 in the Kitano Tenmangu/Kamishichiken area of Kamigyo-ku; that its owner condensed ~35 years as a Kyoto washoku chef into an additive-free (無化調), deliberately low-salt broth drawn only from kombu and mackerel and finished with fried mackerel tatsuta-age; and that the name refers to a school of surfacing fish, suggested by a fishing-loving staffer, with staff wearing Nabura T-shirts.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen/tsukemen noodles are the base of every bowl and the kitchen handles wheat flour for the mackerel tatsuta-age topping, so flour and gluten are present throughout the cooking surfaces.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are fish-based (mackerel and kombu dashi); there is no vegan broth, so no vegan bowl is possible even setting cross-contact aside.

positives.text: Broth is completely additive-free (無化調) using only kombu and mackerel, with no chemical seasonings, fish powder, or animal/pork products - and the kitchen keeps salt low for a lighter, cleaner bowl.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, cash-only neighborhood counter ramen shop run by a veteran Japanese-cuisine chef; no reservations and likely Japanese-only service, so a guide or translation help is useful for ordering and asking about ingredients.

kyr_men_bistro_nakano.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. The ramen is built on wheat noodles, and the shoyu-based tare is almost certainly wheat-containing soy sauce; broths and creative dishes are not allergen-controlled. No celiac-safe accommodation is indicated on any source. Not suitable for strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_men_bistro_nakano.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly destination. Core bowls use chicken broth, dashi (bonito/fish-based 節), shoyu tare, and dairy-rich potage soups (cream-based), plus meat dishes (pork, chicken) and seafood-leaning items. No dedicated plant-based ramen is offered. A vegan could not reliably eat the signature dishes.
kyr_men_bistro_nakano.hours_raw: Tue–Sat 11:30–15:00 (L.O. 14:30) and 18:00–22:00 (L.O. 21:30); Sun & holidays 11:30–15:00 (L.O. 14:30) and 18:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:30); closed Mondays. (Some sources list lunch starting 12:00.)
kyr_men_bistro_nakano.notes: Men Bistro Nakano is run by a chef who came up through French kitchens and now pours that training into a bowl of noodles. The shop took over the space of a former French restaurant, and it kept that room's calm, grown-up feel rather than turning it into a typical narrow ramen co

chef_bio.origin: The space was previously a French restaurant, and it was opened by someone who had run a French establishment — so the bistro atmosphere is not a gimmick but the literal history of the room.
chef_bio.background: Men Bistro Nakano is run by a chef who came up through French kitchens and now pours that training into a bowl of noodles. The shop took over the space of a former French restaurant, and it kept that room's calm, grown-up feel rather than turning it into a typical narrow ramen counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: The guiding idea is a genuine fusion of French, Japanese, and ramen — treating a bowl of ramen with the same care, plating, and finish as a bistro plate. You can pair it with a glass of wine, start with small plates like ratatouille or roasted chicken, and end with a little dessert, which is almost unheard of at a ramen shop.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen builds broths that nod to Japanese cooking — using katsuobushi-style dashi (節) — and finishes them with French herbs and technique. The white and black shoyu bowls anchor the regular menu alongside a tripe-and-tomato ramen and a spicy mazesoba, while seasonal creamed 'potage' noodles (corn, new-onion, edamame, spinach, vichyssoise) rotate through and have become the shop's signature draw. The flavored soft-boiled egg is singled out by regulars as one of the best they've had.

anecdotes.text: Water is served in wine bottles, and the room is so elegant that one writer joked it could go back to being a French or Western restaurant tomorrow — it is notably welcoming even for a solo diner, unusual for a ramen shop.
It is described as a rare 'ramen shop where you can drink wine,' with glasses from around 500 yen and sparkling by the glass, in a space far roomier than a classic ramen counter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site (menbistronakano.net) states the shop is run by a former French chef offering a fusion of French, Japanese and ramen, with seasonal potage noodles, à la carte plates, wine and dessert. kyoto-gourmet confirms the former-French-restaurant space, water served in wine bottles, a solo-friendly elegant room, the black/white shoyu, tripe-tomato ramen and mazesoba, and singles out the soft-boiled egg. kyotopi confirms wine by the glass (~500 yen, sparkling ~800) and the roomy, non-counter layout.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature bowls are white and black shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen, and shoyu tare in Japan is virtually always made with wheat-containing soy sauce; treat the tare as a wheat source.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths lean on chicken stock and Japanese fish dashi (節), and several signature noodles are cream/dairy-based potages, so vegan cross-contact is inherent to the kitchen, not just incidental.

positives.text: Table-only seating in a calm, bistro-style room with small plates and wine makes for an easy, unhurried meal, though the menu itself is not built around dietary restrictions.

cultural_comfort.note: An unusually relaxed, refined ramen room with table seating and an open, bistro-like feel, so a foreign visitor can settle in comfortably; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu go a long way.

kyr_shinuchi_eitaro.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The core menu is wheat: the signature yuzu ramen uses wheat noodles (a low-hydration, low-kansui country-style noodle developed with a noodle maker), and the shop is also a hand-pulled Sanuki udon house, so wheat flour is heavily used throughout the kitchen. The tare/broth is built on soy sauce infused with the udon-shop dashi, and ordinary Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and high airborne-flour and shared-water cross-contamination risk from on-site noodle making. Anyone with celiac disease should avoid; a wheat-allergic diner should not eat here.
kyr_shinuchi_eitaro.vegan_detail: Not vegan/vegetarian-friendly. The signature broth is a 7-hour chicken-bone stock combined with katsuo (bonito) first dashi and Hokkaido kombu, and the yuzu ramen is finished with pork back fat (背脂). Soy-sauce tare carries fish/animal dashi as well. Evening menu centers on wagyu shabu-shabu and udon-sukiyaki hot pots. No advertised plant-based bowl. A vegan would need to ask, and realistically there is no safe option.
kyr_shinuchi_eitaro.hours_raw: Mon–Sat & holidays: 11:30–14:00 (last order 14:00), 17:30–21:00 (last order 21:00). Closed Sun (with occasional special opening days).
kyr_shinuchi_eitaro.notes: [Mom & Pop] Eitaro began roughly four decades ago as a Kyoto noodle shop and built its name first as a hand-pulled Sanuki udon specialist before its owner — a devoted ramen lover — folded a second craft into the kitchen. After years at Shijo-Karasuma where it drew a loyal following and media

chef_bio.background: Eitaro began roughly four decades ago as a Kyoto noodle shop and built its name first as a hand-made Sanuki udon specialist before its owner — a devoted ramen lover — folded a second craft into the kitchen. After around forty years at Shijo-Karasuma where it drew a loyal following and media attention, the shop closed in June 2024, and reopened in November 2024 just steps from Shijo-Omiya Station, bringing back the bowl people kept asking for.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cook so every guest leaves thinking mata tabetai — I want to eat that again. The owner spent years tasting ramen across Kyoto and reportedly three years persuading a noodle maker to produce his low-kansui straight noodle before he was satisfied enough to put the bowl on the menu.
chef_bio.specialty: Yuzu ramen — the shop's signature bowl. The broth is a 7-hour chicken-bone stock layered with katsuo (bonito) first dashi and Hokkaido kombu, seasoned with a soy tare carried over from the udon side of the house, enriched with pork back fat, and finished with a generous squeeze of fresh yuzu so the citrus cuts through the richness. Alongside it the shop still serves hand-made Sanuki udon and, in the evening, hot-pot courses including wagyu shabu-shabu and udon-sukiyaki.

anecdotes.text: The shop closed in June 2024 and only came back because customers kept saying mata ano aji o tabetai — they wanted that flavor again — which pushed the owner to reopen near Shijo-Omiya in November 2024.

The signature yuzu ramen was born from the owner's own obsession: as a ramen lover running an udon shop, he spent years researching ramen around Kyoto before merging his udon dashi expertise with a ramen of his own.
Over its decades in business the shop became known as a spot frequented by entertainers and celebrities.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-eitaro.com (official) confirms a ~40-year Kyoto udon/ramen shop whose owner walked Kyoto eating ramen before creating a yuzu ramen using multiple bonito types and Hokkaido kombu, with daytime noodles and evening hot-pot/izakaya service and celebrity patronage. Tabelog Magazine confirms the June 2024 close and Nov 2024 reopen near Shijo-Omiya by popular demand, the 7-hour chicken broth with bonito dashi, back fat and fresh yuzu, and ~3 years spent getting a maker to produce the reduced-kansui straight noodle. kyotopi confirms the prior 四条烏丸 (Shijo-Karasuma) location.

gf_cross_contamination.text: On-site hand-pulling of Sanuki udon means heavy wheat flour use in the kitchen, with airborne flour and shared boiling water creating cross-contamination risk for any wheat-sensitive diner.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The ramen tare is built on a soy sauce infused with the shop's udon dashi; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the seasoning base is not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is chicken-bone stock plus bonito (katsuo) dashi and kombu, and the yuzu ramen is finished with pork back fat; evening menu centers on wagyu shabu-shabu and sukiyaki, so animal products are pervasive.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, long-running neighborhood noodle shop where a few words of Japanese and a friendly konnichiwa go a long way; English support is not guaranteed.

kyr_akihide.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles and an ultra-thick pork-bone (tonkotsu/kotteri) broth with a tare that almost certainly contains wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free menu, options, or accommodation are advertised, and the single small kitchen makes cross-contact unavoidable. Celiac diners should avoid.
kyr_akihide.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. The shop is a specialist in extremely rich pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth and tops its ramen with chunks of charred pork chashu; the entire concept is animal-based. No plant-based ramen is offered.
kyr_akihide.hours_raw: Basically closed; opens on irregular, unannounced days. When open, dinner service is often around 18:00-20:00 with last order around 23:00. Opening days/times are posted on Twitter/X roughly 30 minutes beforehand (@eigyoakihide for lunch, @eigyoakihide_2 for dinner).
kyr_akihide.notes: [Mom & Pop] Akihide is a cult ramen shop tucked along Ichijoji's famous Ramen Street in Sakyo-ku, northeast Kyoto. chef_bio.background: Akihide is a cult ramen shop tucked along Ichijoji's famous Ramen Street in Sakyo-ku, northeast Kyoto. It is one of the area's most talked-about bowls precisely because it is so hard to catch: the shop is closed by default and opens only on sporadic days that the owner announces on Twitter/X, often just before the doors open. With a single L-shaped counter of nine seats, no phone, no reservations, no parking, and cash-only service, it has the feel of a hidden, owner-run obsession rather than a conventional restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop bills itself as a specialty house for the 'rich-broth tribe' (濃厚民族専門店) — an unapologetic pursuit of maximum richness and intensity over conventional ramen balance, made for diners who want the heaviest, most concentrated bowl possible.
chef_bio.specialty: An ultra-thick kotteri tonkotsu (pork-bone) ramen so concentrated that a ladle is said to stand upright in the soup. The broth has the consistency of a sauce rather than a soup, paired with notably thick, chewy noodles and chunks of soft, fragrantly charred chashu pork that crumble when eaten. The intensity and texture sit somewhere between ramen and tsukemen.

anecdotes.text: The shop keeps no regular hours at all — it is 'basically closed,' and the only way to know it is open is to follow its Twitter/X accounts, which post the operating day (lunch via @eigyoakihide, dinner via @eigyoakihide_2), sometimes roughly half an hour before opening. On the days it does open it draws lines.
The broth is described as so dense that it 'stands a ladle upright,' resembling a thick sauce more than a soup — the shop pitches itself directly to the 'rich-broth tribe.'
A visitor tracked the shop's Twitter to catch an open day during a rainy spell and ate the kotteri bowl topped with two chunks of tender roasted pork and a large sheet of nori.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms Akihide is a 9-seat L-shaped-counter Ichijoji shop that is closed by default and opens only on sporadic days announced on X ~30 minutes ahead (lunch @eigyoakihide, dinner @eigyoakihide_2), with no phone, reservations or parking and cash only; it bills itself a 濃厚民族専門店 serving an ultra-thick kotteri tonkotsu 'so viscous the spoon stands upright,' with thick chewy noodles and soft charred chashu. kyoto-kanko corroborates the tracking-the-Twitter visit and toppings.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 9-seat Japanese-only counter shop with no fixed hours; you'll need to track its Twitter/X in Japanese to know when it's open, so it suits diners comfortable navigating a Japanese-language local ramen experience.

kyr_ramen_akatsuki.gf_detail: This is a traditional back-fat shoyu ramen shop. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles and a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which is essentially always brewed with wheat, over a pork-bone and chicken broth. There is no published gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and shared boiling water for the noodles. Not suitable for celiacs; a wheat-sensitive diner should treat this place as off-limits.
kyr_ramen_akatsuki.vegan_detail: The shop's identity is meat- and fish-based: a pork-bone and chicken broth finished with a Japanese-dashi soy tare, topped with thick hand-cut/braised char siu pork, plus sides like gyoza and karaage. There is no published vegan or vegetarian ramen, and even a plain bowl rests on an animal broth. Not a vegan-friendly option.
kyr_ramen_akatsuki.hours_raw: 11:30–03:00 next day (last order 02:45 next day). Open daily.
kyr_ramen_akatsuki.notes: [Mom & Pop] Ramen Akatsuki is a long-running neighborhood ramen-ya in Kyoto's Kita-Shirakawa quarter of Sakyo Ward, a stone's throw from the Kitashirakawa-kōmae city-bus stop and within walking distance of Mototanaka Station. Reports describe it as approaching its 30th year in business — a g

chef_bio.background: Ramen Akatsuki is a long-running neighborhood ramen-ya in Kyoto's Kita-Shirakawa quarter of Sakyo Ward, a stone's throw from the Kitashirakawa-kōmae city-bus stop and within walking distance of Mototanaka Station. Reports describe it as approaching its 30th year in business — a genuine local fixture rather than a trend shop. It runs from late morning straight through to around 3:00 a.m. every day, making it a dependable late-night bowl for students and locals alike.
chef_bio.philosophy: A straightforward, satisfying bowl that lets a clean pork-and-chicken broth and generous back-fat do the talking — comfort-food Kyoto ramen built for everyday, all-hours eating.
chef_bio.specialty: A Kyoto-style back-fat shoyu ramen built on a long-simmered pork-and-chicken broth finished with a Japanese-dashi soy tare and crowned with a scattering of sweet back-fat. Despite the rich-looking, glistening surface, the soup drinks surprisingly clean and light, with no heavy off-notes. The thick, tender braised char siu is treated as a star in its own right, and regulars are pointed toward extra char siu or the loaded 'Akatsuki Special.'

anecdotes.text: Despite the rich, oily-looking back-fat surface, the broth is described as drinking considerably lighter than it looks, with no distinctive smell or off-flavor.
Beyond the standard bowl, the menu stretches to a loaded 'Akatsuki Special,' a spicy version, and a fish-based ramen, plus sides like gyoza and karaage and set meals.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms Akatsuki is a nearly-30-year Kita-Shirakawa (Sakyo) shop open 11:30–3:00 daily with parking, serving a back-fat pork-and-chicken shoyu ramen that drinks lighter than its glistening surface, with thin straight noodles, melt-in-mouth chashu, and variants including the Akatsuki Special, a spicy version and a fish-based bowl plus gyoza/karaage; Tabelog corroborates the location and menu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water, and the broth is finished with a soy-sauce tare that is essentially always wheat-based — pervasive gluten with no separation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is a shoyu (soy sauce) ramen finished with a Japanese-dashi soy tare; standard Japanese shoyu is brewed with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The base soup is a pork-bone and chicken broth with back-fat and braised pork char siu; there is no animal-free preparation, so all bowls carry animal product.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills neighborhood counter ramen-ya open into the small hours; little to no English, so basic Japanese or pointing at the menu will smooth the visit.

kyr_tokusei_ramen_daichu_hon.gf_detail: Not safe for celiac or strict gluten-free diners. The core dish is wheat ramen noodles (straight-cut noodles from a noodle maker) served in a pork-and-chicken-bone broth seasoned with a shoyu (soy sauce) tare, which is virtually always wheat-based. Recommended toppings include garlic chips and gyoza (wheat dumplings) are on the menu. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, tare, or any allergen accommodation. Treat as off-limits if you must avoid gluten.
kyr_tokusei_ramen_daichu_hon.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The entire identity of the shop is its rich animal broth — large quantities of pork bones (tonkotsu) and chicken bones simmered continuously for 24 hours. Bowls come with chashu (pork) and a soft-boiled egg is a topping; the broth itself is meat-based with no plant-based option mentioned. There is no vegetable or vegan ramen on offer.
kyr_tokusei_ramen_daichu_hon.notes: A Fushimi institution tucked beneath the elevated railway tracks right outside Kintetsu Momoyamagoryomae Station, Daichu has been serving its rich tonkotsu since opening in 1995. The narrow, corridor-shaped space — counter up front, tables behind — keeps a nostalgic Showa-era atm

chef_bio.background: A Fushimi institution tucked beneath the elevated railway tracks right outside Kintetsu Momoyamagoryomae Station, Daichu has been serving its rich tonkotsu since opening in 1995. The narrow, corridor-shaped space — counter up front, tables behind — keeps a nostalgic Showa-era atmosphere, marked from the street by a yellow signboard and a big red lantern. In a district full of izakaya, it runs from late morning until around 2:00 a.m. daily, drawing a steady stream of locals from lunch through late night.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen prides itself on a flavor 'you can't get at a chain' — breaking the bones in-house and simmering large batches of pork and chicken bones for a full 24 hours rather than reconstituting a pre-made base. The shop even posts daily plaques naming that day's noodle-maker and broth-maker, a small signal of how seriously it takes the craft behind each bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: The house bowl is the 大中ラーメン, a 濃厚豚骨醤油 — an intensely rich pork-bone-and-chicken broth seasoned with soy tare, thick enough that it is said a chopstick can stand upright in it, yet finishing with umami rather than heaviness. There is also a 特濃 (extra-rich) version for those who want it even more concentrated. The shop is generous with free customization: noodle firmness, broth richness, extra bean sprouts and green onion, soft-boiled egg, and kimchi, with burnt-garlic oil and garlic chips offered to round out the flavor. Chashu comes in different cuts (shoulder, belly, loin), and a lunch-set adds a side bowl of fried rice, karaage, gyoza, or chashu-don.

anecdotes.text: The broth is famously viscous — described as thick enough to stand a chopstick in — and ranks among Kyoto's most intensely rich kotteri ramen.

Set beneath the railway viaduct with a retro Showa feel, the shop is especially evocative in the evening; the noodles are straight-cut to grab the concentrated broth, and garlic chips are recommended 'to complete the flavor.'

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: palplan (official) states Daichu breaks bones in-house and simmers large batches of pork and chicken bones 24 hours daily to pursue a flavor 'unavailable at chains,' with all toppings free; v-trip confirms the 1995 founding, the 24-hour tonkotsu simmered to a potage, and the displayed name plaques for the day's noodle- and soup-makers. kyotopi confirms the under-viaduct location, yellow signboard/red lantern, chopstick-standing 濃厚豚骨醤油, 特濃 version, chashu cuts and lunch sets; goriluckey confirms the Showa setting, straight-cut noodles and garlic chips.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core dish is wheat ramen noodles in a pork/chicken broth with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; gyoza (wheat) and garlic chips are on the menu. No gluten-free option or allergen handling indicated.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature broth is 濃厚豚骨醤油 (rich pork-bone soy sauce), meaning a wheat-based soy tare is integral to the bowl.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is made by simmering pork bones and chicken bones for 24 hours; there is no plant-based broth or vegan bowl available.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, no-reservations local ramen joint where a few polite Japanese words and pointing at the customizable order sheet will carry you through; staff are used to a steady all-hours crowd rather than overseas guests.

kyr_ganso_jukusei_hosomen_ko.gf_detail: This is a classic Kyoto back-fat shoyu ramen shop. The signature bowls are built on wheat noodles (their custom aged thin noodles), a soy-sauce-based tare (typically brewed soy sauce contains wheat), and a chicken-and-pork bone broth simmered for hours. There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, tamari tare, or allergen handling. A celiac diner cannot safely eat the ramen here. No dedicated gluten-free preparation exists.
kyr_ganso_jukusei_hosomen_ko.vegan_detail: All core bowls are animal-based: the broth is chicken-bone and pork-bone simmered for about 12 hours with back fat, and bowls are topped with chashu pork. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen option indicated. Even the lighter white-shoyu bowl uses Kyoto vegetables but is built on the same animal broth and finished with bonito flakes. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_ganso_jukusei_hosomen_ko.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun 11:00-03:00 (next day); Wed closed. Note: from June 2026, open on public holidays and closed the following day instead.
kyr_ganso_jukusei_hosomen_ko.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kouri is a well-known purveyor of nostalgic Kyoto-style chuka soba in the lively Shijo-Omiya / Mibu quarter, a dense pocket of affordable, beloved eateries near Nijo Castle and a roughly five-minute walk from Hankyu Omiya station. The Mibu shop is the flagship (honten) of the bra

chef_bio.background: Kourai is a well-known purveyor of nostalgic Kyoto-style chuka soba in the lively Shijo-Omiya / Mibu quarter, a dense pocket of affordable, beloved eateries near Nijo Castle and a roughly five-minute walk from Hankyu Omiya station. The Mibu shop is the flagship (honten) of the brand.
chef_bio.philosophy: A devotion to the aged thin-noodle style the shop is named for (熟成細麺, 'aged thin noodle'), pairing custom noodles with a long-simmered broth that balances vegetable sweetness, soy richness and back-fat depth.
chef_bio.specialty: Their signature is the classic Kyoto back-fat shoyu ramen: custom-ordered aged thin noodles with a springy, clean-cutting bite, in a soy-sauce broth made from carefully prepped chicken and pork bones and aromatic vegetables simmered about 12 hours, finished with back fat. It is typically crowned with tender, melt-in-the-mouth chashu.

anecdotes.text: Beyond the classic bowl, the shop has introduced contrasting shoyu variations: a dark 'black' soy ramen with concentrated, robust broth, thicker chashu and menma, and a refined 'white' soy ramen with a clearer broth, Kyoto vegetables and bonito flakes.
The kitchen leans on custom-ordered aged thin noodles prized for a springy texture and clean bite that carries the broth well.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms Kourai in Mibu/Shijo-Omiya (~5 min from Hankyu Omiya) serves a Kyoto-style back-fat shoyu chuka soba on house aged thin noodles (熟成細麺), with a broth of carefully prepped chicken and pork bones plus aromatic vegetables simmered about 12 hours and topped with melt-in-mouth chashu; it also lists a robust dark 'black' soy ramen (thicker chashu, menma) and a refined 'white' soy ramen with Kyoto vegetables and bonito flakes.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are built on a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; brewed Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat, and no wheat-free/tamari alternative is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shared broth is chicken-bone and pork-bone based and bowls are topped with chashu pork; there is no separate vegan preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, casual neighborhood ramen counter open very late; comfortable for solo diners, but expect a Japanese-only menu and minimal English, so come ready to point and order simply.

kyr_chuka_soba_shomen.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The bowl is built on wheat ramen noodles in a chicken-bone broth finished with back fat and an aged soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. There is no gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no indication staff accommodate gluten avoidance. Anyone with celiac disease should not eat the ramen here.
kyr_chuka_soba_shomen.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly option. The signature and essentially only style is a chicken-bone broth enriched with pork back fat and topped with braised pork chashu, so the broth, fat and toppings are all animal-derived and there is no plant-based ramen on the menu.
kyr_chuka_soba_shomen.notes: [Mom & Pop] Open since 1993, Shomen is a small, well-worn ramen counter tucked into the Horikawa Shopping Street on the west side of Horikawa-dori, a short walk toward Marutamachi and Imadegawa. It belongs to the Kyoto back-fat shoyu tradition that traces back to the famous Masutani style —

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Japan — a neighborhood町中華 (town-Chinese / local ramen) shop serving the surrounding residents and after-work salarymen.
chef_bio.background: Open since 1993, Shomen is a small, well-worn ramen counter tucked into the Horikawa Shopping Street on the west side of Horikawa-dori, a short walk toward Marutamachi and Imadegawa. It belongs to the Kyoto back-fat shoyu tradition that traces back to the famous Masutani style — a lineage some regulars argue Shomen executes even better than the original.
chef_bio.philosophy: An almost obsessive devotion to the back fat — the fat is sourced from Kyushu — so that the rich, collagen-laced sheen on the surface is the defining character of the bowl rather than an afterthought.
chef_bio.specialty: Chuka soba: thin, straight noodles in a chicken-bone (鶏ガラ) broth finished with a glistening layer of pork back fat (背脂) and an aged soy-sauce tare, topped with chashu braised until meltingly tender (とろとろ) and firm menma. A bowl runs about ¥650; the ramen-and-fried-rice set about ¥850.

anecdotes.text: A long-time reviewer rates Shomen as the high point of the Kyoto Masutani-style lineage, saying its devotion to the back fat surpasses even the original Masutani shop.
First-time visitors are served the noodles on the softer side by default; regulars who like them firmer just ask for harder noodles when ordering.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Horikawa Shotengai page confirms Shomen's signature chicken-bone back-fat shoyu ramen. A detailed Tabelog review confirms it opened in 1993, works in the ますたに (Masutani) back-fat lineage (which the reviewer rates above the original Masutani), has its back fat direct-shipped from Kyushu, defaults first-timers to softer noodles (firmer on request), and prices a bowl ~¥650 and a ramen-fried-rice set ~¥850, with tender chashu and firm menma.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single small ramen kitchen built around wheat noodles boiled in shared water; no gluten-free protocol or separate prep is indicated, so cross-contact is effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is finished with an aged soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, making the seasoning a wheat source.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is chicken-bone based, enriched with pork back fat and served with pork chashu; no plant-based broth or toppings exist, so there is no vegan path on the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills local Kyoto ramen counter where ordering is straightforward but everything is in Japanese and the welcome is brisk and old-school; a little Japanese or pointing at the menu goes a long way.

kyr_menya_ichimen_senshin.gf_detail: Not safe for celiacs. This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop; the noodles are wheat, the shoyu (soy sauce) tare almost certainly contains wheat, and the kitchen boils flour-based noodles throughout. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no published allergen handling.
kyr_menya_ichimen_senshin.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The entire concept is animal-based: the signature bowl is a super-concentrated tonkotsu made from roughly 1kg of pork bones plus water per bowl, and the other mainstay is a chicken paitan. Even the complimentary warmed vegetables share a meat-broth kitchen.
kyr_menya_ichimen_senshin.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 / 18:00-23:00 (Thursday lunch only, no dinner service on Thursdays)
kyr_menya_ichimen_senshin.notes: [Mom & Pop] A newcomer to Kyoto's ramen scene, Menya Ichimen Senshin opened in March 2024 in a roomy former eatery space in Kamigyo Ward, a short walk northwest toward Nijo Castle. The name carries the spirit of devoting oneself wholeheartedly to a single bowl of noodles.

chef_bio.background: A newcomer to Kyoto's ramen scene, Menya Ichimen Senshin opened on 9 March 2024 in a roomy former eatery space in Kamigyo Ward, a short walk northwest toward Nijo Castle. The name carries the spirit of devoting oneself wholeheartedly to a single bowl of noodles.
chef_bio.philosophy: Single-minded focus on the broth: the tonkotsu is built from bones and water alone, with no extra additives, letting pure pork umami carry the bowl. Diners are also offered free extras on request such as garlic, onions, and a side of warmed vegetables.
chef_bio.specialty: The headline bowl is a super-concentrated tonkotsu ramen made from nothing but pork bones and water, with roughly 1kg of bones per bowl, yielding a thick, viscous, deeply porky broth with restrained sweetness. Alongside it is a chicken paitan (tori-paitan) and a special shoyu ramen priced at just 700 yen.

anecdotes.text: The signature ultra-rich tonkotsu is made with bones and water only, using about 1kg of pork bones per bowl for a thick, high-viscosity soup.
A 700-yen special shoyu ramen is called out as exceptional value.
Warmed vegetables are served alongside the ramen, an unusual touch for a ramen shop.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: noodlers confirms the ultra-rich tonkotsu made from only pork bones and water; kyo-soku (2024/03/29) confirms the 9 March 2024 opening in Senbon-Marutamachi and the ~1kg-of-bones-per-bowl broth alongside a tori-paitan; osumituki and retty confirm the bones-and-water tonkotsu, the 700-yen special shoyu and the free garlic/onion plus warmed-vegetable extras.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A wheat-noodle ramen shop with no gluten-free offering; wheat noodles are boiled throughout the kitchen, so cross-contamination is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The menu includes a special shoyu (soy sauce) ramen; standard ramen shoyu tare is wheat-based, and no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are animal-based, a pork-bone tonkotsu and a chicken paitan, and even the complimentary warmed vegetables come out of a meat-broth kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locally focused independent ramen shop with no sign of English support, so a little Japanese or a translation app will smooth the visit.

kyr_ramen_yucho.gf_detail: Specialist ginger soy-sauce ramen shop. The single menu item is built on wheat noodles (from Menya Teikoku) in a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare that is normally wheat-based, over a fish/dashi broth (horse mackerel, bonito, mackerel). No gluten-free noodle or tare option and no indication of allergen accommodation, so not safe for celiacs. Anyone strictly avoiding gluten should not eat here.
kyr_ramen_yucho.vegan_detail: The bowl is fundamentally a fish/dashi-based broth (horse mackerel, mackerel and bonito stock) topped with chashu pork and roast beef. Not vegetarian or vegan, and there are no plant-based options on the menu, which serves only the ginger soy-sauce ramen.
kyr_ramen_yucho.hours_raw: 11:00-21:30 daily (sources note irregular closures rather than a fixed weekly day off)
kyr_ramen_yucho.notes: [Mom & Pop] Ramen Yucho opened on 18 February 2025 on the second floor of the Iidaya Building, a short walk from Kyoto-Kawaramachi Station in the busy Shijo-Kawaramachi quarter. Styled as a tucked-away hidden-gem shop with a clean, modern Japanese interior and a U-shaped counter, it set out

chef_bio.background: Ramen Yucho opened on 18 February 2025 on the second floor of the Iidaya Building, a short walk from Kyoto-Kawaramachi Station in the busy Shijo-Kawaramachi quarter. Styled as a tucked-away hidden-gem shop with a clean, modern Japanese interior and a U-shaped counter, it set out to do one thing well in a city where ginger-forward ramen is genuinely uncommon.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focused, single-bowl shop: pour everything into one warming, refined ginger soy-sauce ramen rather than a long menu, with broth and ginger meant to leave you physically warmed from the inside.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature and essentially only dish is the Kyoto ginger soy-sauce ramen. A crystal-clear seafood broth is drawn from three kinds of fish dashi (horse mackerel, mackerel and bonito), then driven by ginger both dissolved in the soup and laid on top as fresh needle-cut strips. It is served with thin, supple straight noodles from the Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teikoku, and topped with chashu pork, roast beef, naruto, Kujo green onion, menma and spinach. Diners choose Single, Double or Triple by the number of chashu and roast-beef slices, and a side of ginger dashi rice is also offered.

anecdotes.text: The shop leans into the rarity of ginger ramen in Kyoto, and the broth's pronounced ginger is widely described as leaving diners warmed up and toasty from the inside out.
Diners customize the bowl by selecting how many slices of chashu pork and roast beef they want, scaling from Single (900 yen) to Double (1,250 yen) to Triple (1,700 yen).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-shiyakusho-lunch confirms Ramen Yucho opened 18 Feb 2025 on the 2F of the Iidaya Building near Kyoto-Kawaramachi, a hideaway shop serving a Kyoto ginger soy-sauce ramen: a clear broth of three fish dashi driven by dissolved and needle-cut ginger, on Menya Teikoku (麺屋帝国) noodles, topped with roast beef, pork-shoulder chashu, naruto, Kujo green onion, menma and spinach, scaled Single/Double/Triple at ¥900/¥1,250/¥1,700 with a ¥200 ginger-dashi rice side. osakajinrock corroborates the ginger rarity and warming effect.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the soy-sauce tare is normally wheat-based, so the dish is not gluten-free and no GF accommodation is indicated.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is a ginger soy-sauce ramen built on a special ginger shoyu tare, which in Japanese ramen is virtually always brewed from wheat-containing soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is a fish/dashi base (horse mackerel, mackerel, bonito) and toppings include pork chashu and roast beef, so cross-contact with animal products is inherent to every bowl.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, friendly modern counter ramen shop near Kyoto-Kawaramachi Station where ordering is simple (essentially one bowl, choosing topping count), so a little Japanese and a friendly greeting go a long way.

kyr_menya_kanae.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. This is a Jiro-style shop built on extra-thick wheat noodles with salt or soy (typically wheat-based) tare, served in or with a beef-fat/dashi base — not safe for celiac diners. No gluten-free option is advertised.
kyr_menya_kanae.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The house style centers on wagyu beef fat, beef Achilles tendon, and a dashi-based broth; the wheat noodles and tare make this unsuitable for vegans.
kyr_menya_kanae.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Fri, Sat, Sun & holidays 11:00-14:00 / 17:00-23:00; closed Wed & Thu.
kyr_menya_kanae.notes: [Mom & Pop] Menya Kanae opened in September 2025 in the Shijo-Omiya / Mibu area of Kyoto, tucked along a quiet alley off Koin-dori in a renovated machiya (traditional townhouse) known as the 'Wagyu Kaikan.' You slip off your shoes to enter a snug counter space with a retro, handmade feel, th

chef_bio.background: Menya Kanae opened in September 2025 in the Shijo-Omiya / Mibu area of Kyoto, tucked along a quiet alley off Koin-dori in a renovated machiya (traditional townhouse) known as the 'Wagyu Kaikan.' You slip off your shoes to enter a snug counter space with a retro, handmade feel, then order from your smartphone by QR code — an appealing contrast of old-house atmosphere and modern convenience.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's idea is that wagyu beef fat brings a refined umami and a clean sweetness that pork back-fat lacks, giving a salt-based dashi described as having 'no sharp edges' — a more elegant, mellow spin on the famously heavy Jiro genre. Sourcing such beef fat is difficult, which the shop frames as a mark of its commitment to quality.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is 'KANAE no Jiro' — a new-school take on Jiro-style ramen. In place of the usual pork back-fat it uses the fat of wagyu (Kobe and Omi beef), and instead of pork chashu it tops the bowl with tender, gelatinous beef Achilles tendon, with no cabbage. Extra-thick, wide noodles from veteran maker Tieoh (棣鄂) carry the bowl, which can be ordered with soup (ari) or brothless (nashi), and seasoned with salt (shio) or soy (shoyu).

anecdotes.text: Students get a free upsize of noodles and bean sprouts.
Diners can also order select dishes from the sister izakaya 'Toyo-ta' alongside their ramen.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotopi confirms Menya Kanae opened Sept 2025 in a renovated machiya ('Wagyu Kaikan') off Koin-dori in Shijo-Omiya/Mibu, with shoes-off counter seating and QR smartphone ordering; its 'KANAE no Jiro' replaces pork back-fat with wagyu (Kobe/Omi) fat for a refined, edge-free salt dashi, and uses 棣鄂 (Tieoh) thick wide noodles, with the free student noodle/bean-sprout upsize and access to dishes from sister izakaya Toyo-ta. Tabelog corroborates the location.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop offers a soy-sauce (shoyu) seasoning option; Japanese soy sauce is typically brewed with wheat, so this is not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The bowls are built on wagyu beef fat, beef Achilles tendon, and a dashi-based broth, so the kitchen is not vegan-safe.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual counter ramen shop with QR-code smartphone ordering; little English is to be expected, but the self-service ordering eases the language barrier.

kyr_shinshintei_ichijoji.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop whose signature is white miso ramen; miso tare and the broth setup mean wheat is integral, and there is no published gluten-free option or dedicated handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_shinshintei_ichijoji.vegan_detail: The ramen is built on dashi and pork/meat elements with chashu and other meat toppings, and no vegan or vegetarian bowl is advertised. Plant-only diners cannot reliably be accommodated here.
kyr_shinshintei_ichijoji.hours_raw: 11:00–16:00 (lunch only). Closed Mon and the 3rd Sun.
kyr_shinshintei_ichijoji.notes: [Mom & Pop] Shinshintei is widely credited as the birthplace of Kyoto-style white miso ramen. The lineage began as a humble food stall around 1960 and grew into a brick-and-mortar shop opened in 1972 in the Fushacho area of central Kyoto. Over nearly four decades it built a devoted following

chef_bio.background: Shinshintei is widely credited as the birthplace of Kyoto-style white miso ramen. The lineage began as a humble food stall around 1960 and grew into a brick-and-mortar shop opened in 1972 in the Fushacho area of central Kyoto. Over nearly four decades it built a devoted following before the original first-generation owner retired and closed that location in 2009 due to age. Rather than let the recipe disappear, the founder's younger brother inherited the name and the noren and reopened the shop in the Ichijoji district, where it carries the tradition forward today as a lunch-only neighborhood institution.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep the original white-miso recipe alive and unchanged - a mellow, comforting, deeply flavored bowl made the same way it has been for decades, served simply at lunch.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is white miso ramen (白味噌ラーメン) - a gentle, mellow, slightly sweet white-miso broth that is distinct from the heartier Sapporo style. It pairs a concentrated dashi with a light white miso (淡めの白味噌), is piled with plenty of vegetables, and is served with straight Kyoto-style noodles that meet the smooth broth.

anecdotes.text: The original Fushacho shop became famous enough to draw notable guests, said to include singer Miyuki Nakajima and actor Keanu Reeves, before it closed in 2009.
When the first-generation owner retired, the founder's younger brother took over the name and reopened in Ichijoji to keep the white-miso ramen tradition going (一乗寺で暖簾を受け継いで開業したのが今の新進亭).
Regulars praise the long-unchanged, mellow and deeply flavored miso ramen as something you can only really experience in Kyoto.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki records the 1960 stall, 1972 Fushacho shop, 2009 closure due to the founder's age, the younger brother reopening in Ichijoji, the light white-miso bowl, and the celebrity guests; v-trip confirms the shop as Kyoto's white-miso originator with a long-unchanged mellow flavor and straight noodles.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop's core product is white miso ramen with wheat noodles and a miso-based tare; miso and the broth components typically contain wheat, and no gluten-free preparation is offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bowls are built on dashi and meat elements with chashu and other meat toppings; no vegan or vegetarian broth is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, traditional neighborhood ramen counter where a few words of Japanese and a relaxed lunchtime visit go a long way; English support is unlikely.

kyr_ryuho.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. The karashi soba uses wheat noodles, a wheat-based mustard/soy ankake sauce, and Japanese soy sauce (contains wheat); gyoza and spring rolls are wheat-wrapped. There are no celiac-safe options and no gluten-free accommodation here.
kyr_ryuho.vegan_detail: Not a vegan place. The signature karashi soba is built on a chicken-bone and kombu broth with chicken, shrimp, and animal-based ankake; the wider menu is meat- and seafood-centric town-Chinese. No vegan ramen or vegan set is offered.
kyr_ryuho.hours_raw: 11:30–19:30 (last order 19:00, last entry 18:30). Closed Wed. Note: some sources list lunch-only hours (11:30–16:00), so confirm before visiting.
kyr_ryuho.notes: [Mom & Pop] 龍鳳 is a small, unpretentious Kyoto town-Chinese counter tucked into the Rokkaku lane just off the Shinkyogoku arcade, where it has operated for roughly four decades. Its proprietor, Terada Yasuhiro, trained under two pillars of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking — 第一樓 (Daiichiro), the p

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto-style Chinese (京都中華), Cantonese-rooted but refined and lightly seasoned, in the 鳳舞 (Houmai) / 第一樓 (Daiichiro) lineage.
chef_bio.background: 龍鳳 is a small, unpretentious Kyoto town-Chinese counter tucked into the Rokkaku lane just off the Shinkyogoku arcade, where it has operated for decades. Its proprietor, Terada Yasuhiro, trained under two pillars of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking — 第一樓 (Daiichiro), the postwar restaurant opened around 1951, and the legendary 鳳舞 (Houmai), widely regarded as the fountainhead of 京都中華. He worked as a skilled chef at both before opening his own shop, carrying forward that lineage alongside sister-spirit establishments like 鳳泉.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithful preservation of the original Daiichiro recipe and taste. The dish was born as a course finale at Daiichiro because it travelled to the table more easily than soup noodles; Terada keeps that heritage intact while cooking his version longer to deepen the broth's umami, and historically swapping in seasonal ingredients (matsutake for shiitake in season, fresh bamboo shoots over canned).
chef_bio.specialty: からしそば (karashi soba) — straight noodles pre-coated with mustard paste under a gentle, mildly sweet soy-based ankake, topped with chicken, shrimp, dried shiitake, komatsuna greens and scallion. The mustard gives a sharp 'tsuun' hit to the nose that plays against the sauce's sweetness — a grown-up, unpredictable heat the shop calls a 大人の味.

anecdotes.text: The owner, Terada Yasuhiro, trained at both 第一樓 (Daiichiro, opened around 1951) and the legendary 鳳舞 (Houmai) before opening 龍鳳, and keeps the original Daiichiro karashi-soba recipe alive.
Karashi soba was originally created at Daiichiro as the closer to a Chinese course because it was easier to carry to the table than soup noodles — 'カラシソバはコースの〆によう出してたんです。スープ麺より運びやすいから僕らも重宝してね。'
A craftsman of this trade for a lifetime, the chef is described as over 70 years old yet still running the shop himself — 'ご主人はこの道ひと筋で、御歳70オーバー'.

The dish is served in a nostalgic Showa-era room still set with vintage tabletop condiments — the pepper shaker, soy-sauce dispenser and vinegar bottle that reviewers single out for their retro charm.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Brutus documents Terada Yasuhiro's training at 第一樓 (opened ~1951) and 鳳舞, the karashi-soba course-closer origin quote, longer cooking to concentrate the chicken-and-kombu ankake, and seasonal matsutake/bamboo swaps; kyotopi confirms the over-70 owner devoted to the craft, the Rokkaku/Shinkyogoku location, and the nostalgic condiment-set room.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Karashi soba is wheat-noodle based with a wheat mustard/soy ankake; gyoza and spring rolls are wheat-wrapped, and a small shared kitchen means no gluten isolation is possible.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature dish uses a soy-based ankake sauce (Japanese soy sauce contains wheat).

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is chicken-bone and kombu based, with chicken and shrimp in the dish; no vegan preparation exists, so all cookware contacts animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, old-school Showa-era neighborhood Chinese counter run by a veteran chef; very little English, so a few Japanese phrases and a relaxed, respectful manner go a long way.

kyr_noko_ramen_kyomenya.gf_detail: This is a tonkotsu ramen specialist: wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth, with the usual ramen tare. No gluten-free options are offered and there is no indication of allergy accommodation. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_noko_ramen_kyomenya.vegan_detail: Every bowl is built on a heavy pork-bone (and, in some variants, seafood or chicken) broth, with pork back fat as a customizable topping. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options.
kyr_noko_ramen_kyomenya.hours_raw: Mon/Sat/Sun/holidays 11:30–14:30, 18:00–21:30 (last order 30 min before closing). Closed Tue/Wed/Thu/Fri. Currently open only Sat/Sun/Mon. Additional irregular days off.
kyr_noko_ramen_kyomenya.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kyomenya opened in December 2016 along Ichijoji's famously competitive ramen street in Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, just south of the well-known Ramen Yokozuna. It carved out its niche by going against the grain: while Ichijoji leans toward lighter chicken-based broths, Kyomenya planted i

chef_bio.background: Kyomenya opened on December 12, 2016 along Ichijoji's famously competitive ramen street in Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, near the well-known Ramen Yokozuna. It carved out its niche by going against the grain: while Ichijoji leans toward lighter chicken-based broths, Kyomenya planted its flag on unapologetically heavy, ultra-rich tonkotsu.
chef_bio.philosophy: The aim is a broth that is intensely rich and creamy — dorodoro thick — yet kept smooth and balanced rather than merely heavy (濃厚ですがくどさはありません), with the pork bone simmered long and combined with seafood stock for depth.
chef_bio.specialty: The flagship bowl is the Kyo-no Tonkotsu (驚濃とんこつ) — a viscous, cream-thick pork-bone broth rounded out with seafood dashi, using roughly three times the pork bone of an ordinary tonkotsu ramen (通常の豚骨ラーメンの約3倍). The lineup also includes the Mega Tonkotsu (メガとんこつ, water and pork bones only, simmered for hours), a chicken-enriched Tori Tonkotsu (驚濃とりとんこつ), a milder Maroyaka Tonkotsu (まろやかとんこつ), and mazesoba.

anecdotes.text: The shop earned a runner-up (準グランプリ) in the tonkotsu category of 'Ultimate Ramen 2021' (究極のラーメン2021), a nod to how seriously its dorodoro broth is taken among ramen enthusiasts.
Diners customize each bowl at ordering — noodle firmness, amount of green onion, and amount of pork back fat (① 麺の固さ ② ねぎの多さ ③ 背油の量).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki 84814 confirms the Dec 12 2016 opening near Ramen Yokozuna, the ~3x pork-bone signature 驚濃とんこつ, and the full tonkotsu lineup; gcjapan lists the three order-time adjustments (noodle firmness, green onion, back fat) and the clean pork-plus-seafood broth; the 究極のラーメン2021 tonkotsu 準グランプリ is corroborated via web search.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, no-frills local counter ramen shop where ordering and customizing your bowl in Japanese will go most smoothly; little to no English support should be expected.

kyr_iekei_ramen_saitoya_ichi.gf_detail: This is Yokohama-style iekei ramen: wheat noodles from Sakai Seimen, a wheat-based soy sauce (shoyu) tare, and a pork-bone/chicken broth — all standard wheat-containing components. There is no gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no indication of allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners. Rice bowls are available as sides but are prepared in the same kitchen alongside wheat ramen.
kyr_iekei_ramen_saitoya_ichi.vegan_detail: The entire concept is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken-oil broth with chashu pork, egg, and a soy-sauce tare. There are no vegetarian or vegan ramen options. Toppings such as spinach, seaweed, and negi exist but only as additions to the meat-based bowl. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_iekei_ramen_saitoya_ichi.hours_raw: Tue–Sat 18:00–23:00; Sun & holidays 11:00–21:00; Closed Mondays (or the following Tuesday if Monday is a public holiday). Note: some listings show Fri 11:00–21:00 as well; lunch service is most reliable on Sundays/holidays.
kyr_iekei_ramen_saitoya_ichi.notes: [Mom & Pop] Saitoya is a Yokohama iekei ramen shop whose owner trained at Tagamiya (田上家), a respected Yokohama family-ramen house founded in 2014, and whose lineage traces back to Yoshimuraya (吉村家), the founding shop of the entire iekei genre. The original Saitoya opened in Yokohama's Negish

chef_bio.background: Saitoya is a Yokohama iekei ramen shop whose owner trained at Tagamiya (田上家), a respected Yokohama family-ramen house founded in 2014, and whose lineage traces back to Yoshimuraya (吉村家), the founding shop of the entire iekei genre. The original Saitoya opened in Yokohama's Negishi district in August 2022; this Ichijoji shop, opened July 27, 2024, is the third Saitoya location and the brand's first venture into the Kansai region.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner brews the broth in-house and embraces the iekei idea that the bowl naturally shifts through the day — the flavor you get at the lunch opening differs from the late-evening pour, which they treat as a feature of honest, freshly-simmered cooking rather than a flaw.
chef_bio.specialty: Chashu-men: a rich tonkotsu-and-chicken-oil broth with a soy-based tare, served over Sakai Seimen noodles and topped with tender smoked pork chashu, spinach, nori seaweed, and egg. Diners can customize noodle firmness, oil level, and tare strength in classic iekei fashion, and add cabbage or white negi the Yokohama way.

anecdotes.text: Brought direct-lineage Yokohama family ramen to Ichijoji, one of Kyoto's most competitive ramen districts, billed as the area's first authentic iekei specialist.
Uses Sakai Seimen's premium A-grade noodles, which are reserved for recognized iekei shops in the lineage.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki confirms the owner trained at Yokohama's Tagamiya (est. 2014, drawing on Yoshimuraya), the Negishi original of Aug 2022, the July 27 2024 Ichijoji shop as the third branch and first authentic iekei in the district, the in-house broth, the smoky chashu, and the A-grade Sakai Seimen noodles; noodlers confirms the July 27 2024 Kansai-first opening, self-boiled broth, Sakai Seimen noodles and spinach/nori toppings.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles (Sakai Seimen) and a wheat-based shoyu tare are core to every bowl; there is no gluten-free preparation and no separate handling, so cross-contamination is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare is a soy-sauce base, which in iekei ramen is standard wheat-containing shoyu; reviewers specifically praised the soy-sauce flavor of the broth.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone and chicken-oil based with pork chashu and egg; all bowls are animal-based with no vegan option.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, busy local ramen counter where ordering is in Japanese and there is no English menu — comfortable for travelers used to Japanese ramen shops, but English support should not be expected.

kyr_honki_tsukemen_yamashita.gf_detail: No gluten-free option. This is a dedicated tsukemen specialist: both bowls are built on wheat noodles (described as thick, whole-grain-flour-containing noodles) dipped in a soy-sauce-based fish broth (gyokai shoyu) or a sesame-soy-milk tantan broth, both of which use wheat-based soy sauce tare. The wheat noodles plus wheat shoyu mean neither bowl is safe for celiac or gluten-sensitive diners, and no gluten-free preparation is offered or mentioned anywhere.
kyr_honki_tsukemen_yamashita.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The fish-soy tsukemen broth is made from bonito (katsuo) and dried sardines (niboshi/iriko), and the sesame-soy-milk tantan bowl is topped with meat-miso (niku-miso); both are animal-based. Although the tantan broth uses soy milk (tonyu), it is not a vegan preparation. No vegan or vegetarian option is offered.
kyr_honki_tsukemen_yamashita.hours_raw: 11:00-14:30 (L.O. 14:00) / 17:00-21:30 (L.O. 21:00). Closed Sundays. (Tabelog lists the lunch/dinner blocks as 11:00-14:00 and 17:00-21:00; blog sources list 14:30/21:30 close with L.O. at 14:00/21:00.)
kyr_honki_tsukemen_yamashita.notes: [Mom & Pop] 本気つけ麺山下 opened on May 25, 2026 in the heart of Ichijoji, the neighborhood widely regarded as Kyoto's most fiercely competitive ramen district. It took over the space of the well-loved shop "Tsurukame Ichijoji," which closed at the end of March 2026, refreshing the storefront into

chef_bio.background: 本気つけ麺山下 opened on May 25, 2026 in the heart of Ichijoji, the neighborhood widely regarded as Kyoto's most fiercely competitive ramen district. It took over the space of the well-loved shop "Tsurukame Ichijoji," which closed at the end of March 2026, refreshing the storefront into a clean, bright counter room of eight seats. The proprietor is understood to have trained at a well-known ramen establishment before striking out on his own here.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop keeps its focus deliberately narrow, offering only its two tsukemen and letting the noodles and dip do the talking, with a stated wish to become a place loved by many.
chef_bio.specialty: A two-bowl tsukemen specialist. The signature 魚介醤油つけ麺 pairs thick, springy noodles with a concentrated bonito-and-dried-sardine fish broth balanced by an aromatic soy tare. The second pillar, 胡麻豆乳担々つけ麺, folds rich roasted sesame and creamy soy milk into a tantan dip crowned with meat-miso for a richness-meets-balance bowl.

anecdotes.text: The thick, straight noodles are from a little-known maker called 'はなき' (Hanaki) and are a particular point of pride, praised by reviewers for how well their texture pairs with the rich dip.
The shop occupies the former premises of the popular Tsurukame Ichijoji, which closed on March 31, 2026.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki and kyotopi confirm the May 25 2026 opening in the former Tsurukame space, the two-tsukemen-only concept (魚介醤油 and 胡麻豆乳担々), the 8-seat brighter counter, and an owner who trained at a well-known but undisclosed shop; Tabelog reviewers confirm the noodles come from the little-known 'はなき' (Hanaki) maker and praise their texture.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Both tsukemen use wheat noodles dipped in a wheat-soy-sauce-based tare, so there is no celiac-safe option and gluten is intrinsic to every bowl.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The fish broth is a soy-sauce (shoyu) base, which in Japanese ramen is standard wheat-containing soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Fish broth uses bonito and dried sardines; the tantan bowl is topped with meat-miso, so animal products are central to both dips.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 8-seat counter shop with mobile-order, cash-only service in Kyoto's ramen-mad Ichijoji district; little English is expected, so come ready to order by phone-app and pay cash.

kyr_menya_rennosuke.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The signature bowl uses house-made wheat noodles (Kyoto "Setokirara" wheat), so the ramen contains gluten by definition. The tare/seasoning is unspecified but standard ramen tare typically contains wheat shoyu. No gluten-free menu or noodle option is advertised, and the kitchen is a single small counter operation with shared equipment. Anyone needing strict gluten avoidance should not eat the ramen here.
kyr_menya_rennosuke.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Although the broth is unusually animal-free for ramen — a 100% seafood dashi from two kombu varieties, Ibuki iriko (dried sardines) and saba/urume/katsuo bushi (fish flakes) with no pork or chicken stock — it is fish-based, not plant-based, and the bowl is topped with pork chashu (京の都もち豚). There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen option advertised. The kombu component is plant-derived but the dish as served contains fish and pork.
kyr_menya_rennosuke.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner-chef who trained at 猪一 (Inoichi), a Michelin-recognized Kyoto dashi-soba/ramen establishment, before opening Menya Rennosuke in April 2023 in a renovated traditional wooden house tucked into a quiet Murasakino residential alley.

chef_bio.background: Owner-chef who trained at 猪一 (Inoichi), a Michelin-recognized Kyoto dashi-soba/ramen establishment, before opening Menya Rennosuke in April 2023 in a renovated traditional wooden house tucked into a quiet Murasakino residential alley.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chef set out to 'ラーメン屋というイメージを払拭したかった' — to dispel the everyday image of a ramen shop — pursuing refined, additive-free (無化調; no chemical seasoning) cooking that expresses Kyoto's water and terroir, served in a minimalist, jazz-scored space with Kiyomizu-ware bowls. He also plans seasonal evolution such as cold noodles in summer.
chef_bio.specialty: らぁ麺 — a delicate clear seafood-dashi bowl. The broth is 100% fish-based, built from two kinds of kombu and Ibuki iriko (dried sardines) layered with saba, urume and katsuo bushi, with no animal stock at all. House-made straight noodles use Kyoto 'Setokirara' wheat with Inner Mongolian natural kansui and Kiribati salt, cut at #22. The chashu is Kyoto 京の都もち豚 aged about four days, sliced thin and nearly shabu-like to showcase the pork's natural sweetness, and dessert is a house-made wasanbon pudding.

anecdotes.text: Opened April 2023 and within its first year became the only newly selected ramen shop in the Michelin Guide Kyoto-Osaka 2024, earning a Bib Gourmand — recognition it has retained in the guides since.
Hidden in a residential alley near Kitano, the shop is famously hard to find even with GPS, and its stylish, izakaya-like counter with jazz feels unexpected for a ramen establishment.
The chef apprenticed at Michelin-recognized Inoichi (猪一) before going independent.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyotokurasu names owner 帯刀, his training at a Michelin shop, the April 2023 Murasakino wooden-house opening, the 100%-fish additive-free broth, and 京の都もち豚 chashu; kyotopi 0yOVx confirms the hidden Kitano alley, jazz counter, the two-kombu/Ibuki-iriko/saba-urume-katsuo broth, the Setokirara-wheat / Inner-Mongolian-kansui / Kiribati-salt / #22 noodles, and the 4-day-aged pork; the yahoo expert article confirms the shop as the only newly selected ramen pick in the Michelin Guide Kyoto-Osaka 2024 with a Bib Gourmand.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single small 10-seat counter kitchen built around wheat ramen noodles; no separate gluten-free preparation is advertised, so cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tare/seasoning composition is not published; standard ramen tare typically contains wheat-based soy sauce, so assume wheat unless the shop confirms otherwise.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Although the dashi itself is animal-free (kombu, iriko and fish flakes), it is fish-based and the bowl is topped with pork chashu; no plant-based bowl is offered, so the kitchen is not set up for vegan service.

positives.text: Cooking is explicitly 無化調 — no chemical seasonings, yeast extract or preservatives — which some additive-sensitive diners value, though this does not make it gluten-free or vegan.

The broth is unusually a 100% seafood dashi (no pork or chicken stock), which is relevant for diners avoiding meat/poultry stock specifically — but it still contains fish and the bowl includes pork chashu.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 10-seat counter shop run quietly by its owner-chef in a residential alley; basic Japanese helps and a calm, attentive manner is appreciated in such an intimate space.

kyr_ramen_yume.gf_detail: No gluten-free option. This is a Jiro-style ramen shop built around house-made wheat noodles (the owner invested in a professional noodle machine specifically to make her own wheat noodles), with a typical wheat-soy-sauce tare and pork-based broth. Not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_ramen_yume.vegan_detail: Not a vegan venue. Jiro-style ramen is built on a pork broth with pork (buta) toppings; the signature bowls feature large pork slices. No vegan ramen offering was found.

chef_bio.background: The owner spent years as a hospital nurse, earning her nursing credentials while raising her family and returning to study around age 38 after her children grew more independent. Working grueling night shifts, she found that a bowl of ramen eaten after coming off a night shift restored both her stamina and her spirit. That comfort became a calling: at 53 she set out to open her own shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: She refused to cut corners with wholesale noodles, investing in a professional noodle machine (from Daikoku Manufacturing, around 2.7 million yen) so she could make her own noodles in-house, because she wants customers to taste the difference of truly handmade noodles. Sitting near the universities, she also wants to send students and young people off well-fed and happy, an extension of her caretaking instincts from nursing into feeding her community.
chef_bio.specialty: Jiro-style ramen with generous pork and vegetable toppings; the signature is the 小豚ラーメン (kobuta / small-pork ramen). Bowls are customized at order time by noodle quantity and the classic Jiro toppings of garlic, extra vegetables, and oil.

anecdotes.text: The shop name 夢 (yume, dream) carries a double meaning: it is both her dream of running her own ramen shop and the name of her beloved pet dog.
Her path to ramen began on the mornings after night shifts, when a restorative bowl of ramen moved her so deeply that it eventually inspired a mid-life career change at 53.
She crowdfunded her dream of serving house-made (自家製麺) noodles, buying her own noodle machine rather than relying on store-bought noodles.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Campfire crowdfunding page confirms owner Noriko Fujita (藤田典子), age 53, a former hospital nurse who returned to study at ~38, was restored by ramen after night shifts, invested ~2.7 million yen in a Daikoku noodle machine for house-made noodles, named the shop 夢 after both her dream and her dog, and located near Kyoto's universities to feed students well.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Built entirely around house-made wheat ramen noodles; flour is handled and cooked on-site, so cross-contact with wheat is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Jiro-style tare is soy-sauce based; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Articles describe a soy/salt-balanced broth.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork broth and pork toppings are central to the bowls; no vegan or vegetarian preparation found.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run counter shop with ordering by ticket machine and no English presence; basic Japanese and familiarity with Jiro-style ordering (noodle quantity and the "yasai/ninniku/abura" toppings call) will make the visit smoother.

kyr_shirakawa.gf_detail: This is a classic Kyoto back-fat shoyu ramen shop. The bowl is built on wheat ramen noodles with a soy-sauce tare (Japanese soy sauce almost always contains wheat) over a pork-and-chicken back-fat broth, so the signature dish is not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu, gluten-free noodles, or dedicated handling has been documented, and a shared broth/noodle-boiling workflow makes cross-contact likely. Not suitable for celiac diners; if avoiding gluten you should not rely on this shop.
kyr_shirakawa.vegan_detail: The core product is a meat-based bowl: a pork/chicken-bone broth finished with back fat (背脂チャッチャ系) and topped with chashu and green onion. There is no documented vegan or vegetarian ramen, and the broth itself is animal-based, so there is effectively nothing for a strict vegan here. A vegan diner should plan to eat elsewhere.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Sakyo-ku, Jodoji), in the Masutani back-fat shoyu ramen tradition
chef_bio.background: Shirakawa is a small independent Kyoto-style ramen shop tucked into the Jodoji neighborhood west of Ginkaku-ji, within the Ginkakuji-michi / Kitashirakawa stretch of Sakyo-ku famous as the heartland of Kyoto back-fat shoyu ramen. The owner trained in the renowned Masutani (ますたに) lineage — the Kitashirakawa house generally credited as the origin of Kyoto's back-fat, soy-sauce-and-pork-bone style — before going out on his own to run this counter.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithful to old-school Kyoto ramen: an unpretentious, affordable everyday bowl served in a homey, diner-like room. A telling detail noted by writers is that vinegar is set out on the counter even though gyoza is not on the menu — a sign the owner understands that a splash of vinegar rounds out and lightens this rich Kyoto broth, a small nod to genuine Kyoto-ramen know-how.
chef_bio.specialty: A Kyoto-style back-fat shoyu ramen (背脂チャッチャ系): a pork-and-chicken-bone broth blanketed with melted back fat, soy-sauce tare, wheat noodles, chashu and green onion. Compared with Masutani, regulars describe Shirakawa's bowl as having lighter back fat and a slightly stronger, saltier soy edge — a recognizably personal take on the house style.

anecdotes.text: Diners come specifically because they have heard it is run by someone who trained at Masutani: a reviewer opens with 『ますたに』で修行した人がやってるラーメン屋さんと聞いて ("I heard this is a ramen shop run by someone who trained at Masutani").

Writers point to the counter vinegar as proof of the owner's Kyoto-ramen sensibility: 餃子がメニューにないのに、お酢を置いているということは、店主がちゃんと京都ラーメンにお酢が合うことをわかっている証拠 (the fact that vinegar is offered despite no gyoza on the menu shows the owner knows vinegar suits Kyoto ramen).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: retty confirms the shop is run by someone who trained at Masutani and that its back-fat shoyu bowl runs lighter on fat but saltier than the reviewer expected; kyoto-gourmet places it in Jodoji near Ginkaku-ji, describes the pork-and-chicken back-fat shoyu broth, and highlights the counter vinegar despite no gyoza as evidence of the owner's Kyoto-ramen know-how.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A back-fat shoyu ramen shop with a single shared workflow (one pot of wheat noodles, shared utensils, soy-based tare); cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable for a gluten-sensitive diner.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is a soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen; Japanese soy sauce used for ramen tare almost always contains wheat, and no wheat-free tare is documented here.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth itself is animal-based (pork/chicken bone with back fat), so even non-meat menu items would share an animal-stock kitchen; no vegan-safe preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, old-school neighborhood Kyoto ramen counter run by a local owner; English is unlikely, so a little Japanese or pointing at the menu will help, but it is a casual and welcoming spot.
